engines.label: Engines
engines.description: A voice that makes the sound: oscillators, filters, folders, physical models. Its screen shows the mechanism or the signal path, reshaped by each control.

effects.label: Effects
effects.description: Processes another track's audio: delay, reverb, distortion, filter, dynamics. Its screen shows what happens to the signal on the way through.

players.label: Players
players.description: Generates notes for another engine. Its screen shows the rule that picks the notes, drawn as something with the same shape.

machines.name: Beacon
machines.description: A pulse train through a comb 'lens' that focuses it into a pitch, swept by a rotating light, softened by fog.
machines.concept: A pulse train through a comb 'lens' that focuses it into a pitch, swept by a rotating light, softened by fog.
machines.soundsLike: A clicking pulse train that rings into a clear, glassy pitch as the comb's feedback rises, from a buzzy reed to a bowed-glass tone. The rotating light makes the pitch lean and return like a slow Leslie, and fog darkens and smears it toward a breathy, distant horn.

intake.subject: a pulse train focused by a comb "lens" into a pitch, with a rotating light sweeping the focus and fog softening it; the screen draws that focusing (which object carries it is the subject pass's question, `passes/01-subject/`).
intake.controlSource: new (the "source" is the DSP sketched below; no port)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings. No warnings to justify.

the whole identity of the sound: unpitched clicks at 0, a ringing, sharply pitched tone at 100
0 is static; the pitch lean grows to a wide, seasick swing at 12 st; subtle below ~2 st
dark and smeared at 100, a big tonal change, but the pitch survives

cells.subject: The output itself, traced bright along a chained survey baseline: each input pulse below the chain rings into a run of teeth one comb period apart, surveyed from a station whose bearing ray is the rotating light.
controls: pulse: the grey input pulse train under the chain line widens its pulses, and the bright teeth above widen with them (shape of the input path; the output tooth width follows as a second cue).
lens: the number and height of teeth each pulse rings into (shape of the bright output trace): one lone spike per pulse at 0, a long even run that fills the gap to the next pulse at 100.
sweep: the bearing ray from station a swings up from the chain line, with its angle arc (rotation, 8 to 48 degrees), and the tooth spacing breathes along the chainage as a second cue.
fog: grey survey contours roll in over the plan from the right edge, one more line every ~15 % (count), and the teeth tips flatten as the trace is low-passed.
risks: P3's own pitfall: at a glance it reads as an oscilloscope; the survey furniture (chain, chainage figures, station, offsets) is what makes it a plan and it has to stay.
Two controls (pulse, lens) both touch the bright trace; the rule holds only because pulse's primary is the grey input path. Perceptibility must prove it.
Fog by contour count is empty at the default 0, so the rest frame never shows fog; a contour lines' layer fighting the trace at 100 is untested.
Teeth 18 px apart at lens 100 approach hatching density; keep the comb period on screen ≥ 12 px whatever the note.
cells.alt: Beacon, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The output itself, traced bright along a chained survey baseline: each input pulse below the chain rings into a run of teeth one comb period apart, surveyed from a station whose bearing ray is the rotating light

cells.subject: The comb lens as a stack of sawtooth Fresnel plates receding behind a lamp housing in section, one plate per trip the sound survives round the comb, drawn as a numbered patent figure.
controls: pulse: the tooth profile of the front plate, from sharp sawtooth to blunt flat-topped teeth (shape, on the current layer only).
lens: how many plates stand in the stack, 1 at 0 to 6 at 100, each further one a grey step darker (count).
sweep: the shutter blade on the lamp housing turns about the lamp's axis, its swing drawn as a hairline arc (rotation, -60 to 180 degrees).
fog: the plates drift apart along the recession, the stack loosening from tight to spread (position, 1 to 1.8 times the spacing).
risks: The stack of offset sawtooth plates reads as stairs or a book edge at 1:1; the Fresnel idea needs the axis and the lamp to be legible.
Lamp and plates sit apart, so the brightest element (front plate) is not where the sound starts; the eye splits between two objects.
Lamp plus lens plus light is close to the stock prism engine's idea (a beam through optics); must never draw a beam or rays to stay clear of it.
Section hatching at 6 px pitch on the front plate is near the 3 px floor once scaled; keep it static.
cells.alt: Beacon, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The comb lens as a stack of sawtooth Fresnel plates receding behind a lamp housing in section, one plate per trip the sound survives round the comb, drawn as a numbered patent figure

cells.subject: A hidden-line lens barrel ringed like a comb standing on an isometric sea grid, its lit window and the patch of light it throws on the water turning with the sweep, with the pulse train ticking along the bottom strip.
controls: pulse: the marks in the bottom strip widen, 4 px to 22 px, as each pulse gets wider (shape and size of the strip marks).
lens: the barrel gains evenly spaced rings, 3 at 0 to 12 at 100, the comb's teeth tightening (count on the figure).
sweep: the lit window travels round the barrel's near face and the hidden-line patch on the sea swings with it (position round the barrel; the patch's bearing as the second cue).
fog: a fog bank, a hidden-line wall with black fill, advances across the sea grid toward the barrel and swallows the far grid lines (position).
risks: A ringed cylinder on a grid is close to a generic 3D primitive; it says lighthouse more than comb filter, and the lens/pitch link depends on the rings.
Lens by ring count at 12 rings over 80 px is a 6.7 px pitch: legal but near hatching; the top end may smear.
The lit window and the sea patch move together on rotation-faked-by-position; at the barrel's edge the window hugs the silhouette and nearly vanishes.
Fog wall is not drawn at the default 0; whether it reads as fog or as a building needs a frame at 100.
cells.alt: Beacon, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A hidden-line lens barrel ringed like a comb standing on an isometric sea grid, its lit window and the patch of light it throws on the water turning with the sweep, with the pulse train ticking along the bottom strip

cells.subject: The voice's spectrum charted as a star field on a conic atlas: columns are harmonics, rows are successive trips round the comb, and each star's magnitude comes from the same model as the sound, with the fundamental as the brightest star.
controls: pulse: the field's magnitudes along the harmonic axis follow the pulse's spectrum, so a dark lane of faint stars walks in from the right toward the fundamental as pulses widen (shape of the field, size).
lens: how far down the chart the stars stay bright, from only the top row at 0 to all four rows near equal at 100 (shape of the field, size by row).
sweep: the beam's great-circle track swings about the fundamental star across the chart (rotation, -10 to -50 degrees), lighting the stars it passes.
fog: a nebula boundary drawn as a hairline contour moves in from the high harmonics, and stars inside it drop to hollow wire (position of the boundary, look swap as second cue).
risks: A grid of dots risks reading as a dot-matrix meter or a dashboard rather than an atlas; the conic graticule, labels and the constellation line carry the language.
Pulse and lens both act on star size; it works the P10 way (two operations on one field along different axes) but needs perceptibility to separate them.
48 stars as nodes is cheap, but a sweep that relights stars as it turns can exceed ~20 changed nodes per frame while turning.
Rotating light becomes a line on a chart, the most abstract of the five readings of 'beacon'.
cells.alt: Beacon, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The voice's spectrum charted as a star field on a conic atlas: columns are harmonics, rows are successive trips round the comb, and each star's magnitude comes from the same model as the sound, with the fundamental as the brightest star

cells.subject: An engineering schematic of the comb loop (sum, delay, gain, fog low-pass) whose delay line is woven out below it as cloth: warp threads are the delay taps, and each trip round the loop weaves a fainter row behind the last.
controls: pulse: how many adjacent warp threads carry a raised slab in each row, 1 to 9 (count across the warp).
lens: slab heights fall row by row by the feedback, so at 0 only the front row stands and at 100 four rows stand nearly level (position: slab tops).
sweep: the rows shear sideways against the warp as the light swings the comb's tuning, 0 to 12 px per row (position: row offset).
fog: the raised slabs smear onto their neighbours row by row, the back rows widening and flattening (shape of each row's slab run).
risks: Stretch, and a weak one: P14 is for history over musical time, and the comb's trips last milliseconds, so the cloth shows a physics diagram, not something the player has done. The best case for the exception is that P14 already names an echo field (repeats as rows behind a pulse), and a comb is exactly that.
Schematic plus cloth is two pictures, and the schematic half is a dashboard of blocks with labels that no control moves.
Lens and sweep are both position channels (different parts: slab tops vs row offsets); sweep's shear is small at its default.
Slabs cost three nodes each; 12 threads x 4 rows with flat tiles is ~70 nodes before anything moves.
cells.alt: Beacon, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: An engineering schematic of the comb loop (sum, delay, gain, fog low-pass) whose delay line is woven out below it as cloth: warp threads are the delay taps, and each trip round the loop weaves a fainter row behind the last

cells.subject: The lighthouse's beehive drum lens filling the screen, its dome and pedestal past the frame's edges, the prism rings catching the lamp only round the panel that is flashing while the rest of the glass stays dark, with the flame's image bright in the belt.
controls: pulse: the flame's image in the belt widens from a slit to a broad lens shape, 4 px to 19 px wide (scale of the one bright mass).
lens: the prism rings above and below the belt step in count, 3 to 11 per zone, so the saw-tooth silhouette tightens as the lens focuses (count, with the outline's shape following).

sweep: the drum turns, carrying the lit panel, its brass bars and the flame off the axis toward the right silhouette, 0 to 80 degrees round the drum (rotation, faked by redrawing the bars' positions; the lit arcs slide about 120 px).
fog: diagonal hatching rises from the bottom edge over the glass, clipped to the frame, up to about three quarters of the body (position of the hatched region's top edge; nothing at the default 0).
risks: Cropped this close, a beehive lens can read as a barrel or a lampshade to someone who hasn't seen one; the saw-tooth silhouette is what says lens.
Sweep is a redraw of every bar and lit arc (a 3D turn faked in the plane): heavy on nodes and redraw; the lit run would need to be a few pre-drawn nodes per ring.
At sweep 100 the lit panel reaches the silhouette and the flame is foreshortened to a sliver, so the brightest element nearly disappears; the range may need capping near 60 degrees.
Lens at 0 leaves three rings per zone and a mostly empty drum; fine as 'unfocused', but the top end at 11 rings per zone is about 5 px apart, near the hatching floor.

cells.alt: Beacon, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: The lighthouse's beehive drum lens filling the screen, its dome and pedestal past the frame's edges, the prism rings catching the lamp only round the panel that is flashing while the rest of the glass stays dark, with the flame's image bright in the belt

cells.subject: A stone lighthouse standing on its stepped base at the horizon, drawn as detailed line art from one low camera, coursed masonry, door, windows, corbelled gallery, railing, helical glazing and domed lantern, throwing a hatched beam out to sea.
controls: pulse: the lamp inside the lantern widens behind the glazing bars, 3 px to 13 px (scale of the one bright mass).
lens: the beam's cone closes from a wide hatched fan (18 degrees each side) to a near-parallel shaft (2 degrees), so its far end narrows by over 100 px (shape of the beam outline).
sweep: the beam turns toward the viewer about the lantern, 0 to 55 degrees, so in perspective it rises and shortens across the sky (rotation of the beam node about the lamp).
fog: a hatched bank rises from the sea over the base and up the tower, up to 120 px (position of the bank's top edge; nothing at the default 0).
risks: The most literal of the five: a lighthouse silhouette is close to a postcard or icon if the detail is lost; it depends on the masonry, gallery and glazing reading at 1:1.
The tower is narrow (about 60 px wide) next to a wide frame; the lantern details are 2-4 px apart, at the legibility floor.
Pulse is a small bright mass inside a small lantern; its 3-13 px travel may fall short of the perceptibility floor for a score-3 control without a second cue.
Fog over the tower hatches across masonry lines; the tower stays readable at 60 % in the sanity check but may go grey at 100.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Beacon, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: A stone lighthouse standing on its stepped base at the horizon, drawn as detailed line art from one low camera, coursed masonry, door, windows, corbelled gallery, railing, helical glazing and domed lantern, throwing a hatched beam out to sea

cells.subject: The turning gear in hidden-line 3D: a four-panel flashing lens on a float in its mercury trough, on a cast pedestal, driven by a weight clock with its great wheel, pinion, fly and cable, the lamp flashing through the panel that faces you.
controls: pulse: the flash in the facing panel's bullseye widens, 2.5 px to 10.5 px (scale of the one bright mass).
lens: the bullseye rings in each panel's belt step from 2 to 8 and the reflecting prisms above and below from 1 to 4 (count of hairlines on the glass).

sweep: the carriage turns, 18 to 90 degrees, its panels sliding round and the rack teeth travelling, while the great wheel on the clock turns three times as far (rotation: the wheel is a true in-plane turn, the lens box is redrawn variants).
fog: mist rises up the glass of each visible panel as hatching clipped to the panel, from its foot to its top (position of the hatched band's top; nothing at the default 0).
risks: Rings on a panel are concentric circles, close to the 'target rings' craft warns about; the prism bars above and below cut them to a belt so they read as a Fresnel panel, but this should be checked by eye.
Sweep turns a 3D box, which the device can't tilt: every panel position is a pre-drawn variant (many nodes), only the clock wheel is a cheap true turn.
Two objects (lens carriage and clock) split the eye; the clock is kept smaller and dimmer, but it is still a second thing.
The fly on the clock reads as a small flag at 1:1; it may need redrawing or dropping.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Beacon, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: The turning gear in hidden-line 3D: a four-panel flashing lens on a float in its mercury trough, on a cast pedestal, driven by a weight clock with its great wheel, pinion, fly and cable, the lamp flashing through the panel that faces you

cells.subject: The sea seen from the waterline at night, rows of wave crests as bold closed outlines that hide the ones behind, a glitter path of lit crest edges running toward you beneath a small lighthouse on its rock, whose hatched beam swings across the sky.
controls: pulse: each glint on the lit crests lengthens, from a short dash to a long run along the crest, 0.4 to 2.4 world units (shape of the glint ribbons).

lens: the beam tightens (16 to 2 degrees) and the glitter path reaches further toward you, from the far rows to the nearest (position of the path's near end, about 100 px of travel, with the beam's shape as the second cue).
sweep: the beam swings from lying along the horizon to coming toward you, 14 to 64 degrees, so it rises and widens over the upper left (rotation of the beam about the lantern).
fog: a hatched bank rises over the horizon and swallows the rock and the light (position of the bank's top edge; nothing at the default 0).
risks: The sea of crests is the busiest body of the five (about 80 % black): it can read as texture rather than a picture, and it competes with the small lighthouse.
The lighthouse is small (about 40 px tall); the subject is the light on the water rather than the tower.
At sweep 100 with fog up the beam's hatching and the fog's hatching cross into a crosshatch; the fog needs to sit behind the beam or stop below it.
Lens drives two things (beam width and glitter reach); acceptable as one idea, focus, but the perceptibility check must show the reach clearly.
cells.angle: the material the sound acts on, seen close
cells.alt: Beacon, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: The sea seen from the waterline at night, rows of wave crests as bold closed outlines that hide the ones behind, a glitter path of lit crest edges running toward you beneath a small lighthouse on its rock, whose hatched beam swings across the sky

cells.subject: A headland at night with the lighthouse cut open in section, thick walls, spiral stair treads, floors, the clock's weight in its shaft sunk into the rock, gallery and lantern with the lens profile round the lamp, and a beam carrying hatched bands of light out over the sea.
controls: pulse: each band of light in the beam widens as a share of its period, 3 px to 27 px of every 30 px, from thin flashes to a nearly solid beam (shape: band width).
lens: the beam's spread closes from a wide fan (8 degrees each side) to a parallel shaft, its far end narrowing by about 90 px (shape of the beam outline).
sweep: the beam turns away across the sea and foreshortens, its tip drawing in from the right edge to about 110 px from the lantern (position of the tip).
fog: a hatched bank rises off the sea up the headland and across the lower beam, up to 130 px (position of the bank's top; nothing at the default 0).
risks: The tower is small in a wide scene (about 60 px wide, 130 px tall) and its section detail (treads, floors, lens profile) sits at 3-6 px spacing; it may go busy at 1:1 on the device.
The banded beam is the most model-true picture of the pulse train, but it is also the screen's largest element, so the eye goes to the beam before the tower.
Sweep as foreshortening is a convention: a beam turning away gets shorter; the player may read it as the beam's reach rather than its turn.
Section language risks looking like a patent plate; it carries no labels or callouts, but the cut walls and shaft are technical.
cells.angle: one scene where this happens, with one subject in it
cells.alt: Beacon, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: A headland at night with the lighthouse cut open in section, thick walls, spiral stair treads, floors, the clock's weight in its shaft sunk into the rock, gallery and lantern with the lens profile round the lamp, and a beam carrying hatched bands of light out over the sea

machines.name: Bellows
machines.description: A free-reed voice blown by a bellows whose pressure sags and recovers; leaks add breath, a second reed beats against the first.
machines.concept: A free-reed voice blown by a bellows whose pressure sags and recovers; leaks add breath, a second reed beats against the first.
machines.soundsLike: A harmonium or accordion reed: a buzzy, pulse-like tone whose level and brightness follow the wind pressure, sagging a little through a long note and recovering. Leaks add an airy breath under it; a second reed a few cents off makes it beat like a musette.

intake.subject: a free reed blown from a bellows, where the wind (its pressure, sag and leaks) and the reeds it sounds (one, or two beating) are the object every control acts on.
intake.controlSource: new (source is the DSP to be written)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings. `resources.display` is a placeholder until phase 4.

scores.effect: silence-to-full wind: level and brightness both rise, and the held-note sag deepens; the biggest change on the page
sine-like to hard buzzing pulse; a strong timbre sweep at every press
breath noise grows under the tone and the note sags more; clear above ~30, subtle below
single reed to a slow beat (by 20) to a fast musette shimmer (at 100); unmistakable once past ~10

ranking.note: the mechanism itself, every control a part; fix the graticule weight and give the reed more of the frame.
the strongest single image of the wind sagging and recovering; needs the elevation language pushed so it isn't a scope.
the most explanatory, but split in two.
a true metaphor for choir only.
reads as a meter; wrong pattern for a machine with a mechanism.

pick.reason: Pick 1 is nice; add it.

cells.name: rest
cells.alt: Bellows at rest

cells.subject: The reed's wave drawn in elevation like a facade standing on a datum, its roofline held up by the wind line of the bellows, which sags mid-stroke and recovers.
controls: press: the wind line rises from 30 to 100 px over the datum and the whole wave stands taller under it, the dimension at the right following; scale and position of the wind line.
reed: the wave's profile goes from rounded arches to tall narrow piers as upper partials come in; shape of the bright trace.
leak: a rough band of breath grows along the datum under the wave, 0 to 14 px tall; shape of a second path (the noise band).
choir: a grey second wave behind the first slides out of phase and its piers drift against the bright ones into 0 to 4 beat groups across the width; shape and position of the ghost path.
cells.risks: P3's own warning: it can drift into 'oscilloscope', and an elevation only differs by its ground line, datum ticks and level mark. Three of four controls are shape on paths (trace, breath band, ghost), which is the four-path budget nearly used, and a held note can't re-key them each frame: note response must be node scale on the trace. Rectifying the wave above the datum is a drawing choice, not what the sound does; the shape is truthful, the baseline is not.
cells.cleanNote: Generated by `clean.py` (helpers from `../sketch.py`, unchanged) → `clean.svg`, `clean.png`. Lint: 0 errors, 0 warnings. The owner's pick, copied to `screens/bellows/frames/rest.svg` and `rest.png`.
cells.alt: Bellows, cleaned variant 4: The reed's wave drawn in elevation like a facade standing on a datum, its roofline held up by the wind line of the bellows, which sags mid-stroke and recovers

cells.subject: The wind chest drawn as a schematic plenum of square cells, the air under pressure a lit mass rising from its floor, with the two reed ports on its lid.
controls: press: how high the lit air stands in the plenum (count of lit rows, 1.5 to 6 of 6), the dimension line beside it following; position plus count.
reed: the surface of the lit mass, from long flat runs (stiff, closed reed) to short choppy steps (open, bright reed), and the two port tongues lift; shape of the run length.
leak: the seam on the right wall opens and grey cells bleed out of the mass through it and up the wall, 0 to about 14 cells; count in the grey layer.
choir: vertical beat bands sweep the mass, lit columns dimming to grey in 0 to 4 bands as reed b detunes from reed a; count of bands (pattern across columns), shade as second cue.
cells.risks: Gate 0 fights it: P15 is for sounds that are texture, and bellows has a mechanism (it's air, but air in a box with reeds). The cells read as a level meter if press is the only thing that moves, which is a dashboard; choir as bands and leak as grey cells are both 'how much grey', so one of them must ride run length or position, as P15 warns. Hollow schematic squares plus solid cells is two looks on one grid; at 1:1 the hollow ones could read as a hatch. 96 cells is cheap on nodes but a press turn redraws a whole row of 16 at once.
cells.alt: Bellows, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The wind chest drawn as a schematic plenum of square cells, the air under pressure a lit mass rising from its floor, with the two reed ports on its lid

cells.subject: The bellows and its reed block cut open and plotted on a scope graticule, the pleats a triangle trace that closes as pressure rises and the reed tongue a bright stroke lifted over its slot.
controls: press: the moving board slides left and the pleats close up, the bellows shortening from 250 to 140 px; position of the board, shape of the pleat traces.
reed: the bright tongue over plate a swings open from 6 to 32 px at its tip; rotation about its rivet.
leak: a dotted breath trace streams out between the lower pleats, 0 to about 16 dots and longer as it rises; count.
choir: the second tongue on plate b lifts out of unison and its rivet slides along the plate, 0 to 30 px; position, with a ghost beat-trace across ch2 while playing.
cells.risks: Two languages pulling: a section drawing wants solid cut faces and hatching, a scope wants one phosphor line on a graticule. The graticule is 11 x 5 hairlines across the body and could read as a dashboard grid behind the drawing; it may need to drop to corner ticks. The pleats are the brightest thing, not the reed that sings; at 1:1 the tongue is a 2 px stroke 90 px long, which is right but small. Press both moves a board and reshapes two traces, so its key changes on every press turn (two paths re-keyed).
cells.alt: Bellows, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The bellows and its reed block cut open and plotted on a scope graticule, the pleats a triangle trace that closes as pressure rises and the reed tongue a bright stroke lifted over its slot

cells.subject: A two-figure textbook plate: on the left a weighted wedge reservoir feeding reeds a and b through a wind trunk, on the right the output wave under its envelope, sagging mid-stroke and recovering.
controls: press: the weight on the wedge's top board drops and the board closes from 26 to 8 degrees, while the trace on the right grows in height; rotation of the board (left), the trace's scale as second cue.
reed: the wave on the right goes from nearly a sine to a sharp pulse with its upper partials; shape of the trace, the two tongues lifting as a small echo on the left.
leak: breath leaves the wedge's open mouth as a short column of dots (0 to 12) and the envelope line goes rough; count on the left.
choir: the envelope over the trace pinches into beats, 0 to 4 waists across fig. 2; shape of the envelope line, separate from the trace.
cells.risks: P2 splits the body, so the screen is two smaller pictures rather than one subject; the eye may not know which to read first. Press moves both the board and the trace height, which risks two parts on one control looking like two controls. The figure captions (fig. 1, fig. 2) are honest to a typeset plate but are two extra labels; at 10 px #7D7D7D they're legible but busy. A 200 px trace with five cycles is fine at 64 points; more cycles at higher pitch would not be.
cells.alt: Bellows, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A two-figure textbook plate: on the left a weighted wedge reservoir feeding reeds a and b through a wind trunk, on the right the output wave under its envelope, sagging mid-stroke and recovering

cells.subject: The reed's wave drawn in elevation like a facade standing on a datum, its roofline held up by the wind line of the bellows, which sags mid-stroke and recovers.
controls: press: the wind line rises from 30 to 100 px over the datum and the whole wave stands taller under it, the dimension at the right following; scale and position of the wind line.
reed: the wave's profile goes from rounded arches to tall narrow piers as upper partials come in; shape of the bright trace.
leak: a rough band of breath grows along the datum under the wave, 0 to 14 px tall; shape of a second path (the noise band).
choir: a grey second wave behind the first slides out of phase and its piers drift against the bright ones into 0 to 4 beat groups across the width; shape and position of the ghost path.
cells.risks: P3's own warning: it can drift into 'oscilloscope', and an elevation only differs by its ground line, datum ticks and level mark. Three of four controls are shape on paths (trace, breath band, ghost), which is the four-path budget nearly used, and a held note can't re-key them each frame: note response must be node scale on the trace. Rectifying the wave above the datum is a drawing choice, not what the sound does; the shape is truthful, the baseline is not.
cells.alt: Bellows, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The reed's wave drawn in elevation like a facade standing on a datum, its roofline held up by the wind line of the bellows, which sags mid-stroke and recovers

cells.subject: A survey plan of the reed's cycle: one surveyed ring round the wind chest, with reeds a and b as two stations on it whose angle apart is the beat.
controls: press: the ring's radius grows from 52 to 92 px (and with it the stations' distance from the chest); scale.
reed: the chainage ticks round the ring go from 12 to 36; count.
leak: the ring breaks into a dashed run on its lower side, 0 to 10 gaps, with short bearing lines escaping through them; count.

choir: station b leaves station a and travels round the ring, 0 to 150 degrees apart; rotation. While a note is held the two stations orbit at their two rates, so the gap opens and closes at the beat rate.
cells.risks: Stretch, and only half earns it. The exception: choir is two reeds a few cents apart, and two bodies on one orbit at slightly different rates is literally what beating is, so the orbit is true for choir and, held, shows the beat at the beat rate. It doesn't fit the rest: press as ring radius, reed as tick count and leak as gaps are scenery bolted to the orrery, the failure P13 warns about (Dens and Crpt fit, Scal and Kit didn't). There's no cycle of items here, just two. A plan is flat by definition, so craft.md's 'think in 3D' doesn't apply, but it also loses the orrery's depth. Constant orbital motion while notes are held is a big redraw cost only if the ring itself moves; it doesn't.
cells.alt: Bellows, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: A survey plan of the reed's cycle: one surveyed ring round the wind chest, with reeds a and b as two stations on it whose angle apart is the beat

machines.name: Drill
machines.description: Phase distortion driven by a gear train: the read phase turns with a toothed wheel at a set ratio, stepped by its teeth, rounded by wear, pushed in by bite.
machines.concept: Phase distortion driven by a gear train: the read phase is bent by a toothed wheel whose ratio and wear shape the timbre.
machines.soundsLike: A sine at bite 0 that grows a stepped, buzzy edge as bite rises, its formant-like peak sweeping with ratio the way a CZ resonance sweep does. Few sharp teeth give a coarse, gritty grind; many teeth or heavy wear smooth it back toward a rounder, darker tone.

cells.subject: The toothed wheel itself, drawn as a labelled textbook figure: a big driver rim turning it from the left, a follower lever whose tip rides in its teeth on the right.
controls: ratio: the driver's rim changes size against the fixed wheel (its pitch radius is ratio x the wheel's), sliding its centre and hub off left as the ratio climbs; scale and position of the driver.
teeth: the wheel's outline gains teeth, 3 chunky lugs at 0 to 24 fine ones at 100; shape of the wheel (one mutable outline).
wear: the follower's tip blunts from a sharp point to a round worn nub, its point pulling back about 16 px of outline; shape of the follower tip (a mutable outline).
bite: the follower swings in about its pivot, its tip going from clear of the tips to deep in the roots; rotation of the follower (about 30 deg).
cells.risks: Wear wants to live on the wheel's teeth (that's where it acts in the DSP), but teeth already owns the wheel's shape, so wear is pushed onto the follower; a player may read a blunt stylus as a different control from 'the teeth wore'. The driver at ratio 8 is a near-straight rack off screen left and at 0.5 is smaller than the wheel: both ends need the arc clipped and checked at 1:1. Typeset labels a/b/c are decoration unless a caption line says what they are.
cells.alt: Drill, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The toothed wheel itself, drawn as a labelled textbook figure: a big driver rim turning it from the left, a follower lever whose tip rides in its teeth on the right

cells.subject: Gear pair in front elevation on the left, with centre lines, pitch circle and datum, and the bent output wave it produces on the right, structure under encoders 1-2 and tone under 3-4.
controls: ratio: the driver's rim grows against the wheel and its centre walks off left (position + scale of the driver); on the right the wave carries more humps per cycle as a side effect.
teeth: the wheel's tooth count steps 3 to 24 (shape of the wheel outline), and the tick row under the trace counts teeth passed per cycle (count, ratio x teeth).
wear: the trace's step corners round off and its kinks soften into a smooth bend; shape of the trace, the corners are where some point moves 16 px or more.
bite: the trace bends from a plain windowed sine at 0 into a hard staircase at 100; shape of the trace's amplitude between the steps.
cells.risks: Wear and bite both act on the one trace path (shape on the same part), which the channel rule forbids; at subject stage the fix is to give wear a structural mark on the left too (tooth tips rounding on the wheel) and keep bite on the trace, but then teeth and wear share the wheel. Grey elevation on the left can read as a dashboard of two panels if the trace isn't clearly the brightest thing. The driver rim's teeth are only seen as an arc, which reads as a bracket at ratio near 1.
cells.alt: Drill, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: Gear pair in front elevation on the left, with centre lines, pitch circle and datum, and the bent output wave it produces on the right, structure under encoders 1-2 and tone under 3-4

cells.subject: The output wave drawn as a proposed road alignment on a survey plan, bent off the dashed existing alignment (the plain sine) by the wheel, with one station tick per tooth and chainage along the baseline.
controls: ratio: the chainage marks (one per wheel revolution) spread or bunch along the baseline, 0.5 to 8 turns per cycle; position of the chainage ticks and labels, the alignment's hump count follows.
teeth: the station ticks along the alignment multiply from a few to many (ratio x teeth per cycle); count of stations.
wear: the alignment's step corners round off into easy curves; shape of the bright alignment at its kinks.
bite: the proposed alignment departs further from the dashed existing one, from on top of it at 0 to a hard staircase at 100; shape (offset) of the alignment against the dashed line.
cells.risks: It risks the 'oscilloscope' pitfall P3 names: survey dressing (grid crosses, chainage) on a waveform. Wear and bite both reshape the one alignment path; they differ in where (corners vs overall offset) but the channel rule wants them apart, so one may need the dashed existing line or the verges. At 24 teeth and ratio 8 the station count is 192 per cycle, so stations must cap or thin out, and they cost nodes. No gear is drawn at all; the mechanism only shows through the steps.
cells.alt: Drill, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: The output wave drawn as a proposed road alignment on a survey plan, bent off the dashed existing alignment (the plain sine) by the wheel, with one station tick per tooth and chainage along the baseline

cells.subject: The wheel's rim unrolled into a toothed rack, one sectioned strip per turn stacked receding up and right like a patent figure, with a pawl biting into the front strip.
controls: ratio: the back strips stagger sideways against the front one by the fractional part of the ratio, lined up at whole ratios and offset by up to a tooth between them; position of the four back strips.
teeth: the front strip's teeth go from 3 broad lugs to 24 fine ones across its length; shape of the front strip outline.
wear: the front strip's tooth tips round and wear down unevenly from strip to strip toward the back (older turns are more worn); shape of the back strips, palette swap from crisp to worn variants.
bite: the pawl drops from resting on the tips to the bottom of the roots; position of the pawl tip (about 16 px plus the lever's swing).
cells.risks: Strips 22 px apart with 6 to 24 teeth each turn into hatching at high tooth counts; the back strips need to fade or drop teeth above 12. Ratio's stagger is zero at every whole ratio, including the default 2.00, so at rest the stack looks static and regular, and the stagger wraps (2.9 looks like 1.9), which under-tells the loudest control. Wear on the back strips puts the effect where the eye isn't.
cells.alt: Drill, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The wheel's rim unrolled into a toothed rack, one sectioned strip per turn stacked receding up and right like a patent figure, with a pawl biting into the front strip

cells.subject: The gear train built as an epicyclic orrery in isometric: a sun driver on its arbor, a carrier arm, and one bright planet wheel rolling inside a toothed ring.
controls: ratio: the planet wheel shrinks as the ratio rises (ring/planet = ratio + 1), from nearly filling the ring at 0.5 to a small fast wheel at 8; scale of the planet.
teeth: the ring's internal teeth step from coarse to fine (twice the wheel's count); shape of the ring outline.
wear: the planet's teeth round off and shorten; shape of the planet outline.
bite: the planet slides outward on its arm into the ring's teeth, from just touching to fully meshed; position of the planet along the carrier (about 24 px in iso).
cells.risks: Stretch, and mostly it doesn't fit: P12 earns its keep from a population of items in a cycle (planets as steps, links along orbits) and drill has one continuous phase and one wheel, so nothing here uses what the orrery is good at. The one honest exception is that an orrery is literally a gear train, and planetary gearing is a real way to get a ratio, so the picture is mechanically true. On a note it would want to orbit, which is constant field-wide motion for one voice. Ring teeth at 24 x 2 = 48 teeth blow the 64-point outline unless thinned.
cells.alt: Drill, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: The gear train built as an epicyclic orrery in isometric: a sun driver on its arbor, a carrier arm, and one bright planet wheel rolling inside a toothed ring

cells.subject: The shaving the bit throws: one long helical curl of wood rising out of the bored hole in a plank, its outer face the one bright line.
controls: ratio: the curl winds tighter, 3 loose coils at 0.50 to 12 at 8.00 along the same length (shape of the shaving, one mutable outline per edge).
teeth: chatter marks pressed across the strip, one per tooth on every coil, 3 to 24 per coil (count of short cross-strokes).
wear: the shaving's leading edge goes from a clean cut to torn and ragged, up to about 4 px either side (shape of that edge).
bite: the shaving thickens, a 4 px ribbon at 0 to 22 px at 100, as the bit takes a deeper cut (shape, the strip's width).
cells.risks: Every control is a shape of the same strip, so four shape channels share one subject; on the device ratio and bite both rewrite the helix and need separate keys. At 24 chatter marks per coil and 12 coils the marks fall under 3 px apart on the back runs; draw them on front runs only. The plank is cropped by the frame's left and bottom edges and could read as a ramp; the single weight leaves the hole and the curl at the same line width, so brightness alone separates subject from ground (bright vs mid grey, 5 steps, fine at 1:1). Many tiny ribbon pieces near the hole lint as legibility warnings; merge runs in the real build.
cells.angle: the mark or trace the process leaves behind
cells.alt: Drill, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: The shaving the bit throws: one long helical curl of wood rising out of the bored hole in a plank, its outer face the one bright line

cells.subject: The eggbeater drill's face wheel seen huge and cropped: its hatched cast web and rim of lugs fill the left, the bright pinion sits on the lugs, and the spindle runs off the right edge into a chuck.
controls: ratio: the wheel grows against the pinion, its radius 150 to 300 px, so the rim's arc flattens from a tight curve to nearly straight while its right-most point stays put (shape of the rim and web outline).
teeth: lugs round the rim, 18 to 144 on the whole wheel, about 3 to 20 in view (count).
wear: each lug's corners round off, a crisp block at 0 to a worn lozenge at 100 (shape of the lug outlines).
bite: the pinion slides along the spindle from clear of the rim onto the lug ring, about 40 px of travel (position of the pinion node).
cells.risks: Hatching here is the drawing language for the cast web's mass, not a state; craft.md reserves hatching for semi-opaque or inactive regions, so the owner should say whether a hatched solid reads as 'there but not active'. Ratio reshapes the rim, web edge and every lug at once (one path plus many nodes repositioned): expensive on change. The visible lug count at teeth 3 is under three, and the frame's 20 % hatched area is the densest of the five (82 % black).
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Drill, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: The eggbeater drill's face wheel seen huge and cropped: its hatched cast web and rim of lugs fill the left, the bright pinion sits on the lugs, and the spindle runs off the right edge into a chuck

cells.subject: A carpenter's brace lying level across the screen, head pad, swept crank, grip, ratchet and chuck as black silhouettes lit along their top edges, its auger bit sunk into a board shown in section.
controls: ratio: the brace's sweep deepens, the crank's throw 32 to 72 px (position of the grip and the two bends).
teeth: flute grooves along the auger's twist, 3 to 24 over its cutting length (count of hairline grooves).
wear: the screw point and spurs blunt from a sharp lead into a stub, the point pulling back about 8 px (shape of the bit's tip).
bite: the board slides onto the bit, sinking it 14 to 84 px into the wood (position of the board node, the bore follows).
cells.risks: A long thin object makes the body mostly empty: calm, but the brace is small (rod 7 px) and the lit edges carry everything. The lit edge is one bright element made of several ribbons; light direction must stay fixed as parts move or the rim light jumps. Teeth grooves at 24 are about 4.5 px apart, close to the 3 px floor. Ratio moving the crank changes the rod's outline (two bends), so it's a shape change on device rather than a single translation.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Drill, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: A carpenter's brace lying level across the screen, head pad, swept crank, grip, ratchet and chuck as black silhouettes lit along their top edges, its auger bit sunk into a board shown in section

cells.subject: The eggbeater drill in three-quarter view as a working mechanism: crank and turned grip on the face wheel, lugs on its face driving a bright pinion on the spindle, from the wooden head handle to the chuck and bit.
controls: ratio: the pinion shrinks against the wheel, about 1.6x to 0.8x its rest size (uniform scale of the pinion node).
teeth: lugs on the wheel's face, 3 to 24 (count, each a small solid block with its side walls).
wear: the lugs' outer edges taper and round, crisp square blocks at 0 to worn wedges at 100 (shape of the lug faces).
bite: the bit stands further out of the chuck, 34 to 84 world units (position of the bit node).
cells.risks: Most parts at once: the node count is the highest of the five and lug side walls double the count at teeth 24. Bite as bit length is the weakest link to the sound ('follower depth'); a crank-turn alternative (rotation about the wheel's axle, ≥ 30°) is available if the owner prefers. The pinion at ratio 0.50 scaled 1.6x pushes past the lug ring and nears the spindle head; check extremes. The diagonal of the spindle across the wheel makes a busy centre where crank arm, hub and spindle cross.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Drill, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: The eggbeater drill in three-quarter view as a working mechanism: crank and turned grip on the face wheel, lugs on its face driving a bright pinion on the spindle, from the wooden head handle to the chuck and bit

cells.subject: A laminated block of plywood cut away through the middle of a bored hole, close: plies stacked up its faces, the bore's far wall scored by the bit, its conical floor, and the cut edge of the bore as the one bright line.
controls: ratio: the bit's helical score marks on the bore wall wind tighter, pitch 68 to 4 world units (shape of the score lines).
teeth: the plies the block is laid up from, two per tooth, 6 to 48 glue lines over its height (count of hairlines on the cut face and the side).
wear: the bore's top rim goes from a clean circle to torn fibres, up to 5 px of tear (shape of the top face's hole edge).
bite: the bore deepens from a shallow dish to most of the block's height, 26 to 116 units (position of the floor and the cut edge).
cells.risks: It's a still life of a hole: the drill itself never appears, so the name rests on the bore and the cone the lips cut. Teeth as ply count saturates (needs a cap near 24 plies to keep lines ≥ 3 px apart). Score lines are faint hairlines and may not clear ratio's perceptibility floor at 1:1; give them a Line weight or more of them. Bite moving the floor rewrites the front face's outline (shape) as well as the cut edge.

machines.name: Kiln
machines.description: Modal synthesis of fired ceramic: a struck bowl whose glaze damps it and whose cracks make it inharmonic.
machines.concept: Modal synthesis of fired ceramic: a struck bowl whose glaze damps it and whose cracks make it inharmonic.
machines.soundsLike: A struck ceramic bowl: a clear fundamental with the bowl's stretched upper modes (about 1 : 2.7 : 5.2 : 8.4), ringing long when bare and high-fired, short and thuddy when heavily glazed. Cracks split each mode into a beating doublet and pull the partials apart, from a faint shimmer to a buzzing, broken clink.

intake.subject: a fired ceramic bowl, struck, whose glaze damps its ring and whose cracks pull its modes out of tune.
intake.controlSource: new (the source is the DSP I'm writing: a bank of 8 decaying two-pole resonators excited by a shaped mallet impulse)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings. Nothing to justify. `resources.display` is the placeholder (`stateBytes 4, nodes 1, palette 1`) until phase 4.

scores.effect: Soft thump to glassy ping: excitation bandwidth opens from the first two modes to all eight; big change in attack brightness

Upper modes stretch up to 24 % and ring a little longer; fundamental fixed, so a timbre shift more than a pitch one

cells.subject: The glazed floor of the bowl unrolled into one isometric field of square slab tiles, hidden-line, lit where the mallet's energy is still ringing.
controls: strike: count — the lit patch round the strike point grows from a 3-cell run to ~40 cells (hard mallet reaches more modes), clumped in runs of 2–4.
glaze: count + shade — the share of tiles in the grey glazed layer rises from ~5 % to ~70 % in runs, and lit tiles under glaze dim one step; a damped field.
crack: position — cells along two or three crazing lines drop to hollow wireframe and slip down 4–10 px, so a fissure network opens across the field (none at 0).
fire: position — every slab's thickness grows from 2 to ~14 px (the faces translate, tops rise) as the body vitrifies, so the field reads thin and soft at 0, deep and hard at 100.
cells.risks: P15 is for texture sounds and Gate 0 says a synth with a mechanism gets a drawing of the mechanism; kiln has one (a bowl), so this is the weakest fit of the five. The field isn't recognisably a bowl at 1:1; it reads as a glaze test tile at best. strike and glaze both act on counts of cell states, so glaze must keep its shade step and runs or the two blur. 112 cells x 2 nodes = 224 nodes: inside 256 at sdk 1.7 but no headroom, and a note flaring the patch must stay ≤ ~20 cells a frame. Close kin to toro-blocks' look; must stay a flat cell grid, not a height field, to be its own thing.
cells.alt: Kiln, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The glazed floor of the bowl unrolled into one isometric field of square slab tiles, hidden-line, lit where the mallet's energy is still ringing

cells.subject: The bowl cut through a–a as a bright section, with its ringing modes charted above it as a star chart along an ecliptic and the mallet plotted as a meteor trail falling onto the rim.
controls: strike: rotation — the meteor trail pivots on its impact point at the rim, from a shallow glancing 15° at 0 to a steep 70° at 100, and lengthens with it.
glaze: position — the level of glaze pooled in the well (the meniscus line inside the section) rises from the foot to about half the wall, ~40 px.
crack: shape — a fissure opens in the right wall of the section (the band splits, gap up to 18 px), and each mode star splits into a double star whose companions part along the ecliptic.
fire: scale — the stars' magnitudes: upper-mode stars grow from barely plotted (1.5 px) to ~2× as the fired body rings brighter and longer, and the stars slide right as the modes stretch.
cells.risks: Two languages could fight: a patent section and a star chart. The bowl must stay the subject (brightest, centred) and the chart its caption, or it reads as two pictures. crack does two things (fissure + double stars); keep the fissure primary. The meteor trail risks reading as a pointer/icon unless kept a tapering plotted trail with a radiant. The upper stars are 2 px at rest, under the 3–4 px part floor; fire 0 must hide rather than shrink below it. Labels n2–n7 must stay static.
cells.alt: Kiln, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The bowl cut through a–a as a bright section, with its ringing modes charted above it as a star chart along an ecliptic and the mallet plotted as a meteor trail falling onto the rim

cells.subject: A modal-synthesis schematic: a mallet impulse driving a bank of four tuned resonators through a shared glaze dashpot into a summing junction, with the bowl's ringing output trace on the right.
controls: strike: shape — the impulse in the mallet block narrows from a wide soft pulse (16 px) to a sharp spike (2 px) and grows taller; column 1, left zone.
glaze: position — the dashpot piston sinks ~40 px into its cylinder, the damper engaging every resonator; column 2, left zone.
crack: shape — the output trace's envelope breaks into beating lobes (amplitude dips up to 80 %) and its cycles go uneven; column 3, right zone.
fire: position — the mode ruler's ticks under the trace spread right as the modes stretch (top tick travels ~30 px), and the ratios printed in the resonator boxes follow.
cells.risks: Most at risk of reading as a dashboard: boxes, a slider-like dashpot and a ruler are panel furniture unless the schematic stays drawn in one hairline language with the trace the only bright thing. fire on a tick ruler is thin (1.5 px ticks) and may score under its floor; it may need the trace's cycle spacing too, which collides with crack on the trace's shape. The trace transient is noisy at 64 points: one mutable path can't hold this many cycles, so a real build shows fewer cycles or uses 2–3 paths. Text in the resonator boxes changes with fire, which needs text slots.
cells.alt: Kiln, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A modal-synthesis schematic: a mallet impulse driving a bank of four tuned resonators through a shared glaze dashpot into a summing junction, with the bowl's ringing output trace on the right

cells.subject: The bowl's ring itself, big and bright on a scope graticule: channel 1 is the sum of modes decaying from the trigger, channel 2 below is the highest mode alone, and a cursor marks where it dies away.
controls: strike: scale — channel 1's amplitude grows from ~1 division to ~3 (node scale 0.6 → 1.6 about the axis), harder mallet louder and brighter.
glaze: position — the −40 dB cursor slides left from near the right edge (~400 px) to a third of the way in (~170 px) as glaze damps the ring; the trace past it is drawn at 0.
crack: shape — channel 1's envelope breaks into beating lobes and its cycles go uneven, the doublets of a broken bowl.
fire: shape of channel 2 — the high mode's period shortens and its trace lasts longer, so the grey channel packs from ~8 to ~16 visible cycles.
cells.risks: P3's own pitfall: it's an oscilloscope, which says nothing about ceramic; nothing on screen says bowl, glaze or crack except by inference. Channel 1 is 200+ points at rest; one mutable outline is 64 points, so the real trace shows ~5 cycles or spends 3–4 paths (the whole path budget). glaze's cursor plus a trace that stops is the clearest control here, but glaze and fire both change how long things last, which might confuse. The graticule is 20 hairlines; keep it at #323232 so the trace is the only bright thing.
cells.alt: Kiln, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The bowl's ring itself, big and bright on a scope graticule: channel 1 is the sum of modes decaying from the trigger, channel 2 below is the highest mode alone, and a cursor marks where it dies away

cells.subject: A textbook figure of the bowl in plan as the sun of an orrery, each ringing mode an orbit round it and its antinodes the planets that ride it.
controls: strike: count — how many orbits are populated: a soft mallet lights only n = 2 (4 planets), a hard one fills out to n = 5 (28 planets), stepping in with an ease.
glaze: scale — the planets shrink to ~0.5× as glaze damps the modes, outer orbits first, until n = 5's are points.
crack: position — each planet splits into a doublet whose two halves part along the orbit (up to ~20 px), and the pairs slowly precess while notes ring: the beating of a broken bowl.
fire: scale — the orbits spread outward (outer orbit 1.0× → 1.25×) as the stiffer, vitrified body stretches its upper modes.
cells.risks: Stretch outside the engine column. Why it might be the exception: a bowl's modes really are circular standing waves round the rim with 2n antinodes, and a cracked bowl's split doublets really do beat as their nodes travel round, so orbits and planets are the physics, not a stand-in for a cycle in time. Why it might not fit: P12's strength is a sequence running round a cycle and kiln has none; nothing orbits at rest or between notes, so 'orrery' becomes a static mode diagram, and the pattern's wiring (links, planets that flash when their step sounds) has nothing to do. glaze and fire both use scale (different parts, but close in feel). Honest verdict: it fits as a mode diagram drawn in orrery form, not as an orrery.
cells.alt: Kiln, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: A textbook figure of the bowl in plan as the sun of an orrery, each ringing mode an orbit round it and its antinodes the planets that ride it

cells.subject: A yarn-wound mallet held poised over the rim of a thrown bowl, both modelled and drawn as hidden-line line art, the mallet head the brightest thing.
controls: strike: rotation — the mallet swings back about the wrist, from 10° above the strike line at 0 to 50° at 100 (40° of travel), so a harder strike is a bigger backswing; on a note it swings down to the rim and back.
glaze: position — the glaze line inside the bowl rises from the floor to near the lip (~40 px on screen), with the glazed interior hatched below it.
crack: shape — a hairline crack runs down the front wall from the rim, lengthening and forking (0 to ~40 px) as crack rises; none at 0.
fire: shape — the wall profile tightens and the lip thins and flares a little as the body vitrifies, so the throwing rings and rim ellipse draw stiffer and wider (~16 px at the rim).
cells.risks: Strike is mallet hardness, not force; a backswing reads as force. A swap of head (felt to bare core) is truer but a weaker channel. Glaze and fire both change the bowl, keep fire on the rim outline and glaze on the interior hatching. The mallet must not touch the bowl through strike's range except at the hit.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Kiln, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: A yarn-wound mallet held poised over the rim of a thrown bowl, both modelled and drawn as hidden-line line art, the mallet head the brightest thing

cells.subject: A fragment of the fired bowl wall seen edge-on and close: the clay body with its pores, the glassy glaze skin on its face, and a felt mallet tip resting on the lip.
controls: strike: scale — the mallet tip goes from a broad soft felt ball (r 26) to a small hard tip (r 14), about 1.9×; a note presses it into the lip.
glaze: position — the glaze skin's free surface lifts off the body from 5 to 21 px thick, its hatched glass growing with it.
crack: shape — a fissure opens from the glaze surface down through the body, its two faces parting up to ~16 px at the surface; closed at 0.
fire: count — the pores in the body close up as it vitrifies, from 17 open pores at 0 to 5 at 100 (11 at rest).
cells.risks: Close-up can lose the bowl: it must still read as a rim with a lip, not a banana or a sausage. Fire as pores closing is physically right but counts down; check it eases rather than pops. The tip touches the lip by design; keep it a shared contact point through strike's range.
cells.angle: the material the sound acts on, seen close
cells.alt: Kiln, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: A fragment of the fired bowl wall seen edge-on and close: the clay body with its pores, the glassy glaze skin on its face, and a felt mallet tip resting on the lip

cells.subject: The kiln opened after the firing, cut away in section: brick walls and a sprung arch round one bowl on its shelf, a pyrometric cone bent beside it and a tapping rod ringing the bowl through the spy hole.
controls: strike: position — the tapping rod draws back from the rim through the spy hole, 36 px off at 0 to 6 px at 100; a note taps it in.
glaze: position — the glaze line on the bowl's outside creeps down from just under the rim to near the foot, the glazed band hatched above it.
crack: shape — a dunting crack runs across the bowl's front from the rim, lengthening and stepping as crack rises; none at 0.
fire: rotation — the pyrometric cone bends over, from nearly upright (10°) at 0 to flat on its pad (90°) at 100, the potter's own gauge of how hot the firing went.
cells.risks: The kiln is a frame round the subject; brickwork must stay quiet (darkest grey hairlines) so the bowl stays the one bright thing. The bowl is small (~125 px) and the cone smaller (~35 px), so crack's line and the cone need checking at 1:1. Striking a bowl inside a kiln is a stretch of the scene (potters ring fresh pots by hand at unloading).
cells.angle: one scene where this happens, with one subject in it
cells.alt: Kiln, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: The kiln opened after the firing, cut away in section: brick walls and a sprung arch round one bowl on its shelf, a pyrometric cone bent beside it and a tapping rod ringing the bowl through the spy hole

cells.subject: The bowl taken apart along its axis into four thrown ring courses and its foot, spaced the way its modes are, with the mallet lifted off along its line of strike.
controls: strike: rotation — the exploded mallet turns on its line of strike, from lying back (soft) to pointing steeply at the top course (hard), ~40°.
glaze: position — hatched glaze climbs the inside of the courses from the foot up, course by course, so heavy glaze hatches the whole stack.
crack: shape — each course above the floor opens a split, a gap widening up to ~14 px, so every ring reads as two halves, like the modes splitting into doublets.
fire: position — the gaps between courses stretch more the higher they are (stack top moves ~30 px), the upper modes pulling apart as the body stiffens.
cells.risks: An exploded stack of rings can read as a lampshade or a spring rather than a bowl; the top course must keep the bowl's rim and the foot its foot. Glaze climbing by course is a count in disguise; it has to ease within a course. Stretch on fire is the same channel as nothing else here, but only ~30 px of travel.
cells.angle: the machine's own rule as a physical thing: what turning each knob would do to a real object
cells.alt: Kiln, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: The bowl taken apart along its axis into four thrown ring courses and its foot, spaced the way its modes are, with the mallet lifted off along its line of strike

cells.subject: The ringing bowl cut through its axis and drawn in one line weight: the bright cut wall, the interior's height contours, a glaze pool, and the felt mallet just off the lip.
controls: strike: position — the mallet head stands off the cut lip by 28 px at 0, closing to 4 px at 100; a note brings it in to the lip and the contours ripple.
glaze: position — the pooled glaze's contour rises up the interior contours (from the floor to about two thirds up), the pool hatched in the same weight.
crack: count — crazing lines cross the cut wall and the interior contours, from none to ~14 as crack rises.
fire: shape — the cut wall thins (wall from 0.075 to 0.045 of the radius) and the lip sharpens as the body vitrifies; the section's outline moves ~6–16 px.
cells.risks: Single weight leaves no Subject weight for the cut face; brightness alone has to make it the subject. Hatching in the line weight is heavier than the hairline rule; check it doesn't go grey at 1:1. Fire's wall-thinning travel is small; may need the lip shape to carry it. Close in spirit to pass 01's section, but a 3D cutaway, not a flat a–a section with a chart.
cells.angle: a cutaway of the object at work, so the inside explains it
cells.alt: Kiln, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: The ringing bowl cut through its axis and drawn in one line weight: the bright cut wall, the interior's height contours, a glaze pool, and the felt mallet just off the lip

machines.name: Lattice
machines.description: A 2D waveguide plate: a metal sheet held at its edges, struck at one point and heard at another. Size sets the mesh, tension its stiffness, damp how fast it rings out, pickup where it's heard.
machines.concept: A 2D waveguide plate: a metal sheet held at its edges, excited at one point and heard at another.
machines.soundsLike: A struck sheet of metal tuned to the note: a small tight mesh rings like a tin tray or a bar, a large stiff one like a gong or thunder sheet. Damp takes it from a long shimmering wash to a dead clank, and moving the pickup changes which partials you hear without changing the pitch.

intake.subject: a struck metal plate held at its edges, ringing in a standing-wave pattern that size, tension and damping reshape, with the pickup's place on it marked.
intake.controlSource: new (the DSP sketched below; no port)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings.

scores.effect: mode density from a sparse, almost bar-like few partials (4) to a dense metallic wash (12); the clearest change of character
near-harmonic, almost tonal membrane at 0 to a clangorous stretched plate at 100; strong but the pitch stays put
ring from ~8 s with slow beating to a dead 80 ms clank; the biggest change on the page
timbre shifts as modes drop into and out of nodal lines; clear on sustained notes, subtle on short ones

pick.reason: Pick 1 is good; add it.

cells.alt: Lattice at rest

cells.subject: A metal sheet bolted into a frame, cut away in isometric with its mesh lines bent into the standing wave, a striker rod over one point, a stylus at another and a felt damper hanging above the edge.
controls: size: count and scale, the mesh goes from 4 to 12 lines a side and the plate and frame grow about 1.5x in footprint.
tension: shape, the sheet's surface (mesh polylines) goes from a slack single dome to a taut, finer, inharmonic ripple.
damp: position, the felt damper drops from 40 px above the plate at 0 onto its dashed footprint at 100.
pickup: position, the stylus pin slides across the sheet from beside the striker to the far corner.
cells.risks: The bent mesh is a 3D surface: with 12 x 12 lines it needs mutable outlines well past the 4-path limit, so surface shape must come from pre-drawn variants or translated segments; tension may have to collapse to a few stepped surfaces. The striker head and damper are small (10 px) and could read as icons at 1:1. Grid lines at size 12 come within ~9 px, fine, but hidden-line over self-occluding ripples isn't modelled yet.
cells.cleanNote: Generated by `clean.py` (helpers from `../sketch.py`, unchanged) → `clean.svg`, `clean.png`. Lint: 0 errors, 0 warnings. The owner's pick, copied to `screens/lattice/frames/rest.svg` and `rest.png`.
cells.alt: Lattice, cleaned variant 2: A metal sheet bolted into a frame, cut away in isometric with its mesh lines bent into the standing wave, a striker rod over one point, a stylus at another and a felt damper hanging above the edge

cells.subject: The plate seen face on as a square field of junction cells, each lit by how far it swings, clamped in a hatched section frame and keyed with patent numerals.
controls: size: count, the field steps from 4 x 4 to 12 x 12 junction cells (16 to 144) and the clamp frame grows with it.
tension: shape of the lit pattern (palette swaps across the field), broad lobes at 0 breaking into a finer, stretched checker of nodal lines at 100.
damp: position, the felt band's inner line moves in from the clamp toward the centre and the cells under it go hollow.
pickup: position, the bright outlined pickup cell (numeral 14) walks from the strike point at 0 to the far corner at 100.
cells.risks: P15 is written for noise-like sounds with no mechanism, and this plate has one (Gate 0 pitfall in P15): the cell field is earned only because the waveguide mesh really is a grid of junctions. Tension and damp both act on cell values; damp is kept on geometry (felt line) so the two don't share 'how much grey'. 14 px cells are under P15's 20 px guidance (12 x 12 has to fit 192 px of body); 144 cells + frame fits 256 nodes but tension re-lights many cells per turn, so churn needs a cap. Patent numerals plus words duplicates the key; drop one at frames.

controls: size: count and scale, the mesh goes from 4 to 12 lines a side and the plate and frame grow about 1.5x in footprint.
tension: shape, the sheet's surface (mesh polylines) goes from a slack single dome to a taut, finer, inharmonic ripple.
damp: position, the felt damper drops from 40 px above the plate at 0 onto its dashed footprint at 100.

cells.risks: The bent mesh is a 3D surface: with 12 x 12 lines it needs mutable outlines well past the 4-path limit, so surface shape must come from pre-drawn variants or translated segments; tension may have to collapse to a few stepped surfaces. The striker head and damper are small (10 px) and could read as icons at 1:1. Grid lines at size 12 come within ~9 px, fine, but hidden-line over self-occluding ripples isn't modelled yet.
