cells.subject: A chart of the plate as a star field, junctions plotted as stars by how hard they ring with a constellation line from strike to pickup, beside the light curve the pickup records after each strike.
controls: size: count, the chart holds 4 x 4 to 12 x 12 stars and its neat-line ticks follow the mesh pitch.
tension: shape, the constellation line from strike to pickup sags in a slack arc at 0 and pulls straight at 100.
damp: shape, the light curve on the right runs long and beating at 0 and dies within its first tenth at 100.
pickup: position, the pickup star moves across the chart away from the strike, and the light curve's beating changes with it.
cells.risks: Two subjects in one frame: the chart and the curve compete, and P2 always asks which is the picture. Tension's sag is a metaphor (a constellation line has no tension), honest only as a reading aid; the plate's real tension change is in the curve's partial spacing. The light curve re-keys one 64-point path on damp and pickup and is coarse for high partials (near-reversal at sharp peaks). Stars at 3 px are at the legibility floor.
cells.alt: Lattice, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A chart of the plate as a star field, junctions plotted as stars by how hard they ring with a constellation line from strike to pickup, beside the light curve the pickup records after each strike

cells.subject: The wave itself, cut through the plate along the line from strike to pickup and drawn as a beam between two fixed supports, with a force arrow, a probe to the output terminal and a dimensioned span.
controls: size: position, the supports move apart from a 120 px to a 380 px span and the dimension line follows, letting more half-waves fit.
tension: shape, the trace goes from a few broad bows to a stiffer, crinkled outline as upper modes stretch away.
damp: scale, the trace and its dashed envelope shrink from 44 px of swing to about 15 px.
pickup: position, the probe and its lead to the 'out' terminal slide along the span from the strike arrow toward the far support.
cells.risks: P3's own pitfall: it can drift into 'just an oscilloscope', and a 1D cut throws away the plate's second dimension, which is the whole idea of the machine. At rest the snapshot can sit nearly flat (the default looks calm, maybe too calm); damp as amplitude reads as 'level'. Schematic furniture (title block, chain line) is quiet but adds parts that no control owns.
cells.alt: Lattice, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The wave itself, cut through the plate along the line from strike to pickup and drawn as a beam between two fixed supports, with a force arrow, a probe to the output terminal and a dimensioned span

cells.subject: Each plate mode as a body on its own orbit round the strike point, traced like an oscilloscope in x-y mode, with a phosphor trail behind each body as long as that mode rings.
controls: size: count, 4 to 12 orbits come out, one per mode the mesh can carry.
tension: position, orbit radii follow mode frequency, evenly spaced at 0 and stretched apart toward the rim at 100 as the plate stiffens.
damp: shape, the phosphor trails shorten from nearly full circles at 0 to short ticks behind each body at 100.
pickup: scale, each body's size is that mode's strength at the pickup, so moving the pickup swells some bodies and shrinks others to nothing at a nodal line.
cells.risks: Stretch, outside the engine column, and only half earned: a modal plate really is a set of independent oscillators each turning at its own rate, and an x-y scope does draw a sine pair as a circle, so the orrery is an honest picture of the modes. But concentric rings read as a target (craft.md), the sun does nothing (P13's complaint about P12), the plate's shape is gone entirely, and calm constant orbiting while playing costs a node per body every frame. Planets have no cycle a player can sequence, which is the reason P12 exists. My read: it doesn't fit; the strongest thing in it, trails as ring time, could move to another variant.
cells.alt: Lattice, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: Each plate mode as a body on its own orbit round the strike point, traced like an oscilloscope in x-y mode, with a phosphor trail behind each body as long as that mode rings

machines.name: Pylon
machines.description: An aeolian harp: a span of power line sung by the wind. Wind speed sets which of the wire's modes the shed vortices lock onto, span sets how close those modes sit, gust makes the lock wander, and a mains hum sits under it.
machines.concept: An aeolian harp: power lines sung by wind, the span and gusts setting which modes speak, with a mains hum under it.
machines.soundsLike: An aeolian harp: a breathy, whistling partial that sits on one harmonic of the played note and jumps up the series as the wind rises, with neighbours shimmering in when the span is long. Under it, an optional mains buzz at 50 Hz and its odd harmonics.

intake.subject: a span of power line between two pylons, its wire singing the standing wave the wind locks it into, with the mains humming under it.
intake.controlSource: new (the DSP below is the source)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings.

scores.effect: Climbs the harmonic series (mode 1 → ~15) and rises in level ∝ v²: the biggest change in pitch and loudness
One isolated partial at 20 m to a shimmering, beating cluster at 400 m; also moves the lock up for the same wind
Steady whistle to uneven swells with partials jumping between neighbours; obvious, but the pitch centre stays
A quiet 50 Hz buzz under the voice, never louder than −18 dB

pick.reason: Liked v5; add it, with subtle iconography for ch1 and ch2 instead of text.

cells.name: rest
cells.alt: Pylon at rest

cells.subject: A scope screen weaving the wire's recent shapes into cloth: the newest displacement trace bright at the front, older ones receding row by row, warp threads through the nodes that held.
controls: wind: shape — the front trace and every row behind it change loop count with the locked mode; warp threads follow the nodes.
span: position — the history recedes deeper (6 → 22 px per row), a long span ringing longer.
gust: shape (variance between rows) — rows stop agreeing on their loop count, so the warp columns break; at 0 every row shares its nodes.
hum: scale — the ch2 mains trace on the bottom division grows from flat to a 10 px sine.
cells.risks: Stretch, and mostly doesn't fit. P14 is for sequences and pylon has no steps; the only honest exception is gust, whose whole effect is change over time, and loom rows are one way to show variation in a still (steady wind = warp columns hold, gusts = rows wander). Against it: rows only advance while notes sound, so the rest frame is a memory; it reads as a waterfall/persistence scope, which is P3's 'says nothing new' pitfall; four rows plus the mains trace need five mutable outlines against a limit of 4 (hum would need pre-drawn variants).
cells.cleanNote:
- I removed the `ch1` and `ch2` labels; they were the only text in the drawing (lint now 0 errors, 0 warnings).
- I replaced them with channel marks in the graticule's own hairline: a short tick just outside the left edge at each trace's zero line, one stroke for the wire (y 150), two strokes 4 px apart for the mains (y 196). It's how a scope marks a channel's ground level, so it reads as part of the instrument, not as an icon.
- I kept everything else as the owner picked it: the graticule, the four receding wire rows with the front one the only `#CDCDCD` element, the warp threads and the mains trace, all at the same weights and positions.
- Still open from the sketch, not from this cleanup: the frame binds six outlines (four rows, plus the mains trace split into two pieces), and four rows plus the mains need at least five mutable outlines against a limit of four. Phase 4 has to solve that, e.g. by drawing hum as pre-drawn variants.
cells.alt: Pylon, cleaned variant 5: A scope screen weaving the wire's recent shapes into cloth: the newest displacement trace bright at the front, older ones receding row by row, warp threads through the nodes that held

cells.subject: A field of floating slabs, one row per conductor along the span, whose heights are the standing wave the wind locks into each wire, drawn as a patent figure between two cross-arms cut in hatched section.
controls: wind: shape (heights) — the locked mode number climbs from one broad hump at 0.5 m/s to fine loops at 20 m/s, so the crests multiply along every row.
span: count — the field grows from 10 to 18 slabs along the line while the cross-arms move apart, and the same wind sings a higher mode on a longer span.
gust: shape (row offset) — neighbouring modes join the lock and each row drifts out of step with the next, so the crests stop lining up across the conductors.
hum: shape (texture) — a fine alternating mains ripple lifts every other slab by up to 8 px, an even comb under the wind's loops; none at 0.
cells.risks: Closest to toro's voice field in build (it's the same pattern), so it has to earn its difference in the drawing: hatched section plates and patent numerals, hidden-line slabs, no solid grey faces. At span 100 it's 90 slabs × 3 nodes = 270 nodes, over 256, so it needs sdk 1.8 or a row fewer. Wind, gust and hum all act on heights; hum's comb has to stay visibly a texture rather than another wave, or it reads as a second wind. Crest highlight is several cells, so the 'one brightest element' is a set, not a single part.
cells.alt: Pylon, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A field of floating slabs, one row per conductor along the span, whose heights are the standing wave the wind locks into each wire, drawn as a patent figure between two cross-arms cut in hatched section

cells.subject: The wind's wake behind the wire as a flat isometric grid of cells, each raised cell a shed vortex roll, laid out downwind of one bright conductor on two short masts.
controls: wind: count — how many vortex rolls still stand downwind, from 2 at 0.5 m/s to 7 at 20 m/s (each roll a run of raised cells).
span: run length — the spanwise correlation: rolls go from broken runs of 2 cells to continuous runs of 8 along the wire.
gust: churn — cells are knocked off the street's lattice by 1–2 cells downwind or upwind, so the even rows break into a ragged wake.
hum: grey layer — a regular mains lattice of grey (unraised) cells fills in under the wake, 0 to ~40 cells.
cells.risks: P15 is meant for sounds with no mechanism; pylon has one (a vibrating wire), so Gate 0's 'draw the mechanism' argues against it. The wake is real physics (Kármán street, spanwise correlation), which is why it's worth a try. It shows the wind, not the singing: the wire's modes never appear, so the note itself has nothing obvious to act on beyond a flare near the wire. Isometric cells are rhombi, not the pattern's square cells. Grid of ~104 cells plus raised faces is ~180 nodes.
cells.alt: Pylon, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The wind's wake behind the wire as a flat isometric grid of cells, each raised cell a shed vortex roll, laid out downwind of one bright conductor on two short masts

cells.subject: The span between two pylon heads plotted on a sky chart, its wire a chain of standing-wave loops hung on a catenary across the graticule, with meteors for gusts and an ephemeris band for the hum.
controls: wind: shape — the wire's single mutable outline divides into more loops as the locked mode rises (1 loop at 0.5 m/s, capped near 12 at the top, where loops would drop under ~12 px), each crest marked with a star.
span: position — the two pylon stars slide apart (140 → 360 px) and the catenary sags deeper between them.
gust: count — meteor trails streak in from a fixed radiant upwind, 0 to 12, each a short plotted trail pointing back to it.
hum: position — a hairline ephemeris band opens under the wire, 6 → 30 px below it; folded onto the wire at 0.
cells.risks: It's an elevation against the sky more than a section: P1 says cut the object open, and the atlas language draws it from outside. The loop chain is the one bright subject and reads well, but stars on the antinodes and pylon heads are close in grey to it. Meteors for gust are the obvious atlas move and could read as decoration rather than air. Background field stars must stay static and few, or they become idle noise.
cells.alt: Pylon, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: The span between two pylon heads plotted on a sky chart, its wire a chain of standing-wave loops hung on a catenary across the graticule, with meteors for gusts and an ephemeris band for the hum

cells.subject: A circuit diagram of the harp: a shedding source tapping a ladder of tuned wire modes on the left, summed with a mains line into the output trace on the right.
controls: wind: position — the source's tap slides along the ladder bus to the mode it locks, and that rung lights.
span: count — the ladder holds 4 rungs on a short span and 12 on a long one, packed closer as they multiply.
gust: shape — the output trace's envelope breaks into uneven swells as neighbouring modes cut in.
hum: scale — the mains trace under the sum node grows from a flat line to a 14 px sine.
cells.risks: The most literal and the most explanatory, so it's closest to a dashboard: a ladder and a waveform could be any synth. Controls fall cleanly into the encoder columns (structure on 1–2, trace on 3–4). LC symbols at 10 px rungs are near the 3 px detail floor at 12 rungs. The output trace is a P3-style oscilloscope trace and risks 'says nothing new'. No physical pylon on screen.

machines.name: Silt
machines.description: Additive partials that settle like sediment: each note stirs the high partials up, and they sink back at the settling rate.
machines.concept: Additive partials that settle like sediment: stirring lifts the high partials, which then sink back at a settling rate.
machines.soundsLike: A dull, round additive tone at rest that brightens on every note as the upper partials are stirred up, then darkens again as they sink. Short settle sounds like a plucked brightness; long settle leaves a slow, glassy fall.

intake.subject: a bank of additive partials that lie settled like sediment, which each note stirs up (the high partials lift furthest) and which then sink back at the settling rate.
intake.controlSource: new

cells.subject: A dual-channel scope: the partial spectrum and its decay slope on the left graticule, the summed output waveform on the right.
controls: settle: rotation; the ch2 decay line (level in dB against time, so an exponential settle is a straight line) swings from steep (0.1 s) to nearly flat (10 s), about 56 degrees.
layers: count; the ch1 spectrum gains lines, one per partial, from 2 to 64 across the log-frequency graticule.
stir: shape; the output trace (one mutable outline, 64 points) gains high-partial ripple and sharpens its edges as stir lifts the upper partials.
grain: position; each spectrum line slides off its harmonic tick by a fixed seeded amount, so coarse grain reads as an inharmonic, scattered comb.
risks: Easy to drift into 'oscilloscope', which says nothing new (P3 pitfall applies to the right half).
Three graticules make it read as a dashboard of meters; the subject is split in three boxes, not one object.
At 64 layers the log-spaced top lines bunch under 3 px; cap or thin the upper octave.
Grain's sideways slide is ~3-6 px per line, below the 24 px position floor; needs more travel or shape help.
Settling itself (the sinking) only shows on notes; at rest the screen is a static spectrum.
cells.alt: Silt, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A dual-channel scope: the partial spectrum and its decay slope on the left graticule, the summed output waveform on the right

cells.subject: The stirred wave printed big as a textbook figure, its component partials drawn small beneath it hanging in a band that sinks toward a stippled silt bed.
controls: settle: position; the band of component curves hangs high under the wave at long settle and drops onto the stipple bed at short settle (about 26 px).
layers: count; one printed component curve per partial is added under the wave (capped at eight visible, labelled k2 to kN).
stir: shape; the main wave (the one bright mutable outline) gains high-partial ripple and steeper edges.
grain: scale; the stipple dots of the bed grow from fine silt (3 px) to coarse sand (6 px).
risks: The component band reads as water hatching at 1:1; spacing is exactly at the 7 px limit and amplitude only 2 px.
Layers has to cap at eight curves, so 16..64 differ only in the label; count floor (12 items) fails above 8.
Grain on the bed is small and low-grey; scale 2x of 3 px dots may still under-read for a score-3 control.
Settle shown as a position is a snapshot of a time; it explains 'how far they've sunk', not the rate.
cells.alt: Silt, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The stirred wave printed big as a textbook figure, its component partials drawn small beneath it hanging in a band that sinks toward a stippled silt bed

cells.subject: Octave bands of partials as flat plates in elevation, stepping back from the fundamental on the ground line, the upper plates lifted off their dashed settled positions.
controls: settle: position along the stack; the bright plate (the settle front, the band still falling) moves from the front plate at 0.1 s to the back plate at 10 s.
layers: count; one plate per octave band (k1, k2, k3-4, k5-8 ...), from 2 plates at 2 partials to 7 plates at 64.
stir: position; plates lift vertically off their dashed settled lines, more the further back (higher) they are, up to ~46 px for the top band.
grain: shape; the bright plate's top edge goes from a fine serration to coarse teeth.
risks: Settle and stir both use position, on different parts and axes (bright marker along the stack vs vertical lift); a reviewer may call it a shared channel.
Count by octave grows slowly (2 to 7 plates), under the 12-item floor though it is more than doubling.
Plates read as shelves or a bar chart at 1:1; the elevation conventions (ground hatch, hidden settled lines, dimension ticks) carry the language and must stay crisp.
Grain only shapes one plate; a score-3 control on a 230 px edge with 1.5-5 px teeth is borderline.
cells.alt: Silt, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: Octave bands of partials as flat plates in elevation, stepping back from the fundamental on the ground line, the upper plates lifted off their dashed settled positions

cells.subject: A survey plan of a settling basin: a bright silt plume spreading from the inlet over the faint contoured bed, with its deposit lens on the flow line and one chainage station per partial along the foot.
controls: settle: scale; the plume grows from 0.7x to 1.3x along the flow line (slow-settling silt stays suspended and travels further).
layers: count; chainage stations along the bottom strip, one tick per partial, every fourth numbered.
stir: shape; the plume's edges lobe and billow (high partials lifted) from a smooth fan to a churned outline.
grain: position; the deposit lens slides upstream toward the inlet as grain coarsens (coarse grains drop out first), about 100 px.
risks: The strip of stations is close to a 'strip of cells' at rest (craft: picture, not panel); it earns its place only because it is the partial count.
Contours under 1.5 px (hairline field, lint warns) may vanish on the panel; check on device.
The plume is a metaphor for the spectrum, not a plot of it: stir lobing doesn't literally show which partials lifted.
A blob outline can slide toward an organic or icon-like shape (an earlier draft read as a fish); keep it a fan.
cells.alt: Silt, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: A survey plan of a settling basin: a bright silt plume spreading from the inlet over the faint contoured bed, with its deposit lens on the flow line and one chainage station per partial along the foot

cells.subject: A glass settling column cut open like a patent figure, its partial strata stacked from the bed up to a bright interface, a hinged stirring arm and suspended grains above.
controls: settle: position; the bright interface between settled strata and suspension sits low for a fast settle and high for a slow one (about 100 px).
layers: count; one stratum line per partial from the bed up, to the interface (capped near 24 visible).
stir: rotation; the stirring arm swings on its pivot from hanging straight (0) to 40 degrees (100).
grain: scale; the suspended particles grow from 3 px to 6 px.
risks: Stretch: P11 is for instruments people know by sight, and a settling column (Imhoff cone, elutriation tube) isn't one most players know; recognition is not free here, so the pattern's main reason doesn't hold. Honest verdict: it doesn't fit the pattern well; it survives as a section drawing (closer to P1) of the machine's own metaphor.
Layers counted as strata loses legibility past ~24 lines; strata hide above the interface at slow settle.
The arm rotating is a literal stir, but stir in the DSP lifts high partials; the arm angle doesn't show which partials rise.
Hatched walls are many small static paths; fine for budget but check hatch spacing (5 px) on device.
cells.alt: Silt, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: A glass settling column cut open like a patent figure, its partial strata stacked from the bed up to a bright interface, a hinged stirring arm and suspended grains above

cells.subject: One mica-like platelet per partial, flat hexagonal flakes exploded up a dashed leader line from the big fundamental on the bed to the small high partials, which a stir has lifted furthest.
controls: settle: rotation; each lifted flake tilts as if gliding down, flat at 0.1 s and up to about 26 degrees for the highest flakes at 10 s (pre-drawn tilt variants per flake, since nodes can't tip out of the screen plane).
layers: count; one flake per partial, 2 to 64, each smaller than the one below, so the column gets longer and finer.
stir: position; the gaps between flakes along the leader line, growing with partial number, so the high flakes travel furthest (top flake moves well over 24 px from 0 to 100).
grain: shape; the regular hexagons break into chipped, uneven grains and step off the leader line, each by its own seeded amount.
risks: At 1:1 the column can read as a chain of hexagons rather than flakes; the low flakes crowd into a muddy cluster at the base because they barely lift.
At 64 layers the top flakes get under ~3 px wide; they would need a minimum size or to be capped.
Settle as tilt needs pre-drawn variants for every flake (a node budget question for phase 4).

cells.alt: Silt, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: One mica-like platelet per partial, flat hexagonal flakes exploded up a dashed leader line from the big fundamental on the bed to the small high partials, which a stir has lifted furthest

cells.subject: A pebble has just dropped into a still, shallow stream, and a plume of silt billows up off the bed where it landed and leans away downstream under rings on the water.
controls: settle: rotation; the plume leans downstream, nearly upright at 0.1 s (it drops before the current can carry it) and leaning about 40 degrees at 10 s.
layers: count; one billow per partial, each its own contour folded over the one above, so the plume goes from two lumps to a fine cauliflower.
stir: shape; the plume's height, the high billows rising furthest, capped under the water surface.
grain: shape; the billows scatter off the column into a ragged, uneven plume (seeded per billow).
risks: Single weight: everything is 1.5 px, so hierarchy rests on brightness alone (bright plume outline vs mid-grey scene); a departure from three weights by the direction's own language.
The plume outline at rest can read as a shell or a cabbage; whether it reads as silt depends on the motion (billowing up on a note, leaning and sinking).
Stir and grain are both shape on the plume; they change different things (height vs raggedness) but share the outline path.
cells.angle: one scene where this happens, with one subject in it
cells.alt: Silt, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: A pebble has just dropped into a still, shallow stream, and a plume of silt billows up off the bed where it landed and leans away downstream under rings on the water

cells.subject: A snow globe of silt: shaking it lifts a hatched cloud off the drift on its floor, and the cloud's lifted top edge is the one bright line.
controls: settle: position; how high the cloud's underside still hangs above the drift, resting on it at 0.1 s and floating about 0.4 of the globe higher at 10 s (thicker liquid).
layers: count; the cloud is hatched with exactly one 45-degree hairline per partial, so 2 layers is two strokes and 64 is a dense mass (spacing floors at 3.2 px, so it saturates near 40).
stir: shape; the cloud's top edge (the bright mutable outline) rises and bulges, highest in the middle, from a low skin at 0 to near the top of the glass at 100.
grain: scale; coarse flakes appear under the cloud and grow from nothing to about 10 px, and the top edge roughens.
risks: A snow globe is a known toy and could tip toward novelty; it must stay drawn as an object (glass highlight, banded base), never as an icon.
Layers as hatch count saturates around 40 lines at the 3.2 px floor, so 48 and 64 look alike.
Settle shown as hang height is a snapshot of a time, not the rate.
cells.angle: the machine's own rule as a physical thing: what turning each knob would do to a real object
cells.alt: Silt, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: A snow globe of silt: shaking it lifts a hatched cloud off the drift on its floor, and the cloud's lifted top edge is the one bright line

cells.subject: A prospector's pan cut in half mid-swirl: the water tips up one wall, the fine grains ride up in it while the heavy ones stay in the crease, and the tilted waterline is the bright line.
controls: settle: position; how high the fine grains still hang in the water, back down in the crease at 0.1 s and up near the surface on the high side at 10 s.
layers: count; one grain per partial, from big heavy ones in the crease to small fine ones up the slope.
stir: rotation; the waterline tilts from nearly level at 0 to about 38 degrees at 100, climbing the right-hand wall and taking the fines with it.
grain: scale; every grain grows up to 2.4 times, from fine silt to coarse sand.
risks: At 1:1 the pan reads as a bowl or boat as much as a gold pan; the riffles on the back wall are the only cue.
Grains are 3 to 6 px with a rim light on one side; the smallest sit at the legibility floor.
The cut wall bodies are a #323232 fill (solid bodies); the water is hatching, the grains black with rim light.
cells.angle: a cutaway of the object at work, so the inside explains it
cells.alt: Silt, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: A prospector's pan cut in half mid-swirl: the water tips up one wall, the fine grains ride up in it while the heavy ones stay in the crease, and the tilted waterline is the bright line

cells.subject: A slab of rippled silt lifted out after the water has gone, its cut face showing the cross-laminae each stir-and-settle left, its front ripple profile the one bright line.
controls: settle: shape; the ripples' asymmetry, steep current ripples at 0.1 s (fast drop) easing to round, nearly symmetric ripples at 10 s.
layers: count; one ripple per two partials (crests and cross-lamina sets), 1 to 32 crests, doubling across the range.
stir: shape; ripple height, from a nearly flat bed at 0 to tall ripples at 100 (front profile moves well over 16 px).
grain: shape (planform); the crests go from straight to sinuous, broken linguoid ripples, seeded per crest.
risks: Three controls change the same ripple field by shape (asymmetry, height, crest planform); they read differently on the slab but share one channel family.
Layers below 4 (2 crests) shows a near-empty slab; at 64 the 32 crests sit around 8 px apart, close to the hatching limit with crest lines plus laminae.
Wave and current ripples are geology; the read is 'ripple marks', not necessarily 'partials', without the motion.

machines.name: Spool
machines.description: A single-cycle wave written onto a short tape loop that wears with every pass; bias and wow colour it.
machines.concept: A single-cycle wave written onto a short tape loop that wears with every pass; bias and wow colour it.
machines.soundsLike: A bright single-cycle tone that, held, darkens pass by pass as its high partials wear off the tape, with soft dropouts opening where the oxide thins. Wow bends its pitch once per loop revolution; bias decides whether it saturates hard (under) or goes dull and quiet (over).

intake.subject: a short loop of tape with one cycle written on it, read back pass after pass while it wears, wobbles and saturates.
intake.controlSource: new (the DSP is being written for this machine; the definition is drafted from that intent)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings. Nothing to justify.

scores.effect: Held, a bright cycle dulls toward a sine within a few passes at 100 and dropouts open; at 0 nothing changes. Dramatic, and it keeps working the longer a note sounds
Pitch sways once per revolution, up to ±40 cents; subtle below ~30, obvious above
A soft splice dip once per revolution at any setting, and the pace of wear and wow; with wear and wow at 0 it's only the dip
Under: louder, harder clipping and grit; over: duller and ~2.5 dB quieter. Both ends clearly audible, centre is clean

cells.subject: A labelled diagram of the tape path on the left (loop, capstan, tension roller, record and play heads) with the cycle the play head reads drawn large on the right.
controls: wear: the right-hand trace loses its corners and opens two dropout notches, with the cycle as written ghosted in #4B4B4B behind it (shape, one mutable trace).
wow: the flutter arm resting on the loop's top run swings about its pivot, 0 to 36 degrees (rotation).
length: the tension roller slides right and the loop stretches with it, 80 to 180 px between roller centres (position).
bias: the field lines fringing from the record-head gap into the tape grow from 0.55x to 1.45x (scale).
cells.risks: Hands and screen disagree: P2 wants structure on knobs 1-2 and tone on 3-4, but spool's order puts wear (a trace control) first and length (a structure control) third, so the screen splits left/right while the controls interleave. The left diagram is small at 1:1 (rollers 34 px) and sparse beside the trace; rotating the wow arm lifts its roller off the tape, which is not what wow does physically, so a frames pass should find a truer motion (the arm pressing the run into a dip, say). Wear is the 5-score control but only moves the right half. A ~200 px trace is wider than one mutable outline can be (points within +-64 px of the node), so it needs 2 of the 4 paths.
cells.alt: Spool, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A labelled diagram of the tape path on the left (loop, capstan, tension roller, record and play heads) with the cycle the play head reads drawn large on the right

cells.subject: The magnetised waveform itself, bright along a strip of tape seen in flat front elevation between two diagonal splices, dimensioned like a part drawing.
controls: wear: the repeated cycle along the strip rounds off and sags at two dropouts, every repeat the same (shape of the trace).
wow: the strip's top and bottom edges weave up and down, up to 6 px, as the tape flutters through the guides (shape of the two edge lines, a second and third path).
length: the right-hand splice and the end of the dimension line beneath it slide along the strip, 184 to 454 px from the left edge (position).

bias: the two saturation rails inside the strip close in toward the trace as bias goes under and open to the tape edges as it goes over; under-bias, the trace clips flat against them (position, 20 px travel per rail).
cells.risks: It is the closest of the five to an oscilloscope, which patterns.md warns about; the tape edges, splices and dimension line are what keep it an elevation, and if they read as chrome it collapses into a scope. Four repeats of the cycle across 420 px need four mutable outlines for the trace alone, leaving none for the wow edges, so a device version must repeat one outline as several placed nodes (all re-keyed together when wear moves) or draw fewer repeats. Bias rail travel is ~20 px, just under the 24 px position floor: it needs the clip to show on the trace as well. The 'elevation' label is decoration if nothing else on the page is labelled; cut it in frames.
cells.alt: Spool, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The magnetised waveform itself, bright along a strip of tape seen in flat front elevation between two diagonal splices, dimensioned like a part drawing

cells.subject: Successive passes of the loop surveyed as profiles stacked back in depth, the pass playing now in front and older, fresher passes receding behind it with chainage along the front.
controls: wear: each profile is a little more eroded than the one behind it, so the stack goes from crisp at the back to rounded at the front (shape; only the front profile is a mutable outline, older ones are re-keyed when a pass ages).
wow: the passes shear sideways against each other along the tape, up to 10 px each (position of each layer).
length: the spacing between passes opens from 12 to 26 px, so a longer loop pushes history further back (position along the stack).
bias: the front profile's level, 1.3x under-biased to 0.7x over-biased (scale of the front layer).
cells.risks: At defaults (wear 0) all five profiles are identical, so the rest frame shows only a stack, and the history this subject exists for appears only once wear is up and a note has run. Bias scale spans 1.86x but scaling a node also scales its stroke, so the front line thickens past 2.5 px at the under-bias end; bias may need shape instead, which collides with wear on the same part. Wow as shear at 10 px is under the 24 px floor at 1:1 and needs more travel. Re-keying all five profiles each pass is 5 path redraws per loop period; at 0.05 s loops that is too often, so the stack should advance by moving nodes, not rewriting them.
cells.alt: Spool, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: Successive passes of the loop surveyed as profiles stacked back in depth, the pass playing now in front and older, fresher passes receding behind it with chainage along the front

cells.subject: The record head's laminated core, cut in patent section with hatching, coil turns and reference numerals, standing on a perspective plane of tape with a strip of worn-through segments under it.
controls: wear: segments of the loop in the bottom strip fill in as they wear through, 0 to 24 of 24 (count).
wow: the tape's near edge, the brightest line of the field, weaves in a slow wave up to 4 px (shape of one mutable edge).
length: the splice, a brighter cut across the tape, recedes from the near edge toward the head as the loop lengthens, ~36 px (position).
bias: the field lines fringing out of the head gap into the tape grow from 0.55x to 1.45x (scale).
cells.risks: The figure (the head) is the brightest and largest thing but no control moves the head itself: it is a fixed stage for the gap's field lines, so the screen's subject is the drawing least connected to the sound. Wear, the loudest control (5), lands on the least prominent part, the strip, and at defaults the strip is 24 empty cells; it should probably also cut gaps in the field. Wow at 4 px edge travel is well under the 16 px shape floor. Section hatching and coil turns are static art (fine for cost) but dense: ~60 short ribbons at 6 px pitch, near the 3 px hatching limit in the corners. Patent numerals (10, 12, 14, 16) refer to nothing on screen; they are language, and a reviewer may call them ornament.
cells.alt: Spool, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The record head's laminated core, cut in patent section with hatching, coil turns and reference numerals, standing on a perspective plane of tape with a strip of worn-through segments under it

cells.subject: Each pass of the loop woven as a row of isometric slabs on warp threads, slab heights tracing the cycle, so wear shows as rows that stop matching the row behind.
controls: wear: rows erode front to back, the pass playing now lowest and roundest, the oldest still the written shape (position of slab tops, re-keyed as rows age).
wow: rows slide sideways along the warp against each other, up to 1.4 threads (position of each row).
length: the number of warp threads, 8 to 24, so a longer loop is a wider cloth (count).
bias: under-bias lowers a cap height that the tallest slabs flatten against and turn a lighter grey, over-bias leaves them free (position of the cap, count of capped slabs).
cells.risks: Stretch, outside the engine column. Why spool may be the exception: its sound is literally a history of passes over the same material, and what P14 draws (which positions stay the same pass after pass and which drift) is exactly what wear does; no other engine pattern shows time-by-pass. Why it may not fit: the rows only differ while wear is up and notes run, so at defaults the loom is four identical rows (the 'locked' reading, honest but flat), and a field of bars on a floor reads like a 3D bar chart, i.e. a meter, which the subject gate rejects. Cost is high: 4 rows x 14 threads x 3 faces = 168 nodes, and every pass re-keys all of them as rows age, far over ~20 a frame at short loop lengths; flat tops for older rows (P14's own advice) halve it. At 24 threads the cloth shrinks to fit and slabs get near the 3 px floor.
cells.alt: Spool, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: Each pass of the loop woven as a row of isometric slabs on warp threads, slab heights tracing the cycle, so wear shows as rows that stop matching the row behind

cells.subject: A spool lying on a table, seen low from the front, paying out a trail of thread behind it that lies in the written cycle's shape, repeat after repeat, receding to the far edge.
controls: wear: the trail wears with age, the oldest (far) repeats losing their corners first and opening frayed gaps where the oxide would thin, the newest staying crisp (shape of the trail outline, re-keyed when wear changes).
wow: the spool's heading swings as it rolls, so the free run between the trail's end and the winding pulls round with it, 0 to 36 degrees (rotation of the spool node about its contact point).
length: the wavelength of one repeat laid on the table, so a longer loop lays fewer, longer repeats, 6 down to 3 across the frame (count of repeats, with their spacing).

bias: tension in the free run: under-biased it's pulled straight and taut and the spool sits 24 px nearer the trail; over-biased it sags into a slack loop (position of the spool, with the free run reshaped).
cells.risks: Single weight breaks craft.md's three-weight table on purpose: the language is one 1.5 px contour, with brightness (#CDCDCD thread, #7D7D7D spool) doing the separating; say so if picked. The zigzag trail could read as a chart or a lightning scribble rather than thread if it loses its perspective; it only reads as thread laid on a table because it recedes. Wear acting on the far (small) repeats puts the 5-score control on the least prominent part; it needs to reach the nearest repeat at high wear to clear the 2.5 % floor. The trail is ~5 repeats of 6 points but runs to several mutable outlines once frayed (gaps split it), so the budget is tight on 4 paths. Wow as a spool rotation fakes a 3D turn with a screen-plane turn; it holds only while the camera stays low and the swing is modest.

cells.alt: Spool, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: A spool lying on a table, seen low from the front, paying out a trail of thread behind it that lies in the written cycle's shape, repeat after repeat, receding to the far edge

cells.subject: The lip of one big spool so close that the frame cuts it off: the top flange's rim across the top, the wound mass below it drawn as a hatched mass of turns, and one bright thread peeling off under the rim and out of the frame.
controls: wear: loose fibre loops lift off the wound surface along the turns, 0 to 16 standing loops, and the hatching thins where they leave (count of fibre loops).
wow: the free thread swings about the point where it leaves the winding, as the spool runs untrue, 0 to 32 degrees (rotation of the thread node).
length: how much thread is wound: the face of the wound mass moves out toward the flange rim or back toward the barrel, 30 px of travel at its silhouette (position of the wall and its hatching).
bias: how tightly the turns lie: under-biased the turns pack close (4 px apart), over-biased they lie loose (7 px apart) and the free thread sags further (count of hatch lines).
cells.risks: Hatching here is the thread's own turns, not the semi-opaque convention in craft.md, so the reader has to take the 45-degree-ish hairlines as wound thread; at defaults that's helped by the single bright strand leaving the mass. Bias changes the hatch count, which re-keys the whole hatch (dozens of ribbons) on every turn of the knob; the device version needs the hatch as a few mutable outlines or placed nodes, not 40 static ribbons. The crop hides the whole spool, so nothing at rest says 'spool' except the flange rim and bore; if the rim reads as a lampshade the subject fails. The flange's bore sits near the top edge and competes a little with the thread.
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Spool, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: The lip of one big spool so close that the frame cuts it off: the top flange's rim across the top, the wound mass below it drawn as a hatched mass of turns, and one bright thread peeling off under the rim and out of the frame

cells.subject: A wooden spool of thread standing on end, a black silhouette on black with its right-hand edges caught by a light from behind, the loose end hanging over the bottom flange and curling on the ground.
controls: wear: the lit edge of the winding breaks up into short broken lengths with frayed ends lifting off it, 0 to 14 breaks, and the loose end frays at its tip (count of breaks along the bright edge).
wow: the loose end swings from where it leaves the winding, as the spool turns out of true, 0 to 34 degrees (rotation of the tail node about its exit point).
length: how full the spool is: the wound mass grows out from the barrel toward the flange rims, its lit edge moving 26 px (position of the winding's edge, scale of its outline).
bias: tension in the loose end: under-biased it hangs straight and taut to a short curl; over-biased it drops slack into a wide loose loop on the ground (shape of the tail outline).
cells.risks: Edge-lit means most edges are dim (#323232-#4B4B4B) and only the right-hand ones bright; on the real panel the dim side may vanish and the spool read as a bracket, so the dark outline grey needs a device check. It's the most literal of the five and the plainest: one object, little happening at rest. The winding's bright edge and the tail are both #CDCDCD; they're one thread, but a reviewer may count two brightest elements. Wow and bias both act on the tail (rotation vs. shape); they're different channels on one part, which can blur which knob did what.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Spool, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: A wooden spool of thread standing on end, a black silhouette on black with its right-hand edges caught by a light from behind, the loose end hanging over the bottom flange and curling on the ground

cells.subject: A hand bobbin winder on its base plate: two bearing posts, the spindle and its crank, a bobbin filling with thread, and the thread coming in from the left through a pair of tension discs on a sprung stud.
controls: wear: loose turns and fibre ends stand off the bobbin's winding between the flanges, 0 to 14 of them, and the incoming thread goes from smooth to frayed (count).
wow: the crank's handle swings round the spindle, an uneven stroke drawn as the crank's resting angle, 0 to 40 degrees (rotation of the crank arm and handle about the spindle axis).
length: how full the bobbin is: the wound mass grows from the hub toward the flange rims, 24 px at its top edge (position of the winding outline and its turns).

bias: the tension nut screws along its stud: under-biased it's run in and the spring is short, over-biased it's backed off and the spring opens out, 26 px of travel (position of the nut, with the spring's turns spacing out).
cells.risks: It's the busiest of the five: base, posts, spindle, crank, stud, discs, spring and bobbin. It stays legible at 1:1 because the parts are separate, but it's dense for the 40 % black floor (92 % black measured at rest) and costly in nodes. The crank's angle as wow is a stand-in: a hand crank's angle isn't what wow means, it just reads as 'the stroke'. The tension discs and nut are small (under 30 px), so bias's travel is short in absolute terms; it needs the full 26 px. The thread enters from off-frame top left, near the header line.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Spool, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: A hand bobbin winder on its base plate: two bearing posts, the spindle and its crank, a bobbin filling with thread, and the thread coming in from the left through a pair of tension discs on a sprung stud

cells.subject: A spool on its side seen close, with a quarter of its winding cut away toward the camera so the thread shows in section: every turn a small bright round cut, layer on layer on the barrel, between two whole flanges.
controls: wear: the outer layers' sections go from round and bright to flattened and hatched (worn thin, there but not sounding), from the outside in, 0 to all layers (count of worn sections).
wow: the barrel sits off-centre in the winding, so the layers crowd one cut face and thin on the other, an eccentric reel, 0 to 24 px offset (position of the barrel and bore).
length: the number of layers wound on the barrel, 3 to 9: a longer loop is more thread (count of section rows, with the outer surface moving out).
bias: how the turns pack: under-biased they're pressed tight into a hexagonal stack, over-biased they lie loose in square rows with gaps between them (position of the sections within each row).
cells.risks: Each section is its own small outline: ~330 at rest (326 counted), far beyond the 512-node limit's spirit and the ~20-changed-nodes redraw budget when wear or bias touches them; the device version needs whole rows as one mutable outline each (≤ 64 points per row) and fewer, larger sections. The sections are ~8 px across and touching, so at 1:1 the cut face reads as a mesh before it reads as thread; it may need a closer crop or larger thread. Hidden lines come from a depth buffer in the generator; on the device it's static artwork plus moved rows. Some facet edges break into sub-3 px fragments (lint legibility warnings).

cells.alt: Spool, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: A spool on its side seen close, with a quarter of its winding cut away toward the camera so the thread shows in section: every turn a small bright round cut, layer on layer on the barrel, between two whole flanges

machines.name: Tide
machines.description: Eight tuned resonators in a rock pool, rung by noise that arrives in waves; the note sets the pool's tuning.
machines.concept: A bank of tuned resonators in a rock pool, excited by noise that arrives in waves; notes set the pool's tuning.
machines.soundsLike: A pitched wash: bursts of surf noise that swell in and fall away, leaving a chord of ringing tones at the played note that decays before the next wave. Long depth turns it into a sustained, shimmering drone; short depth leaves tuned hiss.

intake.subject: a rock pool whose tuned hollows ring when the swell's noise washes into them; each candidate in the subject pass draws that pool its own way.
intake.controlSource: new (the source is the DSP below)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 1 warning.

scores.effect: The rhythm of the whole sound: a rapid flutter of surf at 0.25 s, a slow breathing wash at 8 s. Dramatic and constant.
From tuned hiss (50 ms) to a sustained ringing chord (5 s); decides whether it is a pitched instrument at all.
Partials stretch from a clean harmonic chord to bell-like, metallic beating; clear above ~30 %.
Slow chorusing and beating between resonators; subtle under 40 %, a seasick wobble at 100 %.

cells.subject: One phosphor trace of the pool ringing after the latest swell stands bright over dim receding traces of earlier swells, with each wave's arrival ticked along the bottom strip.
controls: swell: the arrival ticks in the bottom strip spread from many (0.25 s) to two (8 s) across the window, and the receding traces step back by one period each (count and position).
depth: the bright trace's ring-down tail stretches from a short burst at the left to a wave that reaches the right edge (shape of the figure).
salt: the trace's later cycles break into an inharmonic beating ripple as the partials stretch (shape, second-order; needs its own region of the trace).
drift: the receding persistence traces slide sideways out of register with each other, so the stack shears (position of the field layers).
cells.risks: P3's warning applies: it can read as a plain oscilloscope that says nothing about a rock pool. Depth and salt both reshape the one trace; salt needs a clearly different kind of change (beating, not length) or it collides with depth. The trace is ~280 points, so on the device it must be four 64-point mutable outlines and re-keyed only on turns. The far persistence traces are small (period ~3.5 px) and close to the hatching floor.
cells.alt: Tide, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: One phosphor trace of the pool ringing after the latest swell stands bright over dim receding traces of earlier swells, with each wave's arrival ticked along the bottom strip

cells.subject: A Hinton chart set like a textbook figure: eight resonator rows across four seconds, each square sized by how loudly that resonator rings, so the swells show as bright columns that fade to the right.
controls: swell: the bright onset columns move closer together or further apart along the time axis, from every column (0.25 s) to only one in the window (8 s) (position/count).
depth: squares stay large for longer after each onset, from one column of decay to a full row of large squares (scale of the cells, i.e. shape of the field).
salt: the row spacing stretches unevenly downward as partials go inharmonic, so f5..f8 spread apart while f1 stays put (position of rows).
drift: each row slides its squares a few pixels left or right of the column grid, so the onset columns go ragged (position per row, different axis to salt).
cells.risks: It is the most legible of the five but the least about a rock pool: no water, no rock, only the model. Row labels f1..f8 and the time axis are static text that the guidelines allow but which push it toward a chart. 128 squares is fine for nodes, but swell moves every column at once, so a swell turn redraws far over 20 nodes (turns only, never at rest). Hinton charts are a known form; it must not drift into a meter grid.
cells.alt: Tide, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: A Hinton chart set like a textbook figure: eight resonator rows across four seconds, each square sized by how loudly that resonator rings, so the swells show as bright columns that fade to the right

cells.subject: The shore cut in elevation as one grid of square cells: hollow cells for rock, grey cells for water, and lit runs where the swell foams over the rim and glints in the pool.
controls: swell: the crest column in the sea grows taller and wider and lights a longer foam run before the rim (count of lit cells).
depth: the pool's water line rises cell by cell and the rock floor under it drops, so the grey water body grows from one row to five (count of grey cells).
salt: lit crystal runs of 2 to 4 cells appear inside the grey water and along the rock edges (density of lit runs).
drift: the pool's surface tilts a cell at a time from one wall to the other, so the water line steps (run length / position of the surface cells).
cells.risks: P15 is meant for sounds with no mechanism, and tide has one (a pool of tuned resonators), so this risks Gate 0's warning. At 20 px cells the shore is coarse and reads like a block game; the hollow rock cells fill a lot of the body, close to the 40% black floor. Salt and swell both add lit cells, so they need different places (in the water vs over the rim) to stay separable.
cells.alt: Tide, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: The shore cut in elevation as one grid of square cells: hollow cells for rock, grey cells for water, and lit runs where the swell foams over the rim and glints in the pool

cells.subject: A surveyed plan of the rock pool: its rim as one bright outline open to the sea, depth contours ringing two basins, spot soundings, a tide mark and the swell fronts arriving through the mouth.
controls: swell: the arc fronts outside the mouth spread apart or crowd together, 3 to 8 visible (position and count).
depth: each basin gains contour rings inward, two to six, and the soundings deepen (count).
salt: the rim outline breaks from a smooth curve into crystalline straight facets (shape of the one mutable outline).
drift: the dotted tide mark slides off concentric and wanders inside the rim (position).
cells.risks: Plan view hides the vertical, so depth has to be read from contour count, not height; that's a convention, not something the eye gets for free. Soundings are body text that should move with depth, which the guidelines discourage (text on things that change); they may have to become fixed labels or go. Notes need a strike: a basin's contours brighten from the centre out, which is a shade change and needs a scale cue too. Contours are many closed outlines, budget must be checked.
cells.alt: Tide, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: A surveyed plan of the rock pool: its rim as one bright outline open to the sea, depth contours ringing two basins, spot soundings, a tide mark and the swell fronts arriving through the mouth

cells.subject: A patent section through the shore: the swell rolling in from the left, the rock rim it overtops, and the pool behind it drilled with three chambers of different depth, each ringing at its own pitch.
controls: swell: the incoming crests spread apart or bunch up along the sea, and the nearest one stands taller against the rim (position).
depth: the chamber floors drop, lengthening each chamber from shallow cups to deep shafts (shape of the rock outline).
salt: crystal facets appear along the chamber walls, a few to a dozen (count).
drift: the pool's water surface tilts and its patent water marks slide, as the pool sloshes off tune (shape/position of the surface).
cells.risks: Stretch outside the engine column. The exception is partial: tide's sound is a capture rule (only the noise that reaches the pool, and only at its tuned frequencies, survives), so the rim-as-threshold is honest. But P13's power in meikyu was that every visual change is a decision the player is making about what gets in; here swell is a period, not a threshold, so the rim does nothing a control moves. Honestly it is a P1 section drawing wearing P13's argument. The hatching is static but dense (7 px), and the numerals are decoration unless they stay few.
cells.alt: Tide, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: A patent section through the shore: the swell rolling in from the left, the rock rim it overtops, and the pool behind it drilled with three chambers of different depth, each ringing at its own pitch

cells.subject: One tuned hollow of the pool, large and running off the frame's bottom edge, exploded: its body of water lifted out on the cup's axis, the inlet stone drawn out of the lip's notch, and the swell's tongue entering from the left edge along the same line.
controls: swell: the crest lines across the swell's tongue at the left edge spread apart or crowd together, about eight across it at 0.25 s and two at 8 s (position).
depth: the cup's floor drops, its far-wall meridians lengthening from a shallow saucer to a deep basin (shape of the cup, floor moves over 30 px).
salt: the standing-wave crests across the lifted water go from evenly spaced to stretched toward the rim (position of the crest lines).
drift: the lifted water slides off the cup's axis, out of register with the hollow it came from, up to about 30 px (position of the lens node).
cells.risks: An exploded view of a cup and a disc can read as a product drawing rather than a rock pool; the rock is carried only by the notch stone and the shelf edge. Depth reshapes the cup's meridians (one mutable outline or pre-drawn steps). The lens lifted above the cup looks like a lid; a note's answer (the lens rippling, the crests brightening) needs designing so it reads as water.
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Tide, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: One tuned hollow of the pool, large and running off the frame's bottom edge, exploded: its body of water lifted out on the cup's axis, the inlet stone drawn out of the lip's notch, and the swell's tongue entering from the left edge along the same line

cells.subject: The tide itself running up a shore: the latest swash's lacy edge as the one bright line, the sea's swell lines beyond it, broken strand marks of earlier swashes, and a rock ledge of eight hollows the water has just filled.
controls: swell: the swell lines out on the sea spread apart or crowd together toward the shore (position).
depth: the strand marks of earlier swashes stay on the beach longer, one at 50 ms up to six at 5 s (count).
salt: the eight hollows' sizes spread from a harmonic series to a stretched one, the small ones shrinking hard (scale per hollow).
drift: the hollows slide off their places on the ledge, each its own way, up to about 24 px (position per hollow).
cells.risks: Single weight leaves value alone to set the hierarchy, so the frame is busy with many grey lines of equal width; the sea lines crowd the swash on the right. The ledge with hollows is small and reads as a pasted blob at 1:1. The swash edge is ~160 points (three paths) if it should move on notes.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Tide, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: The tide itself running up a shore: the latest swash's lacy edge as the one bright line, the sea's swell lines beyond it, broken strand marks of earlier swashes, and a rock ledge of eight hollows the water has just filled

cells.subject: The mechanism as eight stone pipes standing in an arc in the surge, each cut to a partial's length, so every wave that blows across their mouths rings a chord; the stone's turned-away sides are hatched and the fundamental's mouth is the brightest edge.
controls: swell: the surge crests on the water in front of the pipes spread apart or crowd together (position).
depth: the pool stands higher round the pipes, the waterline rising up every pipe, over 24 px (position of the waterline).
salt: the pipes' heights stretch from a harmonic ladder to an inharmonic one, the short pipes getting shorter (shape of the skyline; each pipe a node scaled or pre-drawn).
drift: each pipe leans its own small way about its foot, tops wandering up to ~25 px (rotation per pipe).
cells.risks: A row of graduated cylinders can read as a bar chart or organ pipes rather than a rock pool; the arc helps but it is still close. Hatching on eight pipes is static but dense (~60 hairlines). Salt changing pipe heights needs per-pipe pre-drawn variants or scaled nodes, and scaling would thicken the hatching.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Tide, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: The mechanism as eight stone pipes standing in an arc in the surge, each cut to a partial's length, so every wave that blows across their mouths rings a chord; the stone's turned-away sides are hatched and the fundamental's mouth is the brightest edge

cells.subject: Foam on the pool's surface seen at water level: a raft of bubbles in eight sizes, each ringing at the pitch its size sets, drawn as black domes lit only along their back edges, the largest the brightest.
controls: swell: the ripple lines running under the raft spread apart or crowd together (position).
depth: more bubbles survive in the raft, from 6 at 50 ms to 18 at 5 s (count).
salt: the bubble sizes stretch apart, the small ones shrinking toward the 3 px floor while the largest stays (scale per bubble, up to 1.6x).
drift: the bubbles jostle out of their packed places, each its own way, up to about 24 px (position per bubble).
cells.risks: A bubble's own resonance is real physics, but the link from foam to tuned hollows is a step the player must take; it could read as a bath or a drink. Bright crescents on black domes can tip toward moons if the arcs get too even. The upper half of the body is empty; the raft could sit higher or bigger.
cells.angle: the material the sound acts on, seen close
cells.alt: Tide, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: Foam on the pool's surface seen at water level: a raft of bubbles in eight sizes, each ringing at the pitch its size sets, drawn as black domes lit only along their back edges, the largest the brightest

cells.subject: One boulder at the sea's edge holding a pool in its worn top, drawn as detailed hidden-line facets, with the swell's fronts running in across the sea around it and the pool's water the brightest line.
controls: swell: the wave fronts on the sea spread apart or crowd together as they run in round the boulder (position).
depth: the pool's water sinks lower inside the rim, showing more of the inner wall, over about 20 px (position of the water ring).
salt: a band of salt crust spreads up the boulder's flank above the waterline, drawn as 45-degree hatching (hatched area).
drift: the pool's water ring tips and slides off centre inside the rim (shape of one mutable outline).
cells.risks: The pool is small on the boulder's top and reads partly as a collar; it needs to grow or the camera to rise. A single pool shows one hollow, not eight resonators. Depth moves the water ring only ~15-20 px at this scale, close to the floor. The facets are 40-odd hairlines; static, but count them against the node budget.

cells.alt: Tide, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: One boulder at the sea's edge holding a pool in its worn top, drawn as detailed hidden-line facets, with the swell's fronts running in across the sea around it and the pool's water the brightest line

machines.name: Vapor
machines.description: A breathy formant voice: a glottal pulse through a throat tube and vowel formants, gliding between vowels.
machines.concept: A breathy formant voice: a glottal pulse through a throat tube and vowel formants, gliding between vowels.
machines.soundsLike: A soft sung vowel with air in it, from a hushed whisper to a clear pulsed tone. Each note opens out of a closed "oo" into its vowel, so phrases sound sung rather than switched on.

intake.subject: a breathy voice is a pulse of air shaped by a tube into a vowel, so the screen is that shaping: the tube, the vowel it makes, or the wave that comes out (five candidates in section 3; the pick is the owner's).
intake.controlSource: new (the DSP I'm writing; no port)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings.

scores.effect: F1/F2 sweep through five vowels; the most obvious change the voice has
pure pulse to near-whisper; loudness of the noise and loss of pitch clarity, strong across the whole range
child-small to giant-large voice; every formant moves by an octave across the range
at 5 ms each note simply starts on its vowel; from ~50 ms an audible "w"-like onset, at 2 s a slow diphthong. Only heard at note starts and vowel moves
