cells.subject: A field of square cells laid over the vowel chart, where a bright clump of lit cells sits on the sung vowel and grey breath hangs round it.
controls: vowel: position, the bright clump moves across the field to the vowel's place on the chart (front left, back right, close top, open bottom), up to ~300 px of travel from u to i.
breath: count, grey haze cells in runs of 2-3 gather round the clump, from none at 0 to ~28 cells at 100.
throat: count, the number of lit cells in the clump grows from 4 at 0.75 to ~16 at 1.50, a bigger tract making a bigger, lower mass.
glide: count, a trail of mid-grey cells runs from the closed u corner toward the clump, 0 cells at 5 ms to the full route (~10) at 2 s.
cells.risks: P15 is for sounds that are texture; vapor has a mechanism (pulse through a tube), so Gate 0 argues for drawing the mechanism instead, and the cell field earns its place only because breath really is noise. Typeset diagram wants the five vowel letters in the field, which P15's no-text rule forbids; I kept five 12 px letters as the chart and would defend them as the only labels. Breath and throat both change a count of cells; they differ by value (grey haze vs bright clump) and placement, which is close to a grey-only difference, so throat may need a second cue. A vowel move relights ~25 cells at once, over the ~20 changed nodes/frame guide during a turn. At rest the field is mostly empty dots, so it can read as a screensaver.
cells.alt: Vapor, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A field of square cells laid over the vowel chart, where a bright clump of lit cells sits on the sung vowel and grey breath hangs round it

cells.subject: The throat drawn in elevation as a segmented acoustic tube from glottis to lips, its sections widening and narrowing into the shape of the vowel.
controls: vowel: shape, the sixteen section radii re-profile the tube (one mutable outline): a pinch at the back and a flared mouth for a, a front constriction for i, a closed lip end for u; points move up to ~30 px.
breath: count, short turbulence streaks gather inside the tube just past the glottis, from none at 0 to ~20 at 100.
throat: scale, the whole tube grows uniformly about the glottis from 0.75 to 1.50 (2x) and the dimension line under it reads the length in cm.
glide: count, hairline ghost profiles between the closed u onset and the vowel step in behind the tube, from none at 5 ms to ~6 at 2 s.
cells.risks: Mutable outlines must stay within +/-64 px of the node, so the 240 px tube needs authoring at half size and a node scale of ~1.33 at default, which ties tube width to length (fine physically, a bigger throat). Glide's ghost profiles sit 2-4 px from the subject outline in places and start to read as hatching; they may need to step outward or show only the onset. Breath streaks are small and inside the tube, so breath (scored 4) is under-drawn here; it may need streaks out of the lips too. The dimension label is the only text that changes, and it would need a text slot.
cells.alt: Vapor, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The throat drawn in elevation as a segmented acoustic tube from glottis to lips, its sections widening and narrowing into the shape of the vowel

cells.subject: A survey split in two: the vowel quadrilateral plotted as a parcel with five stations and a traverse to the sung vowel on the left, and the voice's spectral profile drawn as a long section on the right.
controls: vowel: position and shape, the bright station moves between the five plotted vowels on the plan (~150 px) and the formant peaks of the profile walk along the frequency datum.
breath: position, the ground line of aspiration noise under the profile rises from the datum at 0 to ~40 px up at 100, filling the valleys between formants.
throat: scale, the whole plan grows about its low-formant corner from 0.75 to 1.50 as a longer tube lowers every formant, and the profile's peaks shift left with it.
glide: count, chainage ticks along the traverse from the u onset station to the vowel, 0 at 5 ms to ~14 at 2 s.
cells.risks: Two halves split the eye: the profile is the brightest element, but the moving station competes, and with knobs 1-2 driving both halves the P2 column match (structure on 1-2, tone on 3-4) doesn't hold: vowel and breath land right, throat and glide land left. Vowel and throat both move the profile's peaks, so the profile must leave throat's effect to the plan's scale and treat its own shift as secondary. Survey symbols (triangles, a ringed station) risk looking like icons; they must stay hairline and small. Labels (stations, axes, 'plan', 'section') are many for one screen.
cells.alt: Vapor, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A survey split in two: the vowel quadrilateral plotted as a parcel with five stations and a traverse to the sung vowel on the left, and the voice's spectral profile drawn as a long section on the right

cells.subject: The pressure wave at the lips drawn as a patent figure, four glottal periods ringing with the vowel, the early ones still gliding out of a closed u, and the aspiration noise traced beneath with numbered leaders.
controls: vowel: shape, the ringing inside each bright period changes, slow single swings for u and o, a fast double ring for e and i, peaks moving up to ~30 px.
breath: shape, the lower aspiration trace swells from a flat line at 0 to bursts of +/-20 px at every glottal opening at 100.
throat: scale, the main trace grows uniformly about its left end from 0.75 to 1.50, so each ring is longer and the swing taller, as a bigger tract rings lower and louder.
glide: count, how many of the four periods are grey ghosts still moving from u into the vowel, 0 at 5 ms to all but the last at 2 s.
cells.risks: P3's own pitfall: it drifts toward 'oscilloscope'; the patent numerals and the ghosted onset are what keep it a drawing, and the numerals (10/12/14/16) mean nothing to a player without the legend a patent has. A four-period trace is ~240 points, so as a bound subject it needs four mutable outlines, the whole path budget; each period becomes one path and the ghost/solid change is a re-key. Glide is shown as a count of four, under the 12-item floor; it needs the ghost periods to move (shape) as well as change grey to pass perceptibility. Throat scale grows the trace upward toward the header at 1.50; the axis must sit lower.
cells.alt: Vapor, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The pressure wave at the lips drawn as a patent figure, four glottal periods ringing with the vowel, the early ones still gliding out of a closed u, and the aspiration noise traced beneath with numbered leaders

cells.subject: Five vowel resonators stacked into a tower on a narrow throat neck, like the short pipes of a vox humana organ stop, with the sung vowel's chamber standing out solid and breath rising off the top in rings.
controls: vowel: shade and position, the sung chamber fills dark with a bright edge while the others stay hidden-line; moving from u (base) to i (top) walks the solid chamber ~90 px up the tower.
breath: count, rings rise off the top chamber in the same projection, 0 at 0 to ~10 at 100.
throat: position, the neck between the glottal boot and the chambers lengthens from ~26 px at 0.75 to ~52 px at 1.50, lifting the whole stack.
glide: count and shade, the chambers between u and the sung vowel light their edges one by one, the route the onset glides along, none at 5 ms to all of them at 2 s.
cells.risks: Stretch, and plainly a poor fit. P11 works when the player already knows the instrument by sight and the note picks the part; here nobody recognises a vowel resonator stack (the vox humana is real but obscure), and the vowel knob, not the note, picks the chamber, so the tower is an invented diagram dressed as an instrument. The exception case would be that vowel really is a selection among a few named resonances, but vapor's vowel is a continuum and the stack can only show nine enum steps as five tiers. It also sits close to theseus's tower in silhouette, which risks reading as a copy of another machine's drawing. Glide on a five-tier count is under the 12-item floor.
cells.alt: Vapor, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: Five vowel resonators stacked into a tower on a narrow throat neck, like the short pipes of a vox humana organ stop, with the sung vowel's chamber standing out solid and breath rising off the top in rings

cells.subject: A speaking machine pulled apart along its air axis: wedge bellows, reed block, telescoping throat tube, flared horn and a lip iris whose bright aperture is the vowel.
controls: vowel: shape, the lip iris's bright aperture goes from a small round hole (u) through a wide open mouth (a) to a wide flat slit (i), its rim moving well over 16 px.
breath: rotation, the bellows boards swing open about their hinge from 6° to 40° and the leather folds fan out between them.
throat: position, the three tube sections draw out along the axis, pushing the horn and iris about 40 px further from the reed between 0.75 and 1.50.
glide: count, the spring that pulls the iris back to a closed oo winds from 3 coils at 5 ms to 15 at 2 s, a softer spring for a slower opening.
cells.risks: Six parts on one axis is busy, and at 1:1 the reed block and spring are only ~25 px. The speaking machine is a historical object (Kempelen's) most players won't name, though bellows into horn reads as a wind machine that makes a voice. The iris is seen at an angle, so the vowel aperture is an ellipse and u/a/i must stay distinct through foreshortening. Glide as spring coils is a metaphor (stiffness for time) and the coil count is small and at the frame's edge.
cells.angle: the machine's own rule as a physical thing: what turning each knob would do to a real object
cells.alt: Vapor, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: A speaking machine pulled apart along its air axis: wedge bellows, reed block, telescoping throat tube, flared horn and a lip iris whose bright aperture is the vowel

cells.subject: A singer's head cut down the middle mid-note: the tongue's bright dome shaping the vowel under the palate, the larynx low in the throat and breath rising through the airway.
controls: vowel: shape, the tongue's bright dome moves from high at the back (u) through low and flat (a) to high at the front (i), its crest travelling about 30 px while the jaw and lips follow.
breath: count, short dashes of air along the airway from the trachea through the folds to the lips, 4 at 0 to 24 at 100.
throat: position, the larynx (thyroid outline and the vocal folds across the airway) slides 30 px down the throat as the tract lengthens.
glide: shape, a hatched sweep between the tongue and the oo tongue each note opens from, none at 5 ms and the whole sweep back to u at 2 s.
cells.risks: A sagittal head section is the phonetics textbook figure, so it can tip into diagram; it has to stay a drawing with no labels. Single weight leaves hierarchy to grey, apart from the tongue's 2 px line. At vowel a the glide hatch is a thin band. Anatomy can read clinical rather than musical.
cells.angle: a cutaway of the object at work, so the inside explains it
cells.alt: Vapor, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: A singer's head cut down the middle mid-note: the tongue's bright dome shaping the vowel under the palate, the larynx low in the throat and breath rising through the airway

cells.subject: A sung breath fogged onto a cold window pane, a hatched mass of condensation in the mouth's shape with drops running down from it to the glazing bar.
controls: vowel: shape, the fog's dense core goes from a small round patch (u) to a tall open oval (a) to a wide flat ellipse (i).
breath: scale of the halo only, the sparse outer fog spreads from 1.2× to 2.1× the core while the core stays put.
throat: position, the whole patch sits about 30 px higher on the glass as the throat lengthens (a bigger singer, a mouth higher on the pane).
glide: count, drops gather and run from the bottom of the fog, 2 at 5 ms to 14 at 2 s, each a trail ending in a solid bead.
cells.risks: Throat as height on the glass is the weakest mapping of the pass: physical in a story, arbitrary in the sound. A hatched blob needs the window bars to read as fog on glass; without them it's a texture. Many 45° hairlines are costly as nodes and the core's 3 px spacing is at the hatching floor.
cells.angle: the mark or trace the process leaves behind
cells.alt: Vapor, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: A sung breath fogged onto a cold window pane, a hatched mass of condensation in the mouth's shape with drops running down from it to the glazing bar

cells.subject: A singer's lips and jaw at the left edge as a black silhouette lit along its rim, and the breath leaving them into cold air across the frame.
controls: vowel: shape, the rim-lit lips and jaw round and push forward for u, drop open for a and spread for i, the chin moving about 16 px, and the stream's mouth widens with them.
breath: count, billows along the plume's edge from 2 at 0 to 16 at 100, each with a fold line under it.
throat: position, the larynx bump on the neck's rim slides 26 px down toward the bottom edge.
glide: shape, the breath leaves the lips as a narrow round oo stream that holds for 12 px at 5 ms up to 160 px at 2 s before the plume opens.
cells.risks: A human profile can slide toward illustration or icon; it stays a single rim line with no eye or features. The plume is a large hatched area to redraw on a note. Throat lives in a small corner of the frame at the bottom edge, and vowel's lip change is about 16 px, right at the shape floor.
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Vapor, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: A singer's lips and jaw at the left edge as a black silhouette lit along its rim, and the breath leaving them into cold air across the frame

cells.subject: Vapour itself: a ring of breath rising through cold air, modelled as a torus with its rolling flow drawn in hidden-line hairlines, a smaller oo ring following below.
controls: vowel: shape, the ring's plan follows the lips it left: small and round for u, wide for a, flattened and spread for i, the rim travelling about 30 px.
breath: count, wisps peel off the ring's top and trail back, 2 at 0 to 14 at 100.
throat: shape, the ring's core thickens from 14 to 34 units as the throat lengthens, a fatter, slower roll for a lower voice.
glide: position, the small hatched oo ring the note opened from rises up the wake behind the main ring, about 60 px over the range.
cells.risks: A torus can read as a doughnut, a tyre or a lampshade rather than a vapour ring; the wake and the second ring carry the reading. Vowel (plan) and throat (core) both change the ring's size, in different directions, which may blur at a glance. Poloidal hairlines bunch under 3 px near the ring's sides, and the projected sections are many nodes.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Vapor, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: Vapour itself: a ring of breath rising through cold air, modelled as a torus with its rolling flow drawn in hidden-line hairlines, a smaller oo ring following below

machines.name: Bell
machines.description: A compressor as a diving bell: depth is the threshold, the air pocket is the release, the knee is how the bell settles.
machines.concept: A compressor as a diving bell: depth is the threshold, the air pocket is the release, the knee is how the bell settles.
machines.soundsLike: A feed-forward peak compressor on the send: at its default it gently holds the loudest hits down by a few dB and lifts the rest back up, so the return sounds denser and steadier than the dry track. Deep and short it pumps audibly with the beat; shallow, soft and slow it glues the send without being heard as an effect.

intake.subject: a diving bell lowered on its cable, whose depth below the surface is the threshold, whose trapped air pocket is the release, and whose way of settling is the knee, with the signal it presses drawn from the compressor's own model.
intake.controlSource: new
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 1 warning. `resources.display` is a placeholder until phase 4.

ranking.note: keeps the bell as the subject and explains what it does; push fig. 1 to carry more weight (bigger bell, gain on the cable or surface) so the trace doesn't win.
the truest image of compression; needs more height and a bell of some kind or it's a scope with a camera.
the most beautiful and the calmest, but a diagram of the knobs.
clearest explanation of the curve, but too close to a meter.
doesn't fit; keep only as a mascot if the owner wants one.

pick.reason: Refine pick 1, with variations focused on the bell shape and its interaction; drop the signal visualization.

02-revision.focus: Refine v1: the bell's own shape and how each control changes it; no signal or waveform visualization; no text in the drawing.

directions.emphasis: brightest element at the sound source
brightest element where the note lands
brightest element on the most-played control's part

ranking.note: the closest refinement of the pick, and it shows all four controls on the bell itself.
clearest at 1:1, but the hammer and sounding line add parts beside the bell.
the freshest view of the bell, but gain is weak.
strong 3D and gradient, but gain-as-scale is the weakest mapping.
the ring mode is lovely, but the plan view hides the pocket and leans toward a target.

pick.reason: Owner likes v5; remove the hatched background and think about simple environmental grounding.

cells.subject: A patent plate in two figures: the bell in section hanging on its cable under the surface line, water risen inside it to the air pocket, beside the reference passage's output trace pressed down from its grey input.
controls: depth: the bell is lowered on its cable, crown 58 to 130 px below the surface (position), and the threshold dashes in fig. 2 close in on the trace as its crests are pressed lower (shape).

air: the waterline inside the bell drops as the air pocket grows from 35 % to 90 % of the bell (position of the waterline), and in fig. 2 the trace's recovery tail after each hit stretches (shape, same path as depth, so the waterline is the primary).
knee: the bell's shoulders go from a hard corner to a full round crown, shoulder radius 4 to about 30 px (shape of the wall in section).
gain: fig. 2's output trace scales about its centre line, x1 to x16 clipped at the frame of the figure (scale).
cells.risks: P2 splits the body into two half-size pictures, and the bright trace, not the bell, is where the eye lands; the bell is secondary in its own screen. Depth and air both reshape the fig. 2 trace, so their primaries must be the bell's position and the waterline or two knobs read as one. Gain has no part in fig. 1 (a bell has no makeup), so fig. 1 is three controls and fig. 2 is the fourth plus echoes. The trace is the model on a fixed four-hit passage, not the live signal: an effect page gets the slots, not the audio. Patent numerals (10, 12) and fig. captions are four labels; legible at 10 px #7D7D7D but they add up.
cells.alt: Bell, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A patent plate in two figures: the bell in section hanging on its cable under the surface line, water risen inside it to the air pocket, beside the reference passage's output trace pressed down from its grey input

cells.subject: The output envelope of a fixed four-hit passage extruded into a wall in hidden-line isometric, standing on a makeup plinth with its crests pressed down through a water plane, the unpressed input wall standing grey behind it.
controls: depth: the water plane drops down the wall from 0 to -48 dB (position, about 62 world px), and every crest that crosses it is pressed flatter (shape of the bright front face).
air: the slope of the wall after each crest, from a sheer drop back to the input at 20 ms to a long ramp that never recovers between hits at 2 s (shape; the primary for the front face).
knee: two dashed planes open either side of the water plane, 0 to 24 dB apart (position of the band edges), the crests rounding into it.
gain: the plinth under the wall grows from 0 to 24 dB tall and carries the wall and its water plane up with it (position of the whole wall).
cells.risks: P3's own pitfall: an extruded envelope is still an oscilloscope with a camera on it, and nothing in it is a bell except the water plane. Depth and air both reshape the bright front face, which breaks one-channel-per-part unless depth's primary is the plane's position and the crest change is read as consequence. The wall's height is only about 50 px at 1:1 to keep the far corner of the plane out of the header; a taller crest pushes the scene into y 0-20. The front face is one 60-point outline re-keyed on depth, air and knee turns, fine at rest but it's the whole path budget. Like every variant, it's the model on a fixed passage: no live audio on an effect page.
cells.alt: Bell, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The output envelope of a fixed four-hit passage extruded into a wall in hidden-line isometric, standing on a makeup plinth with its crests pressed down through a water plane, the unpressed input wall standing grey behind it

cells.subject: A star atlas of the water column: depth strata stacked as chart plates every 8 dB, receding down and right, with the bell plotted as a body on the plate at its depth, its lit phase the air pocket and its ephemeris track running down from the surface.
controls: depth: the body moves down the stack from plate 0 to plate 48, 26 px right and 20 px down per 8 dB (position), and the plate below it brightens (shade as second cue).
air: the body's phase: the lit air cap above a flat waterline grows from 35 % to 90 % of the disc (shape of the lit part).
knee: the ephemeris track's approach, from a straight drop that stops dead at a hard knee to a long easing curve that settles onto the plate at 24 dB (shape of the track).
gain: the body's magnitude, radius 13 to 26 px, the way an atlas sizes a bright star (scale).
cells.risks: P4 is for things the sound moves through; here it's the threshold setting moving through depth, not the audio, so the stack is a scale, not a set of frames. Seven plates at 20 px steps overlap heavily: plates read as a stack at 1:1, but their tick borders are close to hatching. A disc with a flat waterline sits one step from a 'level indicator' icon; the atlas labels (plate depths, the body's name) and the ephemeris track are what keep it authored. Nothing shows the signal at all: it's a picture of the settings, which ux.md allows but which makes it the most 'diagram of knobs' of the five. Gain as magnitude is a metaphor only (a bell doesn't get louder by being bigger).
cells.alt: Bell, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A star atlas of the water column: depth strata stacked as chart plates every 8 dB, receding down and right, with the bell plotted as a body on the plate at its depth, its lit phase the air pocket and its ephemeris track running down from the surface

cells.subject: A field of identical air columns in engineering elevation, one per input level from -42 to 0 dB, each standing as tall as the bell lets that level out, so the row of crowns is the compressor's transfer curve built from parts, with a second dashed crown in each showing where it still sits 50 ms after the level falls.
controls: depth: the threshold line slides left across the field from x about 420 at 0 dB to past its left edge at -48 dB (position), and every column right of it is pressed down and its crown turns bright (shape of the field, shade as second cue).
air: the dashed second crowns inside the pressed columns sink lower as the air refills more slowly, about 0 to 30 px below the crown (position of 22 marks).
knee: the dashed tolerance band either side of the threshold opens from 0 to about 200 px wide, and the crowns inside it round from a sharp corner to a smooth bend (position of the band edges).
gain: the datum the whole field stands on rises 0 to 60 px with the makeup, dimensioned at the left (position of the field).
cells.risks: It's the transfer curve drawn as bars, which is one step from a level meter or a bar chart, the dashboard the protocol rejects; the schematic furniture (datum, dimensions, tolerance band) is what argues against that, and it may not be enough at 1:1. The dashed second crowns are 9 px marks inside 11 px columns and barely read at 1:1; air needs a stronger channel. 22 columns x 2 nodes is 44 nodes, cheap, but a depth turn redraws most of them at once. At gain x16 the tallest crowns reach y 25, right under the header; the scale needs a ceiling. Static: the field is the curve, so nothing in it reacts to the audio (there's no audio on an effect page anyway).
cells.alt: Bell, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: A field of identical air columns in engineering elevation, one per input level from -42 to 0 dB, each standing as tall as the bell lets that level out, so the row of crowns is the compressor's transfer curve built from parts, with a second dashed crown in each showing where it still sits 50 ms after the level falls

cells.subject: A diver traced in one scope beam, crouched on the stage under a diving bell drawn on the second channel, his helmet in the air pocket, the water line pressing down from the rim and air escaping as dots past the bell's lip.
controls: depth: the bell and its stage are lowered on the cable, crown 54 to 112 px (position of channel 2 and the diver with it).
air: the water line inside the bell drops as the air pocket grows, and the dots of escaping air thin from 14 to 2 as the bell holds its air longer (count).
knee: the diver's knees bend from locked straight (hard knee) to a deep crouch (soft knee), 15 to 75 degrees at the knee joint (rotation of the shins and thighs).
gain: the whole trace, bell and diver, scales about the stage, x1 to x2 (scale).
cells.risks: Stretch, and it doesn't really fit. A compressor has no performer; the only figure the metaphor offers is the bell's occupant, and a diver doesn't do anything a compressor does. Knee as the diver's crouch is a pun on the word, not the sound. The exception would be that a diving bell is person-scale, so a figure gives the screen a size and a body under pressure; that's mood, not mapping. At 1:1 the stick figure reads as clip art, exactly the failure the P6 caution names (toro's bulls), and the scope language makes it look like a vector-display toy. Recommend dropping it unless the owner wants a mascot.
cells.alt: Bell, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: A diver traced in one scope beam, crouched on the stage under a diving bell drawn on the second channel, his helmet in the air pocket, the water line pressing down from the rim and air escaping as dots past the bell's lip

cells.subject: The bell centred in front elevation with its front-right quarter cut away, so the air pocket, the hatched water below it and the clapper hanging inside show, on its cable under one surface line.
controls: depth: the bell is lowered on its cable, crown from just under the surface line to about 70 px below it (position).
air: the waterline inside drops as the air pocket grows from a third to nine tenths of the bell, and the hatched water in the cut shrinks with it (position + hatched area).
knee: the shoulder between crown and wall goes from a hard corner to a full round crown, fillet radius about 2 to 40 px, in the silhouette, the cut wall and every hoop (shape).
gain: the clapper swings out toward the cut, from hanging (4 degrees) to 34 degrees, its travel a dashed hairline arc (rotation); the bright ball is the sound source.
cells.risks: The cutaway adds three hatch fields (wall cut, water cut, and the rear interior seen through) inside a 150 px bell: at 1:1 the wall hatching is only 2-3 lines and could read as a grey band. Gain as a clapper's swing angle is a metaphor for loudness, not makeup gain; a resting drawing that shows a swung clapper must stay still at rest. The quarter cut is a fixed drawing; on device every visible run is redrawn when knee or depth change.
cells.alt: Bell, pass 2 (revision), variant 1: The bell centred in front elevation with its front-right quarter cut away, so the air pocket, the hatched water below it and the clapper hanging inside show, on its cable under one surface line

cells.subject: Looking steeply down through the water at the bell below: a black cut-out in a hatched field, its hidden waterline dashed through the shell and its rim drawn in the ring mode it sounds with.
controls: depth: the bell sinks away from the camera, so it shrinks and drops toward the bottom of the field (size from distance, about 1.7x, plus position).
air: the dashed waterline ring, seen through the shell, slides up or down the bell and widens or narrows with it (position + shape).
knee: the crown's flat top shrinks into a rounded shoulder, so the top hoops close in and the outline rounds (shape).
gain: the rim's oval ring mode about the round rim grows from barely off-round to a strong four-node flex (shape, about 20 px at the extremes); it's the brightest line.
cells.risks: Seen from above, the air pocket is inside an opaque shell, so the waterline is a hidden-line convention the player must learn. The hatched field is all water texture; with the bell small at full depth, the subject could become a dark hole in a grey pattern. Ring-mode oval is a physical picture of ringing but static at rest; it must not move while idle.
cells.alt: Bell, pass 2 (revision), variant 2: Looking steeply down through the water at the bell below: a black cut-out in a hatched field, its hidden waterline dashed through the shell and its rim drawn in the ring mode it sounds with

cells.subject: The bell cut in section on its cable, its parts under their own columns: a sounding line for depth, the air pocket over hatched water, the shoulder's fillet construction, and a hammer drawn back from the sound-bow.
controls: depth: the bell is lowered, and the sounding line in column 1 pays out with it, its lead weight dropping level with the rim (position).
air: the waterline across the section drops as the pocket grows, the hatched water cut below it shrinking (position + hatched area).
knee: the shoulder fillet in column 3 grows from a hard corner to a full round crown; its centre mark and radius lines move with it (shape).
gain: the hammer in column 4 is drawn back from the sound-bow, from 6 to 46 degrees, its swing a dashed arc (rotation); the struck face of the bow is the brightest line.
cells.risks: Column-affine puts four parts in four columns, which edges toward a panel; the sounding line and hammer are additions beside the bell, not the bell itself. The fillet construction lines are drafting marks that could read as decoration. A pure section is the closest to v1 of the five and the least 3D.
cells.alt: Bell, pass 2 (revision), variant 3: The bell cut in section on its cable, its parts under their own columns: a sounding line for depth, the air pocket over hatched water, the shoulder's fillet construction, and a hammer drawn back from the sound-bow

cells.subject: The bell in three-quarter isometric, off to the right below a diagonal surface edge, in water whose hatching closes up with depth, its waterline a dashed hidden ring and its shoulder the bright hoop.
controls: depth: the bell sinks into denser hatching, from the open top bands to the close bottom ones (position + the gradient it sits in).
air: the dashed hidden waterline ring slides along the bell (position + shape).
knee: the bright shoulder hoop moves inward and down as the crown rounds, and the outline softens (shape).
gain: the whole bell grows, x0.80 to x1.32 about its crown (scale).
cells.risks: Four hatch densities are four nested bands of grey value; spaced 11 to 4.5 px they stay line, not tint, but the 4.5 px band is near the limit. Gain as scale reads as 'bigger', not 'louder', and fights the gradient for what depth means. The surface edge diagonal is a projected world line, so it can't move with depth.
cells.alt: Bell, pass 2 (revision), variant 4: The bell in three-quarter isometric, off to the right below a diagonal surface edge, in water whose hatching closes up with depth, its waterline a dashed hidden ring and its shoulder the bright hoop

cells.subject: Looking up into the bell's mouth from below, the bell large in a full-bleed hatched field: inside, the water's surface and the clapper hanging over it; the rim bright.
controls: depth: the bell comes down toward the camera, so it grows and lowers in the frame (size from distance, about 1.3x, plus position); the bright rim leads.
air: the waterline ellipse inside the mouth moves up into the bell or down toward the rim as the pocket grows and shrinks, its hatched water with it (position + area).
knee: the crown's shoulder rounds in the silhouette above the rim (shape).
gain: the clapper's ball grows, x0.7 to x1.3 (scale).
cells.risks: Seen from below, the inside reads only if the mouth is open enough; at full depth the bell fills much of the field. Full-bleed hatching lowers the black share. The clapper hangs on the axis, so gain's change is concentrated in a small spot near the centre; it may miss the 40 px spread floor.
cells.alt: Bell, pass 2 (revision), variant 5: Looking up into the bell's mouth from below, the bell large in a full-bleed hatched field: inside, the water's surface and the clapper hanging over it; the rim bright

sheets.alt: Bell contact sheet: rest, playing and every control at 0, 50 and 100

machines.description: Multi-tap echo shaped by canyon walls: the distance sets the delay, walls set the tap count, rock absorbs highs, wind modulates.
machines.concept: Multi-tap echo shaped by canyon walls: the distance sets the delay, walls set the tap count, rock absorbs highs, wind modulates.
machines.soundsLike: A multi-tap echo whose taps arrive evenly spaced, each one lower and darker than the one before, like a shout coming back off successive canyon walls. Close walls give a slap or a metallic flutter; far walls give slow, separate repeats, and wind makes them waver like a tape echo in a gust.

intake.subject: a shout thrown into a canyon and the train of echoes its walls send back, each one later, quieter and duller than the last.
intake.controlSource: new
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings (two notes: effects have no browser preview yet; effect resources not reviewed beyond structure). `resources.display` is a placeholder (1 path × 64 points, 96 nodes, 8 palette entries) until phase 4.

one slap-back to a long tail of twelve taps; strong at the low end (1 → 4), less from 6 → 12 as late taps are quiet and dark
taps go from as bright as the source to a dull thud after the second wall; clear on bright material, mild on bass
subtle waver below ~40, an audible seasick chorus on the taps above 70

ranking.note: the strongest single scene, every control physical, most authored.
the most self-explaining mapping, at the risk of reading as a meter.
the most original composition, but the plan view needs its labels to read as a canyon.
clean and clear, but split into picture plus dashboard, and a stretch.
wrong pattern for a machine with a mechanism, and the heaviest budget.

cells.subject: A section cut across the canyon, charted like a sky atlas: the two rock walls are the dark limb, a hairline graticule fills the gap, and each echo is plotted as a lettered star of falling magnitude on a constellation line zig-zagging up from the shout.
controls: distance: position; the walls draw apart, the floor from 100 px to 300 px wide, and the constellation's segments stretch with them.
walls: count; more stars are plotted up the chain, a to l, alternating walls, each one higher.
absorb: scale; the stars' magnitudes fall faster bounce by bounce, the later discs shrinking from ~11 px to ~4 px, as the highs die in the rock.
wind: position; each star slides along its own short proper-motion track, up to about 16 px, so the constellation line kinks.
risks: The star atlas is a borrowed language for rock; the graticule may read as decoration rather than as the space inside the canyon.
Twelve stars between the walls get dense at short distance (narrow canyon); lettering has to drop to every other star.
Distance moves the walls, and wind moves the stars: both are position, on different parts; the walls' move must stay much bigger.
Section drawing (P1) wants a part that moves physically; here the walls are fixed for a given distance and nothing physical answers audio except the stars. Audio flare must be on the stars.
Wall rims at width 100 % reach the screen edges; check the extremes for crowding at the sides.

cells.subject: A survey plan of the gorge from above: each reflecting wall is a contoured rock bench, stacked back up a dashed chainage line from the station at the mouth, the nearest bench bright.
controls: distance: position; the benches spread apart along the chainage, 14 px to 54 px per bench (about 160 px of travel at the back of a six-bench stack), and the chainage labels read the metres to each wall.
walls: count; benches step in from 1 to 12 along the line, eased in one by one; past six the extra walls fold behind the last bench and the header carries the real count.

absorb: shape; the bench rims go from jagged rock to smooth, compounding back up the stack, so the far walls are rounded first (the bright front rim is one mutable outline, the rest pre-drawn variants).
wind: rotation; each bench swings about its own centre by a fixed seeded angle, up to about ±18°, so the stack loses its alignment the way modulation smears the tap times.
risks: P4 caps visible layers at 5-6 and walls reach 12; the fold-behind rule has to read, or the top of the range looks like it does nothing.
Absorb's serration change is a few pixels at the rim: it will struggle to reach a score-3 area floor without a second cue (shade down the stack).
Distance and walls both change how far the stack reaches; distance is spacing, walls is count, but at 1:1 they may read alike.
Benches seen from above look like stacked plates or cushions more than canyon walls; the plan needs the chainage labels to explain it.
Rotation of every bench while wind turns redraws up to 12 nodes per frame, fine, but rock outlines with 60 points each cost path budget if more than one is mutable.
cells.alt: Canyon, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A survey plan of the gorge from above: each reflecting wall is a contoured rock bench, stacked back up a dashed chainage line from the station at the mouth, the nearest bench bright

cells.subject: Fig. 1 of a patent: the echo's impulse response cut in longitudinal section as a row of identical hatched rock columns on a section line, each tap rising as a peak, with reference numerals 10, 12, 14.
controls: distance: shape (heights); the peaks spread apart along the row: at 0 the first peak sits in the first column with the rest packed behind it, at 100 it has walked off the far end of the 1.3 s row (about 380 px of travel).
walls: shape (heights); peaks rise one by one along the row, 1 to 12 of them, each lower than the last.
absorb: shape (heights); each peak slumps and broadens into its neighbours, the later ones most, so a hard-rock echo is a row of needles and a soft one is low rolling scree.
wind: position; every column's height jitters by a seeded amount and the peaks drift a column either way, so the clean comb turns ragged.
risks: Three of four controls are all 'heights'; P10 allows that, but distance (spacing), walls (count) and absorb (width) have to stay distinct at 1:1 or two of them read as the same knob.
At distance 0 (40 ms) twelve taps pile into the first few columns; the field reads as one lump and walls appears dead at the short end.
Hatching at 5 px inside 10 px columns is near the 3 px floor once the columns are short; drop hatching under 8 px.
It is close to a bar meter: the patent numerals and section ground are what keep it from reading as a dashboard; if they go, it fails.
Wind as position on the same columns overlaps the shape controls; it needs its own look (a shimmer that only exists while audio passes) to stay separate.
cells.alt: Canyon, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: Fig

cells.subject: The canyon floor as a hidden-line isometric grid of cells, where every returning echo front lights a ring of raised blocks out from the shout's block, the nearest ring brightest and the far rings sinking into grey tiles.
controls: distance: position; the rings widen apart, 1.2 to 4.8 cells between fronts, so the lit arcs sweep out across the floor from the source block.
walls: count; more rings light, 1 to 12, until the floor is combed with arcs (rings past the grid's edge are lost, so the count tops out visibly near 5-6).
absorb: count (raised vs grey layer); in each later ring more raised blocks drop to flat grey tiles, so at 100 only the first ring stands.
wind: position; each ring's cells shift outward or inward by a seeded amount per row, breaking the clean arcs into staggered runs, as if the front was blown.
risks: P15 is for noise-like sounds with no mechanism; an echo has a clear mechanism, so this is the texture of the echo, not its cause. Gate 0 says that is the weaker choice.
Hidden-line cubes on an isometric grid sit close to toro's field in look; the difference (all-wire, rings not heights) must stay obvious.
Rings are a target shape; on a cell grid they read as arcs, but at long distance with few walls the screen is mostly empty floor.
14 × 9 = 126 cells at 3 nodes per raised block is over 200 nodes before anything moves; needs sdk 1.8 or bigger cells.
Walls past ~6 run off the grid, so the top of the range only changes the header.

cells.subject: An engineering elevation of the two canyon walls dimensioned across the gap, standing on a receding floor grid, with the tap train ticked off along a time strip at the bottom edge.
controls: distance: scale; the wall pair scales about the floor centre from 0.7× to 1.3× (the gap and its dimension in metres widen), and the strip's ticks spread with it.
walls: count; the strip gains ticks, 1 to 12, one per reflection along the 1.3 s time line.
absorb: shape; the ticks' heights fall off faster along the strip, from an even comb to one tall first tick and stubs.
wind: position; the floor grid slides and skews sideways up to 30 px under the walls, and the ticks jitter off their even spacing.
risks: Stretch: P5 isn't in the effect column. The exception is that an echo's output is a train of discrete events in time, which is exactly what P5's activity strip is for, and a canyon is a place (the field) with an object in it (the walls). The fit is partial: the strip carries two of the four controls, so it does more work than P5 means it to.
The strip is a meter of taps; with walls and absorb both on it, the screen splits into a picture (top) and a dashboard (bottom).
Wind on the floor grid moves the most pixels for the quietest control (score 2), which over-states it unless the slide is kept small.
Distance is scale ≤ 1.3×, under the 1.6× scale floor; it needs the strip's spacing as its second cue or more range.
The two walls are plain blocks; schematic outline is clean but reads as two pillars, not rock, without the dimension label.

machines.name: Crease
machines.description: A wavefolder for any track: the signal is folded back on itself like paper, with symmetry and a soft paper limit.
machines.soundsLike: A wavefolder for any track: quiet input passes clean, louder input is pushed past the paper's edge and folds back, piling up bright odd harmonics that sweep as the level moves. Sym tips the fold so even harmonics come in; paper rounds the creases so the top end softens.

intake.subject: the track's signal as a strip of paper pushed past its edges and folded back on itself, the folds placed by symmetry and softened by the paper.
intake.controlSource: new (definition drafted here; "source" is the DSP below)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 2 notes (effects have no browser preview yet; effect resources only checked for structure). Nothing to justify.

dry to folded; strong at high crease, moderate at the ×2 default

cells.subject: A folding press drawn in section as an engineering schematic: the paper web festooned over a fixed upper bank of rollers and under a lower bank that drives down between them as far as the signal is pushed past the edge.
controls: crease: the lower roller bank drives down from 12 px to 120 px below the upper bank and the web's loops deepen with it, the depth dimension on the right following; position of the bank, shape of the web.
sym: the lower bank slides sideways up to 26 px either way so the loops lean and go uneven; position.
paper: every roller grows from a 4 px pin (a sharp crease) to a 14 px drum (a soft round bend) and the web's turns round with it; uniform scale of the rollers, shape of the web at the turns.
mix: the diverter blade at the infeed swings 50 degrees from sending the web into the press to dropping it on the straight dry path under the rail, the festooned web dimming as it goes; rotation.
cells.risks: The press is a metaphor for folding, not the signal: the web's loops don't trace the output wave, so a player who knows wavefolders sees a machine, not a waveform. Crease mostly moves the lower bank and the web's depth, which is honest (more drive, deeper fold) but it doesn't add folds; the count of loops is fixed at three. The web is one ribbon of 31 centre points and every control re-keys it (it's the only mutable outline, so fine on budget, but every turn redraws it). The hatched rails and hangers are a lot of hairline structure; at 1:1 they risk competing with the web. The mix blade is small (22 px); at 0 the web needs a second drawn path along the dry route, which is a second mutable outline.
cells.cleanNote: Same press, same composition as `rest.svg`. Generated by `clean.py` → `clean.svg`, `clean.png`. Lint: 0 errors, 0 warnings.
cells.alt: Crease, cleaned variant 4: A folding press drawn in section as an engineering schematic: the paper web festooned over a fixed upper bank of rollers and under a lower bank that drives down between them as far as the signal is pushed past the edge

cells.subject: A paper streamer folded into the shape of the output wave and inked as a one-bit print, front of the paper light dither and back dense, standing on an oscilloscope graticule where the trace would be.
controls: crease: the streamer folds more times across the screen, 2 panels at x1 to 15 or more at x8, every fold a hard white edge; shape of the panel outlines, count of panels.

sym: the scope's trace-position marker on the left edge rides up and down by up to 35 px and the folds go uneven, tall panels on one side and short on the other; position of the marker, shape of the strip.
paper: the folds' corners go from knife creases to soft rolled edges, the short panels at each fold widening; shape at the fold lines.

mix: a plain grey sine (the dry signal) rises behind the streamer as mix drops, and the streamer flattens toward it; count/state of the dry trace (absent at 100, as toro's steam is absent at rest), shape of the strip.
cells.risks: Stretch, and it only half earns it. The exception: crease's subject is a material with two faces, and folding is what makes the back of the paper show, which the one-bit language can say with two dither densities better than greys can; one-bit print is also paper's own medium. Where it fails: P9's dither only lives in still artwork, and here the strip's panels change shape with every control, so on the device they'd be flat palette greys with a white outline, losing the look that justifies the pattern (only the sketch is dithered). The panels overlap where the strip doubles back, and painter's order by time isn't depth order, so some folds will draw over the wrong face. P9 wants a figure; a streamer is barely one, and the scope graticule is a second language competing with the print. Caution from the catalog stands: toro moved off P9 to P10.
cells.cleanNote: Same streamer, same scope, same composition as `rest.svg`. Generated by `clean.py` → `clean.svg`, `clean.png`. Lint: 0 errors, 0 warnings (the sketch had ~350 legibility warnings).
cells.alt: Crease, cleaned variant 5: A paper streamer folded into the shape of the output wave and inked as a one-bit print, front of the paper light dither and back dense, standing on an oscilloscope graticule where the trace would be

cells.subject: The signal as a strip of paper folded back on itself into plies, drawn as a patent figure of the stack seen obliquely, with the folded wave inked on the top ply.
controls: crease: plies are added to the stack, 2 at x1 (one fold) to 6 at x5 and over, the top ply rising 22 px with each, and the wave on it folds more times; count of plies (position of the top ply), shape of the top trace.
sym: alternate plies run long and short so the creases fall off-centre, the ends sliding up to 22 px either way; position of the crease ends.
paper: each crease in section goes from a sharp V to a round bend of half the ply gap; shape of the crease profiles.
mix: the trace on the top ply relaxes from the folded wave back to the plain sine it started as; shape of the trace, the only control that touches it alone at crease x1.
cells.risks: Crease and mix both reshape the one trace on the top ply, so mix needs its own second cue (the ply outlines dimming toward the dry state is the candidate) or it reads as a weaker crease. Count steps a ply at a time (x2, x3, x4, x5), so crease needs the new ply to ease in from under the stack or it's an on/off change per step; six plies at 22 px reach y 48 and fill the body's height. Opaque plies hide everything but their front edges, so the lower plies read as strips and the back creases are hidden. Patent numerals (10, 12, 14) are honest to the language but are three labels for one subject. Plies are parallelograms, so the oblique projection has to be computed (craft.md, Think in 3D), not nudged; this sketch does that, but the crease arcs are only approximately tangent.
cells.alt: Crease, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The signal as a strip of paper folded back on itself into plies, drawn as a patent figure of the stack seen obliquely, with the folded wave inked on the top ply

cells.subject: A hidden-line isometric field of slabs whose heights are the fold surface, the input swept across and its level rising front to back, so the creases run through the field as lit ridges.
controls: crease: the back rows fold into more terraces, 1 ridge at x1 to 7 at x8, the front staying a gentle slope; shape (slab heights).
sym: the ridges slide sideways and the terraces go uneven, high on one side and low on the other; shape (heights) with position of the lit crest slabs.
paper: ridges go from knife-edge crests (one slab at the top) to broad rounded shoulders (three or four slabs near the top); shape (heights near the crests), crest count as second cue.
mix: the field relaxes from folded terraces toward a single plain ramp, with fewer hollow slabs; shape (heights), hollow/solid palette as second cue.
cells.risks: It's toro's visual language on another machine: the brief says not to copy another machine's drawing, and an isometric slab field from the same pattern will look like a sibling, not a new screen. All four controls are shape-of-heights, so they're told apart only by where and how the heights change (back rows, side shift, crest width, overall ramp); paper is the weakest and will need its crest-count cue to clear the floor. 70 slabs x 3 nodes = 210 nodes before the header. Heights over the swept input are a transfer surface, which is truthful but static: notes on an effect have no key position to act on, so note response has to come from the track's level.
cells.alt: Crease, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: A hidden-line isometric field of slabs whose heights are the fold surface, the input swept across and its level rising front to back, so the creases run through the field as lit ridges

cells.subject: The folded signal's harmonics charted as a band of sky across an atlas plate, one column of square cells per harmonic lit about the equator as far as it is strong, odd columns only while sym is centred.
controls: crease: the band reaches further east, from harmonic 1 alone at x1 to bright cells past harmonic 15 at x8; count of lit columns.
sym: the dark even columns fill in as even harmonics appear, from stripes to a solid band; count in the alternate columns (pattern).
paper: the band's eastern half sinks from lit cells to the grey layer as soft folds roll the upper harmonics off; count moved between lit and grey layers.
mix: the band thins toward the equator, every column but the first losing rows as the wet signal drops; run length per column (rows lit).
cells.risks: Gate 0 and P15's own pitfall: a wavefolder isn't texture, it has a mechanism (the fold), and a cell-per-harmonic grid is a spectrum analyser, which is the dashboard-of-meters failure the subject gate rejects. The atlas language sits on it as a frame and tick labels rather than being in the cells; stars on a plate aren't square. Crease and paper both move the band's eastern edge (one adds, one dims), so paper must stay on the lit/grey swap or the two read as one control. Harmonic magnitudes need a DFT per control change on the device, cheap at 19 bins but not free.
cells.alt: Crease, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: The folded signal's harmonics charted as a band of sky across an atlas plate, one column of square cells per harmonic lit about the equator as far as it is strong, odd columns only while sym is centred

machines.description: A rotating speaker drowned in turbulence: spin sets the rotor, flutter adds eddies to its speed, depth sets the doppler.
machines.concept: A rotating speaker drowned in turbulence: spin sets the rotor, flutter adds eddies to its speed, depth sets the doppler.

cells.subject: The horn chamber cut through in plan and drawn by a scope beam: the twin horn is one bright trace on a graticule, its phosphor trail fading behind each mouth.
controls: spin: the phosphor trail behind each horn mouth lengthens from 20 to 280 degrees of arc (shape: sweep), so a fast rotor leaves nearly a full ring of afterglow.
flutter: the trail's radius breaks into irregular ripples, up to 12 % of the horn length (shape), so the eddies show as a trail that no longer follows a clean circle.
depth: the horn grows from 36 to 86 px from the hub (uniform scale, 2.4x), because a longer horn is a larger doppler swing.
mix: the number of ghost horns the beam leaves behind the bright one, 0 to 4 (count, stepped in with an ease), so dry is a lone horn and full wet a fan of afterimages.
cells.risks: A rest frame is a single still horn; the trail is the only thing that says 'spinning', and at spin 0 it is a stub. Ghost horns at 1 px #4B4B4B-#646464 are faint at 1:1 and the count channel needs doubling to clear its floor (0-4 does, 1-2 would not). The graticule must stay at #323232-#4B4B4B or it turns into a dashboard. Effects get no notes, so motion only answers turns unless the host passes an input level.
cells.cleanNote:
- I removed the `rotor 0.82 hz` caption; the header already shows spin as 0.82. It was the only text in the drawing, and lint now shows 0 errors and 0 warnings.

At 1:1 nothing looked broken: the chamber circle (y 30–206) clears the header and the frame, the horn and hub are the one bright element, the trail is drawn as stroked arcs rather than filled shapes, and the body is mostly black.

cells.subject: A typeset signal-path diagram on the left (input, rotor wheel, an eddy line feeding its speed, a dry/wet vane) beside the output trace of a steady tone whose cycles the doppler squeezes and stretches.
controls: spin: the speed ticks set round the rotor wheel step from 3 to 24 (count), in column 1 under its label.
flutter: the eddy line feeding the rotor from below goes from a near-flat rule to a 16 px turbulent scrawl (shape), in column 1-2.
depth: the bright output trace's cycles bunch and spread around the grey dry tone, from identical at 0 to clearly frequency-modulated at 100 (shape, cycle ends move well over 16 px).
mix: the vane at the sum node turns 90 degrees from the dry contact to the wet one (rotation).
cells.risks: Two halves risk reading as a panel: the diagram has labels (in, rotor, dry, wet, eddies, out) and a vane that is close to a schematic switch symbol, which craft.md would call iconic. Spin as a tick count says 'faster' only by convention; the trace does not show rotor speed at all unless depth is up. The trace's 64-point budget over 220 px is coarse once flutter makes cycles irregular.
cells.alt: Eddy, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: A typeset signal-path diagram on the left (input, rotor wheel, an eddy line feeding its speed, a dry/wet vane) beside the output trace of a steady tone whose cycles the doppler squeezes and stretches

cells.subject: The path of the horn mouth through time drawn as a helix in orthographic elevation, front half-turns bright and back half-turns as hidden lines, projected from an end view of the rotor.
controls: spin: the helix pitch tightens from 1 to 12 turns across the elevation (shape/count of half-turns).
flutter: the spacing between turns goes uneven, each half-turn shifted by up to a fifth of a turn (shape).
depth: the helix radius and the end-view circle grow together from 18 to 58 px (shape, ±40 px at the crests), with the r dimension following.
mix: the helix crossfades in from the left: at 0 the elevation is the flat axis (dry), and the point where the helix reaches full radius slides 374 px to the left edge at 100 (position).
cells.risks: Read quickly at 1:1 it is a sine wave with alternate strokes greyed: exactly the 'oscilloscope says nothing new' pitfall P3 warns about. The elevation only reads as a helix if the eye catches the front/back weight change. Two paths (front and back runs) re-key on every spin, flutter and depth turn; runs split per half-turn could need more than 4 mutable outlines unless the helix is one 64-point path with shade per segment, which the device cannot do.
cells.alt: Eddy, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: The path of the horn mouth through time drawn as a helix in orthographic elevation, front half-turns bright and back half-turns as hidden lines, projected from an end view of the rotor

cells.subject: Survey sheets of the rotor, one per past revolution, stacked back in time on a diagonal: the horn's bearing moves on from sheet to sheet, and the front sheet maps the horn's sound throw as contours.
controls: spin: the bearing advance from one sheet to the next opens from 25 to 165 degrees (rotation of each back sheet's horn), so a fast rotor fans its bearings round the stack.
flutter: sheets slip out of register, up to 10 px off the diagonal and half a radian off their bearing (position), so turbulence reads as an untidy stack.
depth: the throw lobe on the front sheet reaches from 30 to 90 px (uniform scale, 3x).
mix: the stack grows from 2 to 5 sheets (count, stepping in with an ease), dry being the present sheet and one echo.
cells.risks: Mix as sheet count gives 2-5 items: under the count floor of 12, so it would need the step plus a second channel (stack depth offset) to pass. A stack of past revolutions shows history, but an effect has no notes, so nothing on screen moves until a knob turns and 'past revolutions' is a fiction at rest. Five overlapping circles plus contour lobes are on the edge of busy; bearing labels and the scale bar must stay #7D7D7D and sparse.
cells.alt: Eddy, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: Survey sheets of the rotor, one per past revolution, stacked back in time on a diagonal: the horn's bearing moves on from sheet to sheet, and the front sheet maps the horn's sound throw as contours

cells.subject: The rotary cabinet cut open as a patent section: one shaft carries the horn and the drum rotor on two orbits like a two-planet orrery, with louvred walls and reference numerals on leaders.
controls: spin: phantom positions of the horn mouth trail along its orbit, from 1 to 13 (count), the stroboscopic way a patent drawing shows a part in motion.
flutter: the drum's orbit loses its circle, rippling by up to 14 % of its radius (shape).
depth: the horn's orbit radius grows from 60 to 120 px about the shaft (uniform scale, 2x), since radius is what makes the doppler.
mix: the louvres in both walls open from 10 to 70 degrees (rotation), letting the rotor's sound into the room.
cells.risks: Stretch: P12 is a player/sequencer pattern, an orbit standing for a cycle of items. The exception is that a rotary speaker is a literal orrery: two bodies circling one shaft at two rates, so the orbits are the mechanism, not a metaphor, and nothing has to stand for steps. What doesn't fit: P12's life is constant calm orbiting, and an effect page has no notes and must be still at rest, so the 'planets' never travel unless a knob turns; the orbit is then just a drawing of the cabinet. The cabinet outline, hatched base and numerals push the frame toward 40 % black territory; louvres at 1:1 are 6 px slats and read as zigzags.
cells.alt: Eddy, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: The rotary cabinet cut open as a patent section: one shaft carries the horn and the drum rotor on two orbits like a two-planet orrery, with louvred walls and reference numerals on leaders

machines.name: Hinge
machines.description: A swinging-door freeze: the door catches a slice of the send's sound and swings it back and forth, creaking as it slows.
machines.concept: A swinging-door freeze: the door catches a slice of sound and swings it back and forth, creaking as it slows.
machines.soundsLike: A caught fragment of whatever is on the send, played forwards then backwards then forwards again, each pass a little slower, lower and quieter, like a door swinging to rest. With creak up, the slowing passes stutter and grind as the playhead sticks and slips.

intake.subject: a door on its hinge that catches a slice of the send's sound and swings it back and forth until it comes to rest; each candidate in the subject pass draws that door and its swing its own way.
intake.controlSource: new (the source is the DSP below)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings (two notes: effects have no browser preview yet, so the page is checked on a device; effect resources aren't reviewed beyond structure).

scores.effect: From a 20 ms buzz (a pitched stutter at the slice's rate) to a 2 s phrase swinging slowly back and forth; changes what the effect is.
Smooth slow-down at 0; clearly grinding, stepped slow-down above ~30 %, mostly on the tail of each swing.
From a quick flick that dies in half a second to a 20 s drone of passes; decides how long the door is heard after each catch.
Balance of dry and frozen; clear but plain, and only as dramatic as the slice is different from the source.

ranking.note: best looking at 1:1 and the only one that draws the swing itself coming to rest; controls map to separate channels.
clearest object and most guessable mapping, but a weak stretch and a static picture of a moving thing.
most honest model of the DSP, held back by tally-mark slats and an implied door.
the right idea (swings stacked on the pin) in a drawing that clips itself into fragments.
crisp but doesn't read as a door, and the wrong pattern for a sound with a mechanism.

cells.subject: The hinge cut in section at the pole of a half-planisphere graduated in degrees, its leaf standing on the meridian, and the swing plotted as an ephemeris: a track spiralling in from the leaf's tip, each turning point a star sized by how loud that pass is.
controls: hold: the leaf's length and the radius where the track starts, 80 to 150 px (scale of the leaf, 1.9x).
creak: the track sticks and slips: smooth arcs become stepped runs where the angle holds while the radius falls, and the turning stars split into close pairs (shape of the track).
swing: how many turning points the track plots before it reaches the pole, 3 to 13 (count of stars and turns).
mix: the stars' magnitude, 0.6x to 1.4x of their size, as an atlas sizes stars by brightness (uniform scale of the star nodes, 2.3x).
cells.risks: Star atlas is a liberty for a section drawing: the hinge in section is small and the chart does the talking, so it can read as a dial or protractor. The track is long (one 64-point outline is coarse for 6+ turns; it needs two or three mutable outlines, re-keyed on hold, creak and swing turns). Inner turns crowd near the pole at high swing. The graduated rim is static art and must stay quieter than the leaf.
cells.cleanNote: Generated by `clean.py` (copies the helpers from `../sketch.py`, which is untouched) → `clean.svg`, `clean.png`. Not picked yet, so it stays here. Lint: 0 errors, 0 warnings.
cells.alt: Hinge, cleaned variant 4: The hinge cut in section at the pole of a half-planisphere graduated in degrees, its leaf standing on the meridian, and the swing plotted as an ephemeris: a track spiralling in from the leaf's tip, each turning point a star sized by how loud that pass is

cells.subject: A survey plan of the doorway drawn once per swing, the plans stacked level above level up the hinge pin, the newest swing bright at the front and each older, wider swing a grey plan behind it.
controls: hold: the leaf's length in every plan (50 to 130 px) and the scale bar under it, because the slice is the leaf (scale of each layer).
creak: each plan's swing arc breaks from a smooth curve into stick-slip steps, more and deeper steps as it rises (shape of the arcs).

swing: how much each swing keeps of the last one: at 0 the front plans collapse almost shut behind a wide oldest swing, at 100 every level swings nearly as wide (rotation of the layer leaves, over 40 degrees on the front leaf).

mix: how far the levels stand apart up the pin, 16 to 32 px each, so the stack of past swings spreads out of the front plan as more of it is heard (position of the back layers, over 60 px at the oldest).
cells.risks: Five overlapping sectors with black fills read as a stack, but the back plans are mostly hidden and their dashed arcs get clipped into fragments at 1:1. The plan oblique (plans squashed to 0.42) is a liberty a survey plan doesn't usually take. Swing and mix both change the stack's silhouette; swing must stay on angle and mix on spacing or they blur together. P4's cap of 5 layers means swing can't be a count.
cells.alt: Hinge, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A survey plan of the doorway drawn once per swing, the plans stacked level above level up the hinge pin, the newest swing bright at the front and each older, wider swing a grey plan behind it

cells.subject: FIG. 1, a section through a louvred door leaf between its hatched stiles: every slat turns on its own pin to the caught slice's level, and each row below is a later, quieter pass played the other way.
controls: hold: how many cycles of the caught sound run across a row of slats, from half a cycle (20 ms) to three and a half (2 s) (rotation pattern across the field).
creak: the slat angles snap to coarse stick-slip steps, from smooth at 0 to 40-degree steps at 100, so rows go from a wave to a staircase (rotation, quantised).
swing: how much angle the later rows keep: at 0 the second and third rows lie nearly flat, at 100 they tilt as far as the first (rotation, row envelope, over 40 degrees in row 3).
mix: the slats' length, 10 px stubs when dry to 34 px when wet, so the leaf goes from shut pins to open louvres (uniform scale per slat, 3.4x).
cells.risks: 66 slats plus pins is about 70 nodes; rotation is pure turn, so a control turn re-poses every slat (66 changed nodes in one frame on a hold or creak turn, far over ~20 average; fine as a one-off ease, but say so). Rows of short marks can read as hatching or tally marks at 1:1, especially row 3. Hold and creak both act on the same rotation; creak's staircase must look different from hold's cycle count. The hinge itself is only a small knuckle at the edge: the door is implied by the louvres, not drawn.
cells.alt: Hinge, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: FIG

cells.subject: An isometric floor of square cells in hidden line, with the door's swing swept into it as a fan of raised cells: the rim where the leaf's edge travels lit, the two extremes it reached in grey, earlier passes as low rings.
controls: hold: the fan's radius, 2.5 to 7.5 cells, because a longer slice is a longer leaf (count of raised cells, roughly 10 to 80).
creak: the lit rim breaks into runs of 2 to 4 with sunken cells between them, the stick-slip of a dry hinge (count of grey-layer cells along the rim).
swing: how far round the fan stays lit, 15 to 115 degrees each side of the closed line (count and position of rim cells).
mix: how high caught cells stand from the floor, 3 to 13 px (position of the raised tops).
cells.risks: P15 is for sounds with no mechanism to draw, and hinge has one (a door), so the category fits but the pattern's own Gate 0 argues against it. At 1:1 the fan reads as an L-shaped wall of blocks rather than a swing; nothing says door without being told. Raised cells are three nodes each, so a big fan passes ~200 nodes with the floor. Hold and swing both change how many cells are lit; they differ only in radius against angle.

cells.subject: A door in elevation as an engineering schematic, its parts stacked on the hinge axis: three knuckled hinges on a dash-dot centreline, a closer and folding arm on the head, a ledged plank leaf standing ajar, with callout balloons and a dimension under the leaf.
controls: hold: how many boards make up the leaf, 3 to 12, and the dimension under it reads the slice (count).
creak: the three hinges' knuckles pull apart along the pin, 1 to 7 px between each, so each barrel lengthens by 24 px (position).
swing: the closer arm's angle at its pivot, 40 to 100 degrees, as a closer's valve sets how slowly a door comes to rest (rotation).
mix: how far the door stands ajar, 10 to 70 degrees: the leaf's seen width narrows and the gap at the latch side opens by ~60 px (position of the free edge).
cells.risks: Stretch, and only a partial fit. P11 is for an instrument the sound is played on and whose parts the player picks between (a kit); a door is recognised by sight just as freely, and its parts do each own one control (hinges creak, the closer sets the swing, the leaf is the slice), which is why it's worth trying. But nothing is selected and nothing is struck, so P11's channel fit (only the struck part moves) doesn't apply; this is really P1 in schematic dress. Mix as how far ajar is a strong reading of wet, but the leaf narrowing also thins the boards, so hold's count gets harder to read at high mix. The hinges and closer are small (8 px barrels, a 42 px closer) next to the bright leaf.
cells.alt: Hinge, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: A door in elevation as an engineering schematic, its parts stacked on the hinge axis: three knuckled hinges on a dash-dot centreline, a closer and folding arm on the head, a ledged plank leaf standing ajar, with callout balloons and a dimension under the leaf

machines.name: Lathe
machines.description: A record-cutting lathe on the send: the signal is cut into a lacquer groove, saturating at the cutter, then played back with inner-groove loss, wear and rumble.
machines.concept: A record-cutting lathe: the signal is cut into a groove, saturating at the cutter, with wear and rumble on playback.
machines.soundsLike: The send comes back as if it had been cut to lacquer and played: warm, rounded saturation and a high-frequency limit as the cutter is driven, getting duller and grittier (tracing distortion) toward the inner grooves. Wear adds crackle, ticks and a dulled top; rumble adds a low, slowly wandering platter rumble under it.

intake.subject: a lacquer disc being cut on a lathe, where the stylus digs the signal into a groove, saturating as it's driven harder, and the groove comes back worn and rumbling on playback.
intake.controlSource: new (the source is the DSP I'm writing: drive into a cutter model of tanh saturation plus a slew limit on the cut velocity, a radius-dependent low-pass and tracing-distortion stage, a crackle/tick generator with a wear-dependent shelf, and a filtered-noise rumble with slow wow)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings (two notes: effects have no browser preview; effect resources not reviewed beyond structure). `resources.display` is the placeholder (`stateBytes 4, nodes 1, palette 1`) until phase 4.

scores.effect: From a 6 dB quieter clean copy, through unity, to dense saturation with rounded transients and a hard top-end limit; the biggest change on the machine
Progressive dulling and a gritty tracing distortion on loud highs toward the label; gentle to ~50, obvious past 70
Light surface noise early (power curve), then ticks, crackle and a dulled top; obvious on quiet material, partly masked on dense
Sub-40 Hz rumble and slow wow; faint until ~60 (squared), and small speakers hide much of it

ranking.note: the subject is the cut itself, every control moves part of it physically, and it's the cheapest.
the best-looking frame and clearly a record, but groove is invisible at the default, and cut takes three paths.
the strongest single drawing language, with an honest mapping; heavy texture, and the physics is abstract.
clear, but it splits into two halves that don't match the hands, and it's boxy.
the stretch doesn't fit; it draws the machine, not what the machine does to the sound.
