cells.subject: The cutting stylus caught mid-cut in a textbook cross-section of the lacquer blank, its V sunk into the coat and a swarf thread coiling off behind it.
controls: cut: shape (node 0, the groove under the stylus) - the V deepens from ~7 to ~22 px and its point bottoms out into a flat floor as the cutter saturates (1.4 to ~9 px flat); the stylus (node 1) rides down with it.

groove: position - the blank slides under the fixed stylus: the rim bevel runs out to the left and the uncut inner lacquer's break line comes in from the right (~160-170 px), so more cut grooves trail the stylus.
wear: count - chips and rounded lips appear on the grooves already cut, left of the stylus (0 to ~14 marks); none at 0.
rumble: shape - the platter line under the blank rises into a slow wave (0 to +-10 px); flat at 0.
cells.risks: Header-wide section (x 160-460) leaves a lot of thin horizontal lines; the lacquer hatching is close to the 3 px floor (5 px spacing, hairline) and could smear on the panel. Rumble's platter line is 420 px long, so as a mutable outline it needs four 64-point runs or it has to be re-thought as a few translated segments. wear's chips are small (3-4 px) and only appear on the 3-4 cut grooves at groove 0. Effects get no note input, so nothing answers playing: the drawing only moves when a knob turns.
cells.alt: Lathe, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The cutting stylus caught mid-cut in a textbook cross-section of the lacquer blank, its V sunk into the coat and a swarf thread coiling off behind it

cells.subject: The lathe drawn side-on as an engineering elevation on the left, with the groove wall as it plays back traced on the right.
controls: cut: shape - the played trace's amplitude grows and its peaks flatten into plateaus as the cutter saturates (nodes 3-4).
groove: position - the cutter head (node 0) travels along the cantilevered rail from the rim toward the spindle, 56 px, and the radius dimension under the plinth lengthens with it.
wear: count - crackle ticks appear above the trace, 0 to 16, a click per tick; none at 0.
rumble: shape - the trace's grey centre line (nodes 1-2) bends into a slow 1.2-cycle wave, 0 to +-12 px; flat at 0.
cells.risks: Two places to look; the left elevation only carries groove, so knobs 1, 3 and 4 all act on the right half and P7's column split doesn't hold. The elevation's plinth, rail and column are boxes and could tip into a 'panel' look. Two languages in one frame (elevation, trace) must share weights. The trace is 200 px, so cut needs two mutable paths and rumble two more: all four paths spent. No note input on an effect, so the trace never scrolls; it is a picture of one turn, not a scope.
cells.alt: Lathe, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The lathe drawn side-on as an engineering elevation on the left, with the groove wall as it plays back traced on the right

cells.subject: A sector of the record side seen from above as a survey plan, the groove being cut drawn bright across it among the grey earlier turns, with chainage marks.
controls: cut: shape - the bright groove's lateral swing grows (about 3 to 9 px) and its crests square off as the cutter saturates (nodes 0-2).
groove: position - the label's edge, an arc below the groove, rises from off-frame to just under the cut (~60 px) as the cut moves inward.
wear: count - spot marks (pits, dust) are plotted along the lands and grooves, 0 to ~20; none at 0.
rumble: position - the set of earlier turns slides off-centre against the bright groove (0 to 24 px), an eccentric, wandering side; concentric at 0.
cells.risks: P3's own pitfall: it could read as a wiggly line rather than a record unless the curvature and earlier turns stay. The bright groove spans 370 px, so cut uses three of the four mutable paths. groove's label arc is off-frame at the default (0), so the rest frame doesn't show where groove is; it only reads once turned. rumble moves five static arcs as one group: five nodes but a whole-width change. Grid crosses must stay faint or they read as icons.
cells.alt: Lathe, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A sector of the record side seen from above as a survey plan, the groove being cut drawn bright across it among the grey earlier turns, with chainage marks

cells.subject: Five section slices taken across the side from rim to label, stacked diagonally like a patent figure, the slice under the stylus lit and the inner ones carrying shorter waves.
controls: cut: shape - the lit slice's grooved top edge (nodes 0-1) swells and flattens at its crests.
groove: position + shade - which slice is lit steps from the front (rim, 10) to the back (label, 18), easing through the grey between; the lit outline and edge move with it (~140 px diagonal travel).
wear: count - nicks are struck into the lit slice's hatched face and edge, 0 to ~12; none at 0.
rumble: position - the five slices ride a slow vertical wave, up to +-10 px each, so the stack goes out of line; aligned at 0.
cells.risks: groove steps between five slices, so between them it must ease (shade fade plus moving the lit edge) or it reads as on/off. Hatching at 4 px is near the 3 px floor and covers five faces: it's static, but it could smear on the panel. The physics is a little abstract: the player has to know that inner grooves carry shorter waves. Reference numerals (10-18) are patent convention and mean nothing to a player; they're decoration in the language.
cells.alt: Lathe, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: Five section slices taken across the side from rim to label, stacked diagonally like a patent figure, the slice under the stylus lit and the inner ones carrying shorter waves

cells.subject: The lathe itself, assembled in hidden-line isometric: plinth, platter and lacquer, the rail behind and the cutter head hanging over the disc on its arm.
controls: cut: scale - the swarf thread coiling from the stylus up to the suction tube grows from ~0.7x to 2x (node 2).
groove: position - the carriage, arm and head slide along the rail from the rim toward the spindle (~34 px on screen) and the cut band of turns widens behind it.
wear: count - dust specks settle on the lacquer, 0 to 14; none at 0.
rumble: rotation - the lacquer's top outline turns in plane about the spindle, up to ~30 deg, so the disc reads as wobbling on a worn bearing; still at 0.
cells.risks: Stretch, and it mostly doesn't fit: P11 works because the instrument's parts are what the note selects (theseus' tiers); here no note selects anything and an effect gets no note input, so the 'stack' is just a portrait of the machine. The exception case is recognition: a lathe reads as a turntable at a glance, so the player knows which part is the head, the disc and the plinth without a legend. Against it: the drawing is about the machine, not the sound; cut's swarf coil is tiny at rest (under ~10 px) and hard to see; rumble's in-plane rotation of an ellipse is a fake tilt that may look like the disc sliding off the platter, and 30 deg is a lot; risk of reading as a stock-style product drawing next to TE's own objects.
cells.alt: Lathe, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: The lathe itself, assembled in hidden-line isometric: plinth, platter and lacquer, the rail behind and the cutter head hanging over the disc on its arm

cells.subject: A turning lathe in profile, the workpiece spinning between chuck and tailstock centre, its turned profile the cut signal and the tool at the shoulder where raw stock becomes waveform.
controls: cut: shape (node 0, the turned profile) - the profile's swings deepen and their crests flatten into lands as the cutter is driven, 8.5 px swing at 1.00 to ~14 px with flat tops at 4.00.
groove: position (node 1, tool and cross-slide) - the cross-slide feeds the tool in toward the axis by 24 px, and the turned radius follows it down (rim = full diameter, label = a thin spindle).
wear: count (hairline chatter marks) - short hairline ticks appear across the turned surface, 0 to ~16, none at 0.

rumble: rotation (node 2, the workpiece and its centre line) - the work runs out, turning in the screen plane about the chuck by up to +-4 deg with a hatched envelope of the swept outline; still at 0.
cells.risks: Single-weight contour: every machine part is one Line-weight outline; the turned profile is the only heavier line and the centre line and chip the only hairlines, so the three weights survive. This is a metal/wood lathe, a pun on the machine's name rather than the record lathe the DSP models; the owner asked for it. rumble's in-plane turn is under the 30 deg rotation floor (the tail end moves ~28 px, so it may pass as position). cut and groove both reshape the profile's path, but groove's primary channel is the tool's position. The profile is one mutable outline of 62 points, close to the 64 limit.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Lathe, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: A turning lathe in profile, the workpiece spinning between chuck and tailstock centre, its turned profile the cut signal and the tool at the shoulder where raw stock becomes waveform

cells.subject: The record lathe's cutter head riding its lead screw side-on, every body a hatched mass, the bright stylus hanging from its pivot into the lacquer it is cutting.
controls: cut: rotation (node 0, the stylus about its pivot) - the stylus swings from a still rest to +-30 deg excursion as drive rises, and at the top of the range it presses against the stop pads in the head's window (saturation drawn as hitting the stops).

groove: position (carriage, column, head and nozzle as one group) - the whole head runs along the screw from the rim (left) toward the label step (right), ~190 px, and the cut turns behind it lengthen.
wear: count - small chips appear on the lacquer behind the stylus among the earlier turns, 0 to ~14, none at 0.
rumble: shape (the lacquer coat's top edge) - the coat and core slab heave into a slow wave under the head, +-6 px; flat at 0.
cells.risks: Hatched masses are a lot of 45 deg texture at 1:1 (spacing 4.5 px, 3.5 px clear); on the panel the hatching may shimmer as the carriage moves, so the moving group may need its hatching pre-drawn per node. The stylus is a filled bright body (the one solid bright mass). groove moves ~6 nodes as a group. The coat notches (earlier turns) sit close to the 3 px floor.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Lathe, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: The record lathe's cutter head riding its lead screw side-on, every body a hatched mass, the bright stylus hanging from its pivot into the lacquer it is cutting

cells.subject: The lacquer coat under the microscope at grazing light, grooves running away from the eye with only their lips catching the light, the newest groove the bright one and the cut face of the coat a notched silhouette at the bottom.
controls: cut: shape (node 0, the bright groove's lit lip) - its swing widens and the crests flatten as the cutter saturates; the V notch it makes in the near face deepens with it.
groove: position (the whole field) - the field slides sideways: the rim's bevel leaves at the right and more turns come in from the left, ~90 px at the near edge.
wear: count - specks and short scratches catch the light on the lands between grooves, 0 to ~16, none at 0.
rumble: rotation (the field about its near centre) - the surface tilts slowly in the screen plane, up to +-3 deg, as the platter heaves; still at 0.
cells.risks: Lines converging upward can read as a retro perspective grid if pushed; the camera looks down so there's no horizon, and each lip stops before it comes within 3 px of its neighbour. groove as a whole-field slide is many lines moving at once (one node per lip, ~25 nodes), expensive on a turn. rumble's rotation is under the 30 deg floor. The bright lip is 44 points split in two ribbons; as one mutable outline it must drop to <= 31 points per side.
cells.angle: the material the sound acts on, seen close
cells.alt: Lathe, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: The lacquer coat under the microscope at grazing light, grooves running away from the eye with only their lips catching the light, the newest groove the bright one and the cut face of the coat a notched silhouette at the bottom

cells.subject: The freshly cut disc playing back on a platter seen close and low, its grooves hairline rings, the tonearm swung in and the one bright arc the groove being read.
controls: cut: shape (node 0, the bright arc of the groove being read) - the arc swings into a modulated ring as drive rises, its crests flattening; a plain arc at low cut.
groove: rotation (the tonearm about its pivot) - the arm swings in from the rim to the last groove before the label, ~35 deg, and the bright arc moves with the stylus.
wear: count - dust specks and short scratch arcs appear across the cut band, 0 to ~16, none at 0.
rumble: position (disc and platter as one group) - the disc rides up and down on its spindle by up to 8 px with a slow wander; still at 0.
cells.risks: The playback deck shows the second half of the machine (wear and rumble live there), so the lathe itself is off stage: it may read as a turntable machine rather than a cutting lathe. The tonearm is small at 1:1 (headshell ~10 px); it needs a closer camera on the device. Hairline rings are drawn as stroked closed outlines (1.0 px), which lint warns about; as ribbons they cost more nodes. Moving the disc for rumble is a big redraw.
cells.angle: one scene where this happens, with one subject in it
cells.alt: Lathe, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: The freshly cut disc playing back on a platter seen close and low, its grooves hairline rings, the tonearm swung in and the one bright arc the groove being read

cells.subject: A specimen block of lacquer on aluminium with one length of modulated groove cut along its top, modelled in hidden-line 3D, its end face sectioned so the V of the groove shows.
controls: cut: shape (node 0, the groove's lit far lip, with its near lip and floor) - the groove widens and sinks and its swings flatten at the crests, half-width 0.25 to 0.37 world (~6 px).

groove: shape on the time axis, carried as position of the block's swing pattern - the same swings pack shorter along the block (inner turns run slower under the stylus), wavelength 1.0 to 0.55 of the rest frame.
wear: count - chips knocked out of the lips, small notches along both edges, 0 to ~14, none at 0.
rumble: position (the whole block) - the block heaves up and down on its bed by up to 10 px with a slow wander, a hatched ghost of its base showing where it rests; still at 0.
cells.risks: cut and groove both change the groove's outline; groove's change is along the length (wavelength), cut's across (width, depth, crest), but both re-key the same paths, so the one-channel rule is bent and must be shown to read on the contact sheet. The cut needs ~cut 1.6 before the widening clears the 16 px shape floor. The block and its three grooves cost ~4 mutable paths (lips, floor), the full budget.
cells.angle: the machine's own rule as a physical thing: what turning each knob would do to a real object
cells.alt: Lathe, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: A specimen block of lacquer on aluminium with one length of modulated groove cut along its top, modelled in hidden-line 3D, its end face sectioned so the V of the groove shows

machines.name: Nave
machines.description: A send reverb modelled on a stone nave: the nave's length sets the decay, the stone's hardness how long the highs survive, the choir's carving how densely the echoes diffuse, and the west doors how long before the first reflection arrives.
machines.concept: A reverb modelled on a stone nave: its length, stone hardness, the choir's diffusion and the doors' pre-delay.
machines.soundsLike: A send reverb modelled on a stone nave: a stone room whose tail runs from a small chapel to a cathedral, bright or dark with the stone. The choir's carving smears early echoes into a wash, and the doors set the gap before the room answers.

intake.subject: a stone nave and the sound it gives back, which the four controls change: how long the nave is, how hard its stone, how carved its choir, how far back its doors.
intake.controlSource: new (the definition below is written against the DSP being designed: an FDN tail with a high-shelf damping filter in the loop, an allpass diffuser chain before it and a pre-delay line in front)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings. Two notes, both informational: effects have no browser preview yet (design from stills, check on a device), and effect resources beyond `display` aren't reviewed by the tool. `resources.display` is a placeholder until phase 4.

scores.effect: 0.4 s room to 12 s cathedral: the biggest change the machine makes
dark, woolly tail to bright ringing one; obvious on cymbals and vocals, smaller on bass
flutter and discrete slaps at 0 to a smooth wash; clear on drums, subtle on pads
under 30 ms barely heard as delay (it separates source and room); above ~80 ms an audible gap

ranking.note: the nave as the subject, in one language, every control moving the building.
the truest to the sound; needs one figure to lead, or the columns realigned.
clean channels and calm, but the metaphor has to be explained.
the strongest shape, blocked by the four-path budget and no sense of place.
the most legible picture, the weakest mapping; it doesn't really fit.

cells.subject: A patent sheet in two figures: fig. 1 cuts the nave lengthwise with its pointed arcade and vault, fig. 2 plots the impulse it returns after the doors' gap.
controls: nave: position (+ count) on fig. 1, the east wall and its half-dome move east about 64 px adding arches; it also stretches the tail of fig. 2 by 100 px as a second cue.
stone: shape on fig. 2; the treble envelope line drops near the floor on soft stone and rides the reflection peaks on hard stone (a quarter of the way into the tail it moves ~30 px).
choir: count on fig. 1; the sound arrow leaving the door fans out from one ray at 0 to fourteen scattered arrows at 100.
doors: position on fig. 2; the first reflection moves away from the bright direct impulse, 6 to 66 px, with a dimension line labelled 'door' over the gap.
risks: Controls don't split by column: fig. 1 carries knobs 1 and 3, fig. 2 knobs 2 and 4, so hands and screen don't agree (P2's main advantage lost).
Fig. 2 is close to a textbook plot; with labels and two figures it can read as a document rather than one subject.
The reflection comb is a 64-point outline of 15 teeth; dense tails at 12 s get coarse, and treble line crossing the teeth can tangle.
The direct impulse is the brightest element, not the nave: the eye lands on fig. 2.

cells.subject: The church measured in plan, cut at sill height: west porch, aisled nave, choir stalls and a round apse, with one sound ray bouncing wall to wall from the door.
controls: nave: position (+ count); the apse slides east about 170 px and arcade bays (piers and bay numbers) are added behind it, from 3 bays at 0.4 s to 10 at 12 s.
stone: count; the ray from the west door survives more wall-to-wall bounces before it ends, 2 legs on soft stone to 14 on hard, folding back at the apse when it runs out of nave.
choir: position; the choir screen walks west along the axis about 90 px, so the stall rows (fine hairlines along both walls) lengthen into the nave.
doors: position; the west porch lengthens about 70 px, pushing the door leaves and their swing arcs away from the nave.
risks: Three of four controls are position; they move different parts in different directions (apse east, screen west, porch west), but the player still has to learn which is which.
The ray is a picture of an acoustic idea, not the DSP: stone sets high-frequency survival, and a single ray doesn't say 'treble'.
Choir stalls are hairline rows 5 px apart: right at the hatching limit, and choir (score 2) is the quietest-looking change.
A plan has no height, so the vault, which is what a listener imagines in a nave, is absent.

cells.subject: The reverb's decay as a hidden-line waterfall: twelve frequency slices from bass in front to treble at the back, each a wedge falling away along time.
controls: nave: shape; every slice's tail lengthens along the time axis, 80 px at 0.4 s to 260 px at 12 s.
stone: shape across depth; the treble slices at the back shorten against the bass, to about a fifth of the bass tail on soft stone and nearly equal on hard stone, so the surface's back edge swings.
choir: shape along the tops; low diffusion breaks each wedge into separate echo peaks with notches between, high diffusion fills it into a smooth slope.
doors: position; the whole surface slides away from the bright direct-sound bar at the time origin, 8 to 68 px.
risks: Three controls are shape on the same surface (P3's pitfall); they act on different dimensions (length, back edge, top texture), but at 1:1 nave and stone can be confused.
Twelve slices are twelve outlines and only four mutable paths exist: slices must become stepped node strips or pre-drawn variants, which the sketch ignores.
It's a waterfall plot: the nave itself never appears, so the 'stone nave' character has to come from the header names alone.
Slice spacing is ~9 px on screen; the back third reads as hatching at 1:1.
cells.alt: Nave, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: The reverb's decay as a hidden-line waterfall: twelve frequency slices from bass in front to treble at the back, each a wedge falling away along time

cells.subject: An atlas of echoes: five charts stacked in depth from the first reflections to the late tail, each plotting its echoes as stars by magnitude, lit from the west door's source star.
controls: nave: position; the charts recede further apart, the back chart travelling about 60 px up and to the right, so a long nave is a deep stack.
stone: scale; star magnitudes fall from chart to chart, steeply on soft stone (back charts nearly empty) and hardly at all on hard stone.
choir: count; each chart plots 4 bright stars at 0 (discrete echoes) up to 26 fainter ones at 100 (a diffuse wash).
doors: position; the whole stack moves away from the source star along a dashed trail, 18 to 98 px.
risks: The stack reads as cards or windows before it reads as time; the 'first' and 'V' labels carry a lot.
Stars on back charts only show in the thin uncovered strip, so stone's change lives mostly in that strip and in small dots (lint warns on dots under 3 px).
Choir changes count and star size together; star size is stone's channel too, so the two blur on the front chart.
Star atlas is a borrowed language for a building; nothing says 'stone nave' except the source labelled 'door'.
cells.alt: Nave, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: An atlas of echoes: five charts stacked in depth from the first reflections to the late tail, each plotting its echoes as stars by magnitude, lit from the west door's source star

cells.subject: A one-bit church in side elevation, west tower, lancet-windowed nave and apse in hard white outline with dithered stone, annotated with schematic dimension and decay glyphs.
controls: nave: shape (+ count); the nave wall and roof lengthen east about 150 px and lancet windows are added, one per bay, the apse riding at the end.
stone: tone + shape; the walls' dither level goes from sparse (soft, dark) to dense (hard, bright), and the decay glyph over the roof keeps its fine teeth longer on hard stone.
choir: count; a scatter of 4 px ink squares over the east end grows from 2 to 16.
doors: position; a dimension line from the west door to a first-reflection mark lengthens 14 to 84 px.
risks: Stretch, and it only partly earns it: a church is recognisable by sight the way toro's bull was, and an effect page keeps one subject on screen so static dither is affordable; but nothing on the figure performs the sound, so the figure is a mascot and the controls end up on glyphs.
Dither can't change on the device (static art only), so stone's tone has to swap to flat greys; the sketch's dither is the look, not the build. Lint warns on ~1,700 2 px dither cells.
Mixing one-bit print with schematic callouts is two languages unless the glyphs are drawn in the same hard ink; the 'ring' squiggle and 'pre' dimension are close to icons.
Choir's ink squares mean nothing a player could guess; it's the weakest mapping of the five.
Figurative screens are where toro failed nine times (caution in pass.json).
cells.alt: Nave, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: A one-bit church in side elevation, west tower, lancet-windowed nave and apse in hard white outline with dithered stone, annotated with schematic dimension and decay glyphs

machines.name: Relay
machines.description: A bucket-brigade delay with failing stages: a chain of charge buckets passes the signal along on each clock tick; some buckets leak, the clock wanders, and the output recirculates to the input.
machines.concept: A bucket-brigade delay with failing stages: some buckets leak, the clock wanders, feedback recirculates.
machines.soundsLike: A dark, slightly grainy analogue delay: from flanger-short slap to a 1 s echo, the repeats softening each pass. Turned up, the repeats lose level and pieces as buckets leak, and warble in pitch as the clock wanders.

intake.subject: the bucket chain itself, with a test note passing down it and coming round again, so the player sees how many buckets it has, which of them leak, how unevenly they're clocked and how often the note recirculates.
intake.controlSource: new (source is the DSP to be written)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings (2 notes: effects have no browser preview yet; effect resources not reviewed beyond structure). `resources.display` is a placeholder until phase 4.

scores.effect: delay time 10 ms → 1 s: comb/flange colour through slapback to a clear echo; the biggest change in what the effect is
repeats lose level and highs and break up into grit as failing buckets drop charge; obvious from ~30 %, subtle below
pitch warble of the repeats, chorus-like at low settings to seasick at 1 st; quieter than leak, and only on the wet signal
from one repeat to a long recirculating tail near self-oscillation; dramatic at the top

cells.subject: Every trip the test note makes round the chain is one oscilloscope sweep, and the sweeps stack back into depth, the newest bright in front and each recirculation a dimmer screen behind it.
controls: stages: the echo burst slides along every sweep's time axis from just after the dry mark (10 ms) to the far end (1 s), log time, all screens together (position, ~200 px).
leak: the front trace's burst sags and goes to staircase: the leaky buckets' held samples show as flat steps and its peaks droop, the back screens inheriting it (shape of the bright front trace).

clock: the screens behind shear sideways by uneven amounts, so successive passes stop lining up, the way a wandering clock smears each recirculation's arrival (position of the back layers, up to ~24 px each).
feedback: how many screens the stack holds, one at 0 up to six at 100, each further back dimmer and lower (count of layers, with shade as the second cue).
risks: P3's oscilloscope pitfall applies to every layer: it can read as a stock scope view; the stacked screens are what make it this machine.
stages and clock are both position; they move different parts (the burst within every screen vs the screens themselves), but perceptibility has to prove the player can tell them apart.
At the default (leak 0, clock 0) the stack is pristine; the machine's failing character only shows when the player turns it up.
An effect page gets no audio, so the bursts are a notional test note, not what is playing.
cells.alt: Relay, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: Every trip the test note makes round the chain is one oscilloscope sweep, and the sweeps stack back into depth, the newest bright in front and each recirculation a dimmer screen behind it

cells.subject: The bucket chain coiled into a printed spiral figure: one radial bar per bucket, its length the charge it holds, each turn of the coil one more pass of recirculation winding inward.
controls: stages: how many bucket bars stand on each turn, 24 at 0 to 72 at 100, so the coil goes from coarse comb to dense fringe (count).
leak: a fixed seeded set of failing buckets loses its charge and their bars sink to stubs, more of them and lower as leak rises, so the note's lump on each turn gets gaps (shape: bar lengths).

clock: the bars lose their even angular spacing and bunch and spread around the coil, and the note's lump drifts round a little further on each inner turn instead of lining up radially (rotation of bars about the centre, up to ~30°).
feedback: how many turns the coil winds before the lump dies away, one at 0 to four at 100, inner turns shorter-barred and dimmer (count of turns).
risks: Inner turns crowd: at 72 bars on the fourth turn bars sit ~2.4 px apart, under the 3 px hatching floor; cap stages' count on inner turns or cap turns at 3.
~190 bar nodes at default stages and four turns; clock moves every bar, far past ~20 changed nodes per frame while it turns.
Typeset labels (in, out, pass numerals, caption) must stay off moving bars; the numerals at nine o'clock collide when clock bunches bars there.
Spiral plus ticks risks reading as a dial or a record, an icon; the figure caption and numerals are what keep it a diagram.
cells.alt: Relay, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The bucket chain coiled into a printed spiral figure: one radial bar per bucket, its length the charge it holds, each turn of the coil one more pass of recirculation winding inward

cells.subject: A wall of bucket compartments seen face on, the chain running back and forth along its rows, each compartment's held charge drawn as how full and how bright it stands.
controls: stages: how far apart the recirculated runs sit along the wall, from runs almost touching their note at 10 ms to one echo per two rows at 1 s (field statistic: spacing of lit runs, a position channel).
leak: a growing seeded share of compartments drain to empty, black where the standing bias charge was, and runs passing them lose cells (count of the grey layer).
clock: runs smear and break up, 3-cell runs stretching to ragged 6-cell runs with a cell missing, because a wandering clock spreads each packet over more buckets (run length).
feedback: how many lit runs follow each note before the wall goes back to bias, one at 0 to the whole wall lit at 100 (density of lit cells).
risks: Gate 0 tension: a BBD has a mechanism (v4 draws it), and P15 is for sounds that are texture; this wall argues the chain's state is the texture, which the owner may not buy.
A grid of level-filled compartments can read as a meter bank, the dashboard the protocol rejects; the elevation reading (fill from the floor, bias always there) has to carry it.
216 cell nodes; feedback and clock churn far more than ~20 cells a frame while turning, and the wall shows a notional test phrase since effect pages get no audio.
stages as spacing of runs is a weak statistic at the long end (one echo every two rows); check it clears the position floor.
cells.alt: Relay, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A wall of bucket compartments seen face on, the chain running back and forth along its rows, each compartment's held charge drawn as how full and how bright it stands

cells.subject: The chip's charge channel cut open lengthwise and drawn as a surveyor's long-section: a row of wells under their clock gates, each holding a pool of charge whose surfaces trace the note, over a datum with chainage in stages and a return leg beneath.
controls: stages: the chainage compresses, more and narrower wells across the section, 8 at 0 to 24 at 100, the chainage figures rising to match (count of wells, with the gate row following).
leak: failing wells get a seep notch in their floor and their pool surfaces sink toward empty, breaking the note's line (shape of the bright pool-surface profile).

clock: the gate electrodes above the wells slip off their even pitch, and the walls of each well follow them, so the wells come out uneven in width (position of the gates and wells, up to ~12 px each, ≥ 24 px end to end).
feedback: the hydraulic grade line in the return leg rises from the invert at 0 to just under the datum at 100, the level the output is fed back in at (position, ~50 px).
risks: The most literal of the five: it explains the device (a CCD potential-well diagram) more than the sound; leak and clock read clearly, stages and feedback are diagram furniture.
Sixteen pools each with a surface ribbon plus the profile and gates is detailed for the node budget; the profile and pool surfaces want to be one or two mutable outlines.
Survey labels (ch, figures, in, out, hgl, return) are many for 480 × 220; cut to what the player needs.
Pools show a notional test note frozen mid-chain; effect pages get no audio.
cells.alt: Relay, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The chip's charge channel cut open lengthwise and drawn as a surveyor's long-section: a row of wells under their clock gates, each holding a pool of charge whose surfaces trace the note, over a datum with chainage in stages and a return leg beneath

cells.subject: The name taken literally, as a patent drawing of a cascade of tipping buckets hung from a sloped frame, each one pouring its charge into the next, the note's bucket tipped and bright, with a riser carrying the overflow back to the top.
controls: stages: how many buckets hang in the cascade, 4 at 0 to 10 at 100, closer together as they multiply (count).
leak: holes open in a seeded set of buckets, with drops falling from them, and their water levels sink (count of drops, with level as a second cue).
clock: the buckets that should hang level tilt by uneven amounts, some early to tip and some late, up to ±20° (rotation about each axle).
feedback: the water column in the return riser climbs from the basin to the top bucket's inlet (position, ~160 px).
risks: Stretch, and honestly a weak one: P11 earns its place when the machine plays an instrument people know by sight, and nobody plays buckets. The exception argument is only that the bucket brigade is named after one, so recognition is free; the picture is a metaphor, not the mechanism or the sound.
Buckets on hangers flirt with clip-art; it has to stay a patent section (cut walls, numerals, leaders) or it becomes an icon row.
stages as count is coarse (4..10 buckets for 100..10000 stages): the drawing can't show the delay time it controls, only more or fewer steps.
Water in tipped buckets is a mutable outline per bucket; clock moving every bucket redraws all of them while it turns.
cells.alt: Relay, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: The name taken literally, as a patent drawing of a cascade of tipping buckets hung from a sloped frame, each one pouring its charge into the next, the note's bucket tipped and bright, with a riser carrying the overflow back to the top

cells.subject: The charge the chain holds, seen close: a stretch of the chain's buckets drawn as thin capacitor plates pulled apart along their line, each as tall as the charge it holds, with the test note riding down the row and each recirculation a smaller copy further on.
controls: stages: how many plates lie between one pass of the note and the next, 5 at 10 ms to 30 at 1 s, so the repeats slide along the row and off its far end (position of the repeat groups, ~60 to 400+ px).
leak: a seeded share of plates come out short, and the charge each has lost stands above it as a hatched ghost of the plate's full height (shape of the plate heights, hatching as the second cue).
clock: the plates drift off their even pitch, bunching and spreading along the axis like an exploded view drawn by an unsteady hand (position of each plate, up to ~40% of the pitch).
feedback: how many groups of plates carry a copy of the note and how tall each is, one group at 0 to five or six at the top (count of repeat groups, height as the second cue).
risks: At 1:1 the plates can read as a row of dominoes or glass panes; the exploded-view axis, the source block and the electrode insets are what make them plates.
stages and clock both move plates along the row; stages moves whole repeat groups, clock jitters every plate, so perceptibility has to prove they read apart.
Thirty plates of three faces each is ~120 nodes before hatching; leak's hatched ghosts add more, and clock moves every plate while it turns.
The row is a notional window on the chain with the note and its echoes in it at once; an effect page gets no audio.
cells.angle: the material the sound acts on, seen close
cells.alt: Relay, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: The charge the chain holds, seen close: a stretch of the chain's buckets drawn as thin capacitor plates pulled apart along their line, each as tall as the charge it holds, with the test note riding down the row and each recirculation a smaller copy further on

cells.subject: A telegraph line running away over open ground, the old relay that handed a signal on from station to station: the poles are the stages and the note is a lit span of the top wire, its recirculations dimmer spans further down the line.
controls: stages: how many poles stand between the viewer and the horizon, 7 at 10 ms to 20 at 1 s, the spans shortening as they multiply (count of poles and spans).
leak: in a seeded set of spans the top wire has come loose from its insulator and hangs in a deep sag, so the pulse's path droops there (shape of the wire, up to ~20 px of sag per span).
clock: the poles lean by uneven amounts and stand at uneven spacing, so the wire's rhythm down the line goes ragged (rotation of each pole, up to ~9°, with position as the second cue).
feedback: how many spans further down the line carry a dimmer copy of the lit pulse, one at 0 to five or six at the top (count of lit spans).
risks: The pulse is a 2 px span on a long scene; at 1:1 it's the one bright thing but small, and the note response (rest to playing) has to clear 2% of the body.
Single-weight contour asks for one line; the frame keeps three (scene 1.5, pulse 2, distance in hairline), so the language is bent to the house rule.
Far poles crowd toward the vanishing point at 20 stages; anything under 3 px is dropped, so the count's top end is partly invisible.
It's a metaphor (telegraph relay) rather than the chip; it reads as 'a signal handed along stages' but not as a bucket-brigade specifically.
cells.angle: one scene where this happens, with one subject in it
cells.alt: Relay, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: A telegraph line running away over open ground, the old relay that handed a signal on from station to station: the poles are the stages and the note is a lit span of the top wire, its recirculations dimmer spans further down the line

cells.subject: A long cradle of hanging steel balls: a blow knocked into one end is handed ball to ball down the row and out the far end, then swings back in, so each ball is a stage and the swing that returns is the recirculation.
controls: stages: how many balls hang in the frame, 7 at 10 ms to 18 at 1 s, smaller as they multiply so the row keeps its length (count).
leak: a seeded set of balls take a dent, a flat on the lit side, and stop touching their neighbours, so the blow is lost there (shape of the dented balls, with the gap they leave).
clock: the balls hang on uneven strings and at uneven gaps, so the row goes from a straight touching line to a ragged one (position of each ball, up to ~1.6 units of drop).
feedback: how far the input ball swings back up as the output returns, from a small nudge at 0 to almost as high as the outgoing ball at 100 (rotation of the input ball's strings, 6° to 40°).
risks: A Newton's cradle is a well-known desk toy and can read as an icon of momentum, not of a delay; the swing arcs and the returning input ball have to carry the recirculation.
Hatched shadow sides on every ball are many short hairlines; at 18 balls they approach the node budget and the 3 px floor on small balls.
Strings from both rails to every ball are hairlines that fan and cross; at high clock they tangle (seen at the extremes).
The two swung balls are a frozen moment; the screen still shows a notional test note, not what's playing.

cells.alt: Relay, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: A long cradle of hanging steel balls: a blow knocked into one end is handed ball to ball down the row and out the far end, then swings back in, so each ball is a stage and the swing that returns is the recirculation

cells.subject: An eight-pin bucket-brigade chip with the top of its moulding cut away, showing the die on its lead frame and the chain itself as a meander of stages folded across the silicon, the test note a lit stretch of it and a return trace carrying it round again.
controls: stages: how many folds the meander makes across the die, 3 at 10 ms to 9 at 1 s, the chain getting longer inside the same silicon (count of folds).
leak: a seeded set of stages break out of the meander as gaps, each with a small hatched patch where the charge escapes into the substrate (count of gaps, hatching as the second cue).
clock: the folds lose their even pitch and bunch and spread across the die (position of each fold, up to ~35% of the pitch).
feedback: how many lit stretches are travelling round the meander and its return trace, one at 0 to five or six at the top, each further one dimmer (count of lit stretches).
risks: The subject is the chip, not the sound: it explains the device, and the meander that every control acts on is about a quarter of the frame at 1:1.
Edge-lit silhouette leaves most edges dark grey; on the real screen the #323232 outlines may vanish and the package may read as fragments.
Meander folds sit ~10 px apart at 9 folds and the folds are close to the 3 px floor where clock bunches them.
Lit stretches on one meander for several passes is a notional picture (the chain holds one copy at a time); the screen shows a test note, not what's playing.
cells.angle: a cutaway of the object at work, so the inside explains it
cells.alt: Relay, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: An eight-pin bucket-brigade chip with the top of its moulding cut away, showing the die on its lead frame and the chain itself as a meander of stages folded across the silicon, the test note a lit stretch of it and a return trace carrying it round again

cells.subject: The ring stains a bucket brigade leaves on a plank floor: a row of wet rings where each bucket stood, later passes set down over the first, fainter and more broken, and the freshest ring, where the note is now, the bright one.
controls: stages: how many rings make the row, 5 at 10 ms to 15 at 1 s, closer together as they multiply (count).
leak: drip trails of small spots run from a seeded set of rings toward the next, where those buckets leaked on their way along (count of drip spots).
clock: the rings lose their even spacing and step off the line, as if the buckets were set down in a hurry (position of each ring, up to ~40% of the pitch).
feedback: how many rings are set down over each first ring, offset and broken, one at 0 to five or six at the top, each fainter and more broken than the last (count of overlapping rings).
risks: Rings with an inner tide-mark can drift toward a target or a coffee-cup icon; the overlapping offset rings and the plank floor keep them stains.
The plank floor fills the frame; it's hairline and dark, but it's the busiest ground of the five and must not compete with the rings on the device.
At 15 rings with feedback high, overlapping rings crowd into a chain-link pattern (seen at the extremes).
The trace is a still record, so a note answers by a ring brightening and a new one being set down; motion is the design's to prove later.

machines.name: Sieve
machines.description: A harmonic sieve: a comb filter tuned to the input's fundamental keeps only chosen multiples, shaken to let others through.
machines.concept: A harmonic sieve: a comb filter tuned to the input's fundamental keeps only chosen multiples, shaken to let others through.
machines.soundsLike: A pitch tracker follows the input's fundamental and a bank of comb resonances sits on the harmonics it keeps, so a bass line through the sieve at 2nd comes out an octave up and glassy, at 3rd a twelfth up and hollow. Shake lets rejected harmonics flicker through at random, so a held note rattles and sparkles instead of ringing pure.

intake.subject: the sieve itself, a mesh that the input's harmonic series falls onto, with only the multiples it keeps getting through. (Five readings of it are in the subject pass below.)
intake.controlSource: new (the DSP is being written alongside this brief)

scores.effect: Jumps the heard pitch up by octaves, twelfths and beyond while thinning the tone from full to a few glassy partials; the biggest change on the machine
Nothing at 0, a faint shimmer by 30, a busy rattle of flickering partials by 100
Short plucky colour at 10 ms to a long singing drone at 2 s that outlasts the input
On a send the dry path is already in the track, so it mostly sets how much the sieve dominates; clear but not dramatic

cells.subject: Fig. 1: the sieved wave itself, emerging from a hatched wall in section and ringing out between dashed envelope lines, with reference numerals.
controls: mesh: the trace's period (shape): at 'all' one fundamental cycle per half, at 2nd an octave up, at 8th eight times as many cycles, so the pitch the sieve leaves is drawn.
shake: chaff, a count of grey grains scattered under the trace (0 → 24), each a leaked harmonic let through for a moment.
keep: the dashed envelope lines (shape of their own part): they close in near the wall at 10 ms and run almost parallel to the far end at 2 s, and the trace's amplitude follows them.
mix: a grey dry trace behind the bright one, scaled from flat on the axis at 100 % to full height at 0 % (scale).
cells.risks: Closest to 'oscilloscope', the pattern's own pitfall: what makes it authored is the patent apparatus (wall in section, numerals, leaders), which must stay sparing. At 8th the trace needs more points than one 64-point outline: 2–3 of the 4 paths, which spends the whole path budget on one part. Mesh and keep both reshape the visible trace even though keep's primary part is the envelope.

cells.subject: An atlas plate of a constellation drawn as an organ rank, twelve pipes in figure lines with a star at each mouth, the sieve's kept partials the bright named stars joined by the figure line.
controls: mesh: which stars are named and joined by the figure line (count: 12 at 'all', 6 at 2nd, down to 1 at 8th within the twelve drawn).
shake: rejected stars drift off their mouths along short proper-motion tracks (position, up to 24 px), brightening as they pass.
keep: the magnitude of the kept stars (scale, 0.8× → 1.6×), since a longer ring is a brighter, longer-lived partial.
mix: the magnitude of the unsieved stars (scale of a different part, pinpoints at 100 % to full size at 0 %).
cells.risks: Stretch, outside the effect column. The case for it: an organ's mutation and mixture stops are literally harmonic sieves (a 2 2/3' stop keeps the 3rd harmonic), so a rank of pipes is the one instrument people know by sight whose parts are the harmonic series, and atlases have always drawn constellations as instruments (Lyra, Pyxis). The case against: an effect acts on another track's sound, and the pipes suggest the sieve makes sound. P11's channel fit (only the struck part moves) doesn't map onto a filter. Two of the four controls are star-size scale on different parts. Twelve pipes cover only h1–h12, so 7th and 8th keep one star each.

cells.subject: A riddle seen dead side-on in elevation: the input's harmonics fall as rods onto its mesh plate, and only the rods over a hole drop through.
controls: mesh: the holes in the plate (count channel): every rod at 'all', every 2nd at 2nd, down to two holes at 8th; the plate's bright ribbon re-segments around them.
shake: the whole riddle slides sideways on its dimension line (position, ±24 px), and rods that land half over a hole leak through as grey stubs.
keep: how far the passed rods hang below the plate (position of their lower ends, 24 → 90 px): a short ring is a short rod.
mix: the bypass gate hinged on the left rim (rotation, 0° flush at 100 % to 70° open at 0 %) through which the unsieved column falls past the riddle.
cells.risks: Sixteen rods plus eight plate segments is a lot of uprights at 15 px pitch; at 8th the plate is nearly whole and the drawing goes quiet, which is honest but reads as 'off'. Shake as a slide only works if leaked stubs also appear, otherwise it's a position change of the whole thing with no sieve meaning. The gate is the weakest part: mix has no physical twin in a riddle.

cells.subject: A surveyed plan of the sieve from above on the left, sixteen numbered stations open or closed, beside a long-section profile of the output spectrum on the right.
controls: mesh: which stations in the plan are open rings and which are survey crosses (count, 16 → 2 open), with the profile's peaks following.
shake: the station lattice slides off the rim's datum (position, up to 40 px right), and small leaked peaks rise between the kept ones on the profile.
keep: the width of each profile peak (shape: broad hills at 10 ms, needles at 2 s), because a longer ring is a narrower resonance.
mix: a grey dry profile lifts off the datum line under the trace (position, 0 px at 100 % to 60 px at 0 %).
cells.risks: Two zones split attention; the plan is the explanation and the profile the result, so neither is clearly the subject. The profile is a spectrum, which drifts toward 'analyser'. Mix at its default (100 %) shows nothing, so the dry line only appears once turned. Two controls touch the profile (keep on shape, shake on leaked peaks); shake's primary channel has to stay the lattice slide.

machines.name: Tilt
machines.description: Tilt-shift for sound: a spectral tilt about a focal band, with a blur that smears everything outside the band in frequency and in time.
machines.concept: Tilt-shift for sound: a spectral tilt with a blur that smears everything outside a focal band.
machines.soundsLike: A one-octave band around the focus passes untouched while the rest of the spectrum is smeared, in frequency (partials melt into a wash) and a little in time (transients outside the band soften into swells), so the band seems to sit in front of a blurred background. A tilt filter pivoting on the focus darkens or brightens everything around it.

intake.subject: the sound's spectrum with one band held in focus, crisp, while everything outside it goes soft and the whole thing tilts about that band.
intake.controlSource: new (no source engine; "source" is the DSP sketched in `passes/01-subject/sketch.py`: flat-topped band window ±0.5 oct, log-frequency Gaussian smear outside it, ±6 dB/oct tilt about the focus)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 2 notes (effects have no browser preview yet; effect resources not reviewed beyond structure). Nothing to justify.

strongest picture of what the effect does to texture; the cost and the hatching read are the open questions.
depth-as-focus is right, but the echoes need taming.
best story, weakest fit; half its controls are scenery.
right idea, wrong look; it's the closest to a dashboard and has a channel clash.

cells.alt: Tilt at rest

cells.subject: One bright spectrum line, set like a textbook figure on a log-frequency axis, crisp and jagged inside the focal band and smoothed to a soft hump outside it.
controls: focus: position. The focal span (a 1.5 px bracket on the axis) and the dense, jagged stretch of the line slide together along the axis, 100 Hz to 8 kHz, about 290 px; the line re-keys where it's sharp.
tilt: rotation. The whole line turns about its point at the focus, ±18° (36° over the range; a little more than the true ±6 dB/oct slope so it clears the 30° floor).
blur: shape. Outside the band the line is smoothed by a wider kernel: at 0 the partials stand as sharp peaks right across, at 100 the line outside the band is a soft hump with no peaks.

mix: position. A dark hairline ghost of the dry, untouched spectrum sits under the bright line; mix drops it from on the line (0) to 34 px below (100), so the gap is how far the result has left the input.
risks: Easy to read as an analyser: the line is a fixed test spectrum (an effect page gets no audio), so it shows what the settings do, not what's playing. That has to be obvious or it reads as broken.

Tilt as rotation is slightly exaggerated (±18° for ±6 dB/oct) to clear the 30° floor; a 400 px line turned 18° pokes towards the header at the ends, so the pivot height and the turn need checking on the contact sheet.
Mix is the weakest channel: a ghost dropping away is a convention, not the sound. At the default (mix 100) the ghost is permanently 34 px down and adds clutter.
Budget: sharp-in-band needs dense points, so the line is three mutable outlines (left, band, right) of 31 centre points each; focus re-keys all three. Four paths is the cap.

cells.subject: Six octave bands stood up as cards in an oblique elevation, low at the front, high at the back; the card at the focus is drawn crisp and bright and the cards either side go soft with an echoed outline.
controls: focus: shade and position. The crisp bright outline and its detailed wave top step from card to card along the stack (front card at 100 Hz, back card at 8 kHz); five card steps, about 180 px of travel.
tilt: scale. Each card's height scales with its band's gain, so the stack's silhouette tilts: at −6 dB/oct the front cards stand tall and the back ones sink, at +6 the reverse (heights 0.6× to 1.6×).
blur: position. Every out-of-focus card's top contour is echoed by a dark hairline lifted above it, and its own wave flattens; blur lifts the echo from 3 px to 24 px and irons the wave out.
mix: position. The spacing of the stack: at 0 the six cards collapse onto one plane (dry: no depth, nothing separated), at 100 they spread to 36 px apart diagonally.
risks: Front cards hide most of the cards behind; only their tops and right edges show, so the focal card's detail is only visible in a strip ~36 px wide when it isn't the front card.
The echoed contours of six cards cross each other and read as a nest of wavy lines on the left at blur 40 %; at blur 100 it may turn into hatching.

Focus steps in six cards while the control has twenty positions; between octaves the bright card can't move, so focus needs a second cue (the crisp detail sliding across the card) or it reads as stepped.
Six stacked cards is at the 5–6 cap from P4.

cells.subject: A surveyed plot of square markers laid out frequency by time, where a vertical strip at the focus is surveyed sharp (bright solid markers, crisp hits) and the rest of the ground is smeared into even, hollow, mid-size markers.
controls: focus: position. The two strip boundary lines (1.5 px, past the neat line) and the solid bright markers between them slide across the plan, 100 Hz to 8 kHz, about 330 px.
tilt: scale. Marker size ramps across the plan from low to high frequency: at −6 the low side swells and the high side shrinks to 4 px, +6 the reverse (each marker 4–14 px).

blur: scale over time. Outside the strip each column's markers even out down the time axis: at 0 every column has the strip's crisp pattern (big at the three hits, tiny between), at 100 every row is the same mid size, the hits smeared away.
mix: count. A seeded scatter of markers outside the strip swaps between the dry look (the crisp pattern) and the wet look (smeared); mix sets how many have swapped, 0 to all 160.
risks: At 1:1 it reads as a matrix of LEDs or graph paper: a regular grid of identical squares is close to the 'dashboard of meters' the subject gate rejects.

Tilt and blur both change marker size (one across frequency, one down time); two controls on the scale channel of the same parts breaks the one-channel-per-control rule unless blur moves to shape (stretching markers into streaks along time) instead.
Size differences inside the haze are small at the default; the field looks uniform outside the strip, which is right for the sound but dull.
192 markers is fine for the node budget, but tilt and blur each resize nearly all of them: a turn redraws ~160 nodes, well past ~20 per frame while easing.
cells.alt: Tilt, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A surveyed plot of square markers laid out frequency by time, where a vertical strip at the focus is surveyed sharp (bright solid markers, crisp hits) and the rest of the ground is smeared into even, hollow, mid-size markers

cells.subject: The sound's texture cut through like a patent section, a block of square cells frequency by time in which the focal band stays as crisp solid cells on the hits and everything outside is cross-hatched cut material smeared into long runs.
controls: focus: position. The column pair that stays solid (bright, hits only) moves across the block, 100 Hz to 8 kHz, about 400 px; the hatching closes behind it.
tilt: count. The density of hatched cells ramps across the block: at −6 the low side fills and the high side empties, at +6 the reverse; about 40 cells change sides over the range.
blur: run length. Outside the band, hatched cells join into longer vertical runs (time smeared): at 0 they're single cells on the hit rows like the band, at 100 they run most of the block's height.
mix: count, second look. A seeded scatter of out-of-band cells keeps the dry look (a solid mid-grey cell on the hit rows, no hatching) instead of the cut look; mix 0 is all dry, 100 all hatched.
risks: Hatching is static art (hundreds of 1 px ribbons) and can't be swapped by palette, so each cell needs a pre-hatched variant to show or hide: two nodes per cell, 320 nodes, needs sdk 1.8 and is heavy.
P15 is for noise-like sounds; tilt processes whatever is sent to it, so this only fits by saying the drawing is the effect's texture, not the source. Gate 0 has to be argued.
Hatched regions at 5 px pitch look like 'disabled' stipple from desktop UIs; a patent reader sees cut material, a player may see greyed-out.
Tilt and mix are both counts on the same cells; they differ by which look (hatched vs dry solid) and where (gradient vs scatter), which may not be enough to tell them apart.
cells.alt: Tilt, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The sound's texture cut through like a patent section, a block of square cells frequency by time in which the focal band stays as crisp solid cells on the hits and everything outside is cross-hatched cut material smeared into long runs

cells.subject: A tilt-shift miniature: the spectrum built as a row of thin fins on a model base, with an upright glass plane of focus standing across it that captures the fins inside its depth of field as solid and leaves the rest hollow and doubled.
controls: focus: position. The plane of focus and its two depth-of-field lines on the base slide along the row, 100 Hz to 8 kHz, about 260 px of screen travel; fins entering it turn solid, fins leaving it go hollow.
tilt: shape. The base tips: fin heights ramp along the row about the plane of focus, so at −6 the near end towers and the far end sinks to stubs, at +6 the reverse (each fin 8–56 px).
blur: position. Each fin outside the depth of field casts a hollow ghost of itself set back into the base; blur pushes the ghost from 0 to ~14 px back, further for fins further from focus.
mix: position. No twin in the optics; a plain scale along the base's front edge (octave ticks, a 1.5 px bar) fills from 0 to the full length.
risks: Honest verdict on the stretch: it fits for focus and blur, and doesn't for tilt (a sloped base is a stand-in) or mix (a ruler in the corner, which P13 itself warns looks bolted on).
Twenty-two fins in a row read as a bookshelf or dominoes before they read as a spectrum; the glass plane is the only cue that this is about focus.
The camera is dimetric (24°/30°), not true isometric, to fit 300 px of row into a 200 px body; a strict 30° row would need ~170 px of drop.
Close to toro's hidden-line block field in look; the composition (one row, one plane) has to keep it from reading as a copy.
cells.alt: Tilt, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: A tilt-shift miniature: the spectrum built as a row of thin fins on a model base, with an upright glass plane of focus standing across it that captures the fins inside its depth of field as solid and leaves the rest hollow and doubled

machines.name: Ants
machines.description: A note player on aux track 12: ants walk a lattice of scale degrees leaving scent; trails strengthen into repeated phrases and fade when unused.
machines.concept: Ants walk a lattice of scale degrees leaving scent; trails strengthen into repeated phrases and fade when unused.
machines.soundsLike: Makes no sound of its own: it plays notes on the instrument tracks it steers, one note per ant per step it lands on a degree. With few ants and strong scent it settles into a short repeating figure; with many ants and fast fade it wanders, half-repeating, like a melody that keeps rewriting its ending.

intake.subject: a colony walking a lattice of scale degrees, where the trail it keeps using brightens into a phrase and the trails it leaves fade away.
intake.controlSource: new (the source is the control code I'm writing: ants step on the lattice each clock tick, choosing the next edge with weight `(ε + τ)^k` where τ is the edge's pheromone and k follows scent; every edge loses a fraction of τ each step set by fade; a walked edge gains a fixed deposit)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings, 1 note (trackControl: runs on aux track 12 with its own page on M1; show muted). `machine.json` declares `kind: synth`, `sdk: 1.9`; `resources.trackControl` is `{stateBytes 256, stateAlignment 8, savedBytes 128, aux [12], unique true}`. `resources.display` is the placeholder (`stateBytes 4, nodes 1, palette 1`) until phase 4.

scores.effect: One voice line to eight overlapping ones: note density and polyphony rise at every step, the largest change on the machine
Random wandering at 0 to a locked repeating phrase at 100; the change is in whether you hear repetition, clear within a bar or two
How long a phrase survives once ants leave it: slow to hear (takes several passes), subtle until ~40, then phrases visibly fail to settle
Changes the pitch set at once: pent to chrom is dramatic, neighbouring modes differ by one or two degrees

ranking.note: the strongest single picture of the rule, and fade (the hardest control to show) gets the clearest channel; its phrase-order gap is the thing to solve.
tells the phrase story best and is the cleanest at 1:1; needs to look less like a chart.
a sound P12, but the trail doubling and the idle nest need a redraw.
recognisable and well drawn, but a stretch that doesn't earn its exception.
the best lattice model in the weakest picture.

cells.subject: The colony seen as a textbook orrery: the nest a dark sphere at the centre, each octave of the scale an orbit round it, each degree a planet fixed at its pitch-class angle, and the reinforced trail a bright run of links from planet to planet with the ants walking on it.
controls: ants: count, the number of ant marks on the trail links, 1 to 8 (4 at default); each new ant eases in at the nest and walks out onto the trail, so 1 → 8 is three doublings of bodies spread round the orbits.

scent: shape, the bright trail itself: at 0 the links scatter into short one-step arcs between many planets, at 100 they close into one loop that repeats, so the run of bright links contracts by ≥ 16 px on its outer points as it locks onto a phrase.

fade: count + shade, the older trails behind the live one: at 0 up to six grey trail runs stay on the orbits, stepping darker with age; at 100 only the live trail is left, the rest gone within a pass.

scale: count + position, planets per orbit and the spokes under them: pent 5, major/minor/modes 7, chrom 12 per orbit, each planet sliding to its pitch-class angle so the rings fill from a pentagon to an even clock.
cells.risks: The trail returns over its own arcs (a phrase reuses edges), so at 1:1 the reinforced links double up beside the orbits on the left and read as a thick ring rather than a path. Cross-octave steps can't stay on one orbit (P12's pitfall: links across orbits); here they are short spiral links, which is the one place the pattern is bent. The nest does nothing a control drives, the same objection P13 makes of P12's sun. Ants on a 2.4 px bright link are only a bead; at 1:1 they read as knots, not bodies, and the brightest-element rule makes trail and ants compete. 24 bound nodes at rest in the sketch; twelve planets per orbit at chrom plus 8 ants plus up to 4 trail outlines stays well under 256.
cells.alt: Ants, variant 1 kept as sequencer

cells.subject: The colony seen as a textbook orrery: the nest a dark sphere at the centre, each octave of the scale an orbit round it, each degree a planet fixed at its pitch-class angle, and the reinforced trail a bright run of links from planet to planet with the ants walking on it.

scale: count + position, planets per orbit and the spokes under them: pent 5, major/minor/modes 7, chrom 12 per orbit, each planet sliding to its pitch-class angle so the rings fill from a pentagon to an even clock.
cells.risks: The trail returns over its own arcs (a phrase reuses edges), so at 1:1 the reinforced links double up beside the orbits on the left and read as a thick ring rather than a path.
