cells.alt: Ants, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The colony seen as a textbook orrery: the nest a dark sphere at the centre, each octave of the scale an orbit round it, each degree a planet fixed at its pitch-class angle, and the reinforced trail a bright run of links from planet to planet with the ants walking on it

cells.subject: An elevation cut across the lattice where every walked degree has built a mound of scent and fade is a waterline: what the colony keeps walking stands dry and plays, what it leaves is drowned.
controls: ants: count, the ants standing on the dry crests, one per crest, 1 to 8; the extra ants take the next-highest crests in order, so the row of bodies spreads from one mound to most of the lattice.
scent: shape, the mound profile: each crossing builds its mound in proportion to scent, so at 0 the profile is a low even ripple and at 100 the reinforced degrees stand ≥ 40 px taller than the rest.

fade: position, the waterline rises from just above the ground at 0 to two thirds of the tallest crest at 100 (≥ 60 px), and every mound below it drops from the bright line weight to the drowned grey.
scale: count + position, the number of mounds and their spacing along the ground: 11 at pent (two octaves) to 25 at chrom, with the degree names under the ground line moving with them.
cells.risks: The elevation loses the walk's order: it shows which degrees the colony favours, not the phrase it repeats, so 'trails strengthen into repeated phrases' is half told. A row of rounded peaks above a band reads as a waveform or a bar meter at a glance; the earth ticks and the elevation label carry the 'ground' reading, and that may not be enough at arm's length (P3's oscilloscope trap, by another road). The profile needs two or three 64-point mutable outlines and re-keys on every scent or fade turn; the waterline splitting it into dry and drowned runs also re-keys on fade, so turning fade redraws the most.
cells.alt: Ants, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: An elevation cut across the lattice where every walked degree has built a mound of scent and fade is a waterline: what the colony keeps walking stands dry and plays, what it leaves is drowned

cells.subject: A survey plan of the colony's recent passes, eight step stations across, each pass plotted as one traverse whose height on its row is the degree it played, the newest at the front and older ones stepping back and greying, so a phrase that has set shows as the same line repeated down the plan.
controls: ants: count, the ant marks walking the newest traverse between its stations, 1 to 8, one per leg the ants are on; at 8 every leg of the front pass carries a body.
scent: shape, how alike the passes are: at 0 each older traverse wanders off the front one by up to three degrees per station (≥ 16 px), at 100 all rows lie as copies of the same line.
fade: count + shade, how many past passes are still plotted behind the front one, six at 0 to none at 100, each older row one grey step darker and on a finer line.

scale: shape + count, the degree ruler at the left margin and the height step per degree: pent quantises the traverses to 5 levels per octave with coarse steps, chrom to 12 with fine ones, so every row redraws finer or coarser.
cells.risks: The plan is honest but cool: at 1:1 it reads close to a line chart with a history, and the 'picture, not panel' rule is the one it leans on hardest. Loom's own strength (slabs and depth) is given up for a flat plan, so depth-as-earlier is carried only by row position and grey steps. Eight stations assumes an eight-step phrase; the machine's phrases are whatever the trail makes, so the station count would come from the trail's length, and a long trail crowds the plan. Each row is one mutable outline and there are only 4 paths, so at most four rows can change shape; older rows have to be frozen copies.
cells.alt: Ants, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A survey plan of the colony's recent passes, eight step stations across, each pass plotted as one traverse whose height on its row is the degree it played, the newest at the front and older ones stepping back and greying, so a phrase that has set shows as the same line repeated down the plan

cells.subject: A patent figure of the lattice as a ground field of degree nodes, step neighbours across and third neighbours into depth, cut along its front edge, with the reinforced trail as one bright closed loop over it, the ants on that loop, and the phrase's steps in a strip below.
controls: ants: count, ant marks spaced along the loop and the lit cells in the step strip, 1 to 8; the strip's lit cells show how many ants landed on a note in the last pass.
scent: shape, the figure: at 0 the loop frays into three loose strands wandering across the field, at 100 they draw together into one tight loop on the same nodes (strand points move ≥ 16 px).
fade: count + shade, the dashed ghost loops left on the field by abandoned trails: up to five at 0, stepping darker with age, none at 100.
scale: count + position, the field's columns: pent's 10 node columns to chrom's 24, the mesh closing up as the lattice gets finer while the loop stays on the degrees it uses.
cells.risks: The patent section (hatched cut face, reference numerals, FIG. 2) is the most decorative language of the five and nothing in the section moves; it may read as costume over P5. The skewed Tonnetz-like field is right for the lattice but at 1:1 its diagonals converge into a fan that reads as perspective noise, and at chrom 24 columns the back rows fall under the 3 px hatching floor and must fade out. The figure is one smooth loop through seven nodes; a real trail can cross itself, so the loop sometimes becomes a figure-eight that needs both 64-point outlines. Closest to the reference's composition (field, one figure, strip), so care is needed not to borrow its look.
cells.alt: Ants, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: A patent figure of the lattice as a ground field of degree nodes, step neighbours across and third neighbours into depth, cut along its front edge, with the reinforced trail as one bright closed loop over it, the ants on that loop, and the phrase's steps in a strip below

cells.subject: A glass-sided formicarium on a plinth in hidden-line isometric, one chamber dug for every degree, the octaves as galleries winding back and forth up the slab, and the reinforced trail as the bright tunnel the ants keep using.
controls: ants: count, ants in the tunnels, 1 to 8, each walking the live trail; the ones not on the trail sit in the nest chamber at the top.
scent: scale + shape, tunnel bore: the live trail's tunnels widen from a hairline at 0 to a full 2.4 px bore with chambers rimmed bright at 100, while unused tunnels stay hairline.
fade: count, old tunnels left dashed and collapsing: at 0 every tunnel ever dug stays open (up to ten dashed runs), at 100 only the live trail's tunnels are left.
scale: count + position, chambers per gallery: 5 at pent to 12 at chrom, sliding closer along each gallery so the slab stays the same size.
cells.risks: Outside the category's column (see stretch). At 1:1 the octave-one gallery's tunnels bunch along the isometric diagonal and the trail reads as a tangle; galleries that wind back and forth help but don't cure it. The slab takes a third of the screen as a frame that never changes. Close to theseus' hidden-line look (black-filled parts, grey edges, a plinth); the shapes are its own, but the family resemblance is strong. A chamber per degree at chrom is 25 chambers on a 184 px gallery, 14 px apart, close to the touching limit.
cells.alt: Ants, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: A glass-sided formicarium on a plinth in hidden-line isometric, one chamber dug for every degree, the octaves as galleries winding back and forth up the slab, and the reinforced trail as the bright tunnel the ants keep using

cells.subject: The colony walking a glockenspiel, one bar per degree, so the loop the ants keep treading across the bars is the phrase they play.
controls: ants: count, contour ants walking the bright loop over the bars, 1 to 8, spaced evenly round it; each new one eases in at the lowest bar.

scent: shape, the loop itself: at 0 it frays into a loose scribble that wanders over many bars, at 100 it pulls into one tight oval over the few bars the phrase uses (outer points move well over 16 px).
fade: count, the dashed old routes still lying across the bars: two at 0 and default, none by 100, each one thinning out from its far end as it goes.
scale: count + position, the bars themselves: 11 at pent (two octaves) up to 25 at chrom, bars narrowing and sliding closer so the instrument keeps its width, the rails following.
cells.risks: A glockenspiel is a picture of any melodic machine; only the ants and the loop make it this one, so it lives or dies on the ants reading at 26 px. The loop is a smooth oval, so which bars actually sound (landings, not crossings) isn't drawn; a note flash on the struck bar has to carry that. At chrom 25 bars are ~12 px wide with 6 px gaps, close to crowding. Single weight means the trail stands out by brightness alone (it's drawn 0.5 px heavier as the one exception).
cells.angle: the machine's own rule as a physical thing: what turning each knob would do to a real object
cells.alt: Ants, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: The colony walking a glockenspiel, one bar per degree, so the loop the ants keep treading across the bars is the phrase they play

cells.subject: One ant at large scale in side elevation, its gaster cut open to show the gland and duct laying the scent trail behind it, its antennae reading the trail, followers walking the trail it leaves.
controls: ants: count, the small ants following in file on the trail behind the big one, 0 to 7 (1 to 8 with it), each easing in from the left edge.
scent: rotation, the flagellum of the near antenna pivots at its elbow from raised and searching (about −35°) at 0 to pressed down onto the ground trail (about +70°) at 100, over 100°.

fade: position, where the deposited trail dies: the bright fresh stretch runs back from the sting, then a hatched evaporating stretch, whose far end moves from the left edge at 0 to just behind the ant at 100 (over 100 px).
scale: count + position, the stone slabs under the ground line, one per degree: 11 at pent to 25 at chrom.
cells.risks: It explains the rule (deposit, sense, evaporate) better than it shows the phrase: the trail is a straight line along the ground, so the repeating melody isn't visible; the ant is the subject but the bright element is the trail. Hatched masses on head and thorax plus a hatched cut wall is a lot of hatching; at 1:1 it holds, but on the device it may read grey. The followers are 30 px and only just read as ants. The scale slabs along the bottom are close to a strip of cells.
cells.angle: a cutaway of the object at work, so the inside explains it
cells.alt: Ants, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: One ant at large scale in side elevation, its gaster cut open to show the gland and duct laying the scent trail behind it, its antennae reading the trail, followers walking the trail it leaves

cells.subject: A leaf held against low light, black with its margin and veins edge-lit, one side vein per degree, and the glistening trail the colony has worn across it as the loop it keeps walking.
controls: ants: count, edge-lit ant silhouettes on the trail, 1 to 8, spaced round the loop.
scent: shape, the trail: at 0 it frays into several faint wandering threads across the leaf, at 100 it is one tight bright loop through the phrase's veins (points move ≥ 16 px).
fade: count, the dashed dull traces of trails no longer walked: two at 0–30, none at 100, each shortening from its old end.
scale: count + position, side veins per side: 5 (pent) to 12 (chrom), sliding closer along the midrib; lower side octave one, upper side octave two.
cells.risks: The leaf is beautiful but arbitrary: nothing about ants requires it, and veins as degrees is a mapping the player has to be told. The loop crosses itself (the phrase revisits a degree), which at 1:1 reads as a zigzag in the middle. Edge-lit silhouettes need the ants to sit on something lit; on black leaf they read only by their hairline edge.
cells.angle: the mark or trace the process leaves behind
cells.alt: Ants, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: A leaf held against low light, black with its margin and veins edge-lit, one side vein per degree, and the glistening trail the colony has worn across it as the loop it keeps walking

cells.subject: One fork of the lattice at large scale: a twig junction where a step can go to any degree of the octave, one branch per degree, a scout ant on the knot turning onto the scented branch and the rest of the lattice past the frame's edge.
controls: ants: count, ants already out along the scented branch, 0 to 7 behind the scout, the farthest ones leaving the frame.
scent: rotation, the scout's heading on the knot swings from between branches at 0 to square onto the scented branch at 100 (about 70°).
fade: position, how far the old scent (hatched band) still reaches up the unused branches: to the frame edge at 0, shrinking back to the knot by 100.
scale: count + rotation, branches out of the knot: 5 at pent, 7 for the modes, 12 at chrom, fanning closer together.
cells.risks: Shows one decision, not the phrase: what the colony plays over time isn't drawn, only which way it goes next, so the player sees the rule more than the result. Branches per degree of the octave is a simplification of the real lattice (step and third neighbours). At chrom twelve branches crowd into a fan near the knot. Twigs could pass for roads at a glance; the bark fissures carry the reading.
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Ants, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: One fork of the lattice at large scale: a twig junction where a step can go to any degree of the octave, one branch per degree, a scout ant on the knot turning onto the scented branch and the rest of the lattice past the frame's edge

cells.subject: Ants drawn literally: a few hidden-line 3D ants, modelled from ellipsoids with segmented gasters and jointed legs, walking the bright trail between low degree stones in two rows, under one camera.
controls: ants: count, modelled ants on the trail, 1 to 8, nearer ones larger, each easing in from the nest end of the loop.
scent: position, how closely the ants keep to the trail: at 0 they straggle up to a stone's width off it at random headings, at 100 they walk nose to tail on it (≥ 24 px).
fade: count, the dashed old routes between stones: two at 0–30, none at 100.
scale: count + position, the stones per row: 5 at pent to 12 at chrom per octave, closing up along each row.
cells.risks: The ants need pre-drawn variants per heading (a node can't turn out of the screen plane), so 8 ants × several headings is the costliest of the five. At 1:1 the far ants overlap stones and the legs read busy; three weights and hidden-line keep it legible but it's the most cluttered frame. Close in look to theseus' black-with-grey-edge family. The near row runs off both sides of the frame.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Ants, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: Ants drawn literally: a few hidden-line 3D ants, modelled from ellipsoids with segmented gasters and jointed legs, walking the bright trail between low degree stones in two rows, under one camera

cells.subject: A hand-held marble board whose rocker gates are pushed toward each side a marble takes and sprung back to centre, so the route the marbles keep taking wears into one bright groove through the cascade.
controls: ants: count, marbles rolling down the worn groove, 1 to 8, spaced along the route from the entry to the outlets.
scent: rotation, how far the gates on the worn route are thrown across the branch not taken, from a slight lean (about 11°) at 0 to hard over (about 33°) at 100.
fade: count, how many older routes still show hatched residue in their channels, several at 0 down to none at 100 (the springs win).
scale: count, columns of gates and outlets on the board: 5 outlets at pent, 7 for the modes, 12 at chrom, the diamonds narrowing to fit.
cells.risks: A Galton-style board reads as chance first; only the thrown gates and the one bright groove say 'reinforced'. It shows which outlet the colony prefers, not the phrase's order. At chrom (11 columns) the diamonds get small and the gates crowd; the board's hatching is a lot of lines (cost and calm), and the route's residue hatch is close in look to the board's own.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Ants, pass 3 (subject), variant 1: A hand-held marble board whose rocker gates are pushed toward each side a marble takes and sprung back to centre, so the route the marbles keep taking wears into one bright groove through the cascade

cells.subject: The ground the colony works, seen close and low: sand grains lit along their upper edges, a channel swept clear through them that bends past pebbles, scent lying on its floor as beads that shrink and dry back along it.
controls: ants: count, fresh beads at the head of the channel with a bright rim, 1 to 8; the nearest is the note just landed.
scent: shape, the channel's width and how cleanly it is swept, from a scuffed narrow track to a wide clean channel.
fade: scale + count, how fast the beads shrink back along the channel and how far back they last before drying to a mark; the old branch fills with grains.
scale: count, pebbles the channel bends around: 5 at pent, 7 for the modes, 12 at chrom, closer together.
cells.risks: Hundreds of grains: far over the node and redraw budget, so a device version would need the grains as a few fixed textured paths. At 1:1 the grain field can read as gravel or a starfield, and the beads are small; the channel's bends don't give pitch, only order. The grain field's rounded far boundary reads a little like a mound.
cells.angle: the material the sound acts on, seen close
cells.alt: Ants, pass 3 (subject), variant 2: The ground the colony works, seen close and low: sand grains lit along their upper edges, a channel swept clear through them that bends past pebbles, scent lying on its floor as beads that shrink and dry back along it

cells.subject: A ford of stepping stones across a stream, one row per step and one stone per degree, where the crossing everyone takes is worn smooth and dished while the stones nobody uses are mossed over.
controls: ants: count, stones on the worn route that are still wet from a crossing (a short sheen on the near lip), 1 to 8.
scent: shape, how deep the polished dish is on the route stones and how bare their tops are, from barely worn to a deep tread.
fade: shape, how far the moss (hatching) has grown back over the old route's bare patches, none at 0 to closed over at 100.
scale: count, stones per row: 5 at pent, 7 for the modes, 12 at chrom, smaller and closer across the stream.
cells.risks: Thirty stones each with flank lines, ripples and hatched moss is far over budget and close to busy at 1:1; the hatched tops can read as biscuits. The route is told by bare against hatched more than by line weight, and reading rows as steps needs the frame to cross from bank to bank, so the crossing's order is only implied. Twelve stones a row at chrom will crowd.
cells.angle: one scene where this happens, with one subject in it
cells.alt: Ants, pass 3 (subject), variant 3: A ford of stepping stones across a stream, one row per step and one stone per degree, where the crossing everyone takes is worn smooth and dished while the stones nobody uses are mossed over

cells.subject: One iron mooring ring at large scale with ropes running off the frame to the rest of the lattice, the way the colony keeps using laid up thick and taut, the ways it leaves hanging slack and frayed through.
controls: ants: count, strands laid into the taut rope (its lay lines and its girth), 1 to 8.
scent: shape, how slack the unused ropes hang, all taut alike at 0 to deep sags at 100.
fade: position, where the slack ropes have frayed through, the break running from the frame edge at 0 back toward the ring at 100, hatched beyond it.
scale: count, ropes hitched to the ring: 5 at pent, 7 for the modes, 12 at chrom.
cells.risks: A ring with ropes is a mooring or a lifebuoy before it is a colony; the metaphor (more strands, more trail) needs saying once. It shows one junction's state, not the phrase. Thin ropes are only ~5 px, so their hatched ghosts barely read, and slack curves are mutable outlines (4-path limit) if they move.
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Ants, pass 3 (subject), variant 4: One iron mooring ring at large scale with ropes running off the frame to the rest of the lattice, the way the colony keeps using laid up thick and taut, the ways it leaves hanging slack and frayed through

cells.subject: The trail itself, drawn as the thing it is: a band swept clear through the litter in one closed loop past the stones it plays, old spurs fading out from it, seeds carried round it.
controls: ants: count, seeds carried round the loop, 1 to 8.
scent: shape, the band's width, a narrow scuffed track at 0 to a wide cleared road at 100.
fade: position, how far the old spurs (hatched) still reach out from the loop before they give out, long at 0, stubs at 100.
scale: count, stones in the clearing: 5 at pent, 7 for the modes, 12 at chrom; the loop touches the ones its phrase plays.
cells.risks: A closed band in oblique view can read as a race track or a pool; the loop is in a plan-like view that sits near pass 01's field-and-figure loop, though there's no lattice field here. Twig capsules and spur ends are the weakest drawing; the stones the phrase plays are only told by sitting on the loop.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well

machines.name: Ebb
machines.description: A track-control player on aux track 12: notes rise and fall with a tide over a scale; the tide's height picks the register, foam scatters grace notes at the turn.
machines.concept: Notes rise and fall with a tide over a scale: the tide's height picks the register, foam scatters grace notes at the turn.
machines.soundsLike: A slow melodic swell that climbs and falls through the target track's register on a scale, like water up and down a flight of steps. At the top and bottom of each tide, foam adds quick neighbour-note flurries before it turns.

intake.subject: the tide itself, a water level that rises and falls over a scale's steps on a slow period, picking the register from its height and throwing foam (grace notes) at each turn.
intake.controlSource: new (the DSP is the control code written for this machine)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 1 warning (plus the trackControl note).

scores.effect: From one repeated note (0 st) to a three-octave swing; the register sweep is the machine's main gesture.
From a fast warble (1 s) to a contour that takes 32 s to come round; changes the music's whole pace.
Nothing at 0; flurries of grace notes only near the turns, so it's heard twice a period, not continuously.
Every note's interval changes, the contour doesn't; clear to the ear but the shape stays.

pick.reason: Cleaning up v5 would work well.

cells.name: rest
cells.alt: Ebb at rest

cells.subject: A star chart of the last sixteen seconds where every scale degree at every moment is a star sized by how near the tide passes it, so the notes rise and set along a sinuous ecliptic toward the brightest star, now.
controls: tide: the ecliptic band's swing between declinations widens from a flat line of stars at the mean at 0 st to the full +0 to +36 chart at 36 st (shape of the field).
period: the band's wavelength across right ascension stretches from 16 crests in the window at 1 s to half a crest at 32 s (shape of the field, along the other axis).
foam: faint stars scatter off the band at its crests and troughs, none to about 30, like a cluster round each turning point (count).
scale: the rows of stars re-space to the scale's degrees, so pentatonic draws five widely spaced rows per octave and hirajoshi five unevenly spaced ones (position of the rows).
cells.risks: Stretch outside the player column. The case for the exception: ebb's rule is a continuous function of time (a sine quantised to a scale), so like an engine's signal it can be computed into a field of identical parts, and each control does to the field what it does to the notes. The honest case against: what results is a scatter plot of pitch over time, a piano roll with star dots; P10's charm is that the field is the sound's shape, and here the shape is just the melody, which any sequencer page already shows. It reads as a graph at 1:1, not as an atlas, despite the graticule and labels. Budget: 40 columns x 22 degrees is 880 cells, past 512 nodes, so only the ~3 nearest degrees per column can be nodes (120), placed per column; the chart scrolls every column step, far over ~20 nodes a frame. Muted: the band stops scrolling and the now star goes hollow.
cells.cleanNote: Same star chart, same rule, same composition as `rest.svg`. Generated by `clean.py` → `clean.svg`, `clean.png`, copied to `screens/ebb/frames/rest.svg` / `rest.png` as the pick. Lint: 0 errors, 0 warnings (the sketch had 7 text-in-drawing and 20 legibility warnings).
cells.alt: Ebb, cleaned variant 5: A star chart of the last sixteen seconds where every scale degree at every moment is a star sized by how near the tide passes it, so the notes rise and set along a sinuous ecliptic toward the brightest star, now

cells.subject: A stepped sea wall seen in elevation, one tread per scale degree rising with pitch, where the water level is the capture line and the highest tread it covers is the note that plays.
controls: tide: the painted hw and lw marks and their range dimension spread apart up the wall face, from one line at 0 st to 144 px apart at 36 st, and the water's travel between them with it (position of the marks).
period: the swell on the water surface stretches from a tight chop (about 8 px wavelength at 1 s) to one long gentle wave across the pool at 32 s (shape of the surface line).
foam: spray marks spring up the wall face where the water meets it, none at 0 % to a cloud of about 24 at 100 %, grouped at the turn (count).

scale: the staircase re-cuts itself: tread heights follow the scale's intervals, so pentatonic gives fewer, taller risers and hirajoshi a lopsided run of short and tall ones (shape of the wall profile).
cells.risks: Capture's strength is that the threshold is the player's choice; here the water's height is the tide, which the player sets only in range, so the capture line moves on its own while playing (that's the point, but it means the subject animates with the clock, a slow continuous redraw). The wall profile is up to 46 points and reshapes on every scale change, and the water polygon is a second mutable outline that follows the level every frame it moves: 2 of 4 paths, re-keyed on level change, so throttle level updates to whole semitones. 22 risers at 17 px are fine for the seven-note scales; pentatonic and hirajoshi give 16, so the wall's width changes with scale unless tread width is fitted. Muted: the water drains to datum and the captured block goes hollow grey, a change in position, not shade alone. It is the most literal of the five; it may read as a bar chart from across a room.
cells.alt: Ebb, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A stepped sea wall seen in elevation, one tread per scale degree rising with pitch, where the water level is the capture line and the highest tread it covers is the note that plays

cells.subject: A surveyed sheet of the last four rows of tide, woven as weft threads across sixteen chainage lines, each note a slab sounded on its line and the newest row bright at the front.
controls: tide: every row's weft swings further from its dashed mean-water contour, from flat rows at 0 st to arcs spanning 36 px of the 40 px row at 36 st (shape of the rows).
period: the weft's waves tighten or relax across the rows: at 1 s each row holds four crests, at 8 s each row is one half arc, at 32 s each row is an almost straight slope (shape, across all rows).

foam: hollow grace slabs appear beside the solid ones near each crest and trough, scattered differently in every row, so the cloth shows what changed pass to pass (count, and the loom's solid vs hollow role).

scale: the scale bar in the sheet's corner re-divides into alternating blocks at the scale's degrees, and the slabs snap to its steps so the weft turns from smooth to terraced (shape of the corner bar, second cue in the rows).
cells.risks: Loom's power is history that varies; with foam at 0 every row is the same tide, so at defaults it shows no history worth reading, only a periodic wave. Flat on a plan, it loses P14's depth cue (rows recede in 3D) and leans toward a grid of dashes: dashboard-of-meters risk at 1:1. 64 slabs plus 4 weft outlines (all 4 paths) is fine for nodes, but each step shifts every row back (a whole-sheet redraw per eighth note), far over ~20 nodes a frame; it needs a scroll-only-on-bar rule or a playhead instead. The corner scale bar is a legend, the kind of thing P13 permits but craft calls panel. Muted: the newest row's slabs go hollow and the weft stops being added (rows stop moving).
cells.alt: Ebb, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: A surveyed sheet of the last four rows of tide, woven as weft threads across sixteen chainage lines, each note a slab sounded on its line and the newest row bright at the front

cells.subject: Fig. 1, a float cut in section riding a receding sea, its graduated spar sliding past a fixed index arm on a pile, with the notes it has read ticked along a strip below.
controls: tide: the two stop collars (16) on the pile spread apart from touching at 0 st to 108 px at 36 st, and the float rides between them when playing (position).
period: the swell lines of the receding sea lengthen from a tight chop to long rollers, front wavelength 9 px at 1 s to 288 px at 32 s (shape of the field, re-keyed only on turns).
foam: spray strokes break off the hull at the waterline, none to about 20, thrown highest at the turns (count).
scale: the spar's graduations re-space to the scale's degrees, octave ticks long, so pentatonic reads as sparse wide marks and lydian as dense ones (position of the ticks).
cells.risks: A patent drawing carries reference numerals and leaders that are decoration once you know the parts; they must stay few and static. The receding field is ten full-width lines of about 220 points each: as static art it is free, but period reshapes all of them, which needs four 64-point mutable outlines at most, so the field has to drop to four lines on the device or period moves something smaller. The spar's major-scale ticks sit 3 px apart at semitone steps, on the hatching floor. Muted: a lock bar drops across the spar at the index, a shape cue, and the float sits on its lower stop.
cells.alt: Ebb, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: Fig

cells.subject: The moon on its orbit drawing the sea out into a bright spheroid round a dashed, hidden earth, with the twelve pitch classes as beads on a ring between them.
controls: tide: the water spheroid stretches toward the moon, from a sphere just over the earth at 0 st to a long lemon 2.2x its width at 36 st (shape of the brightest outline).
period: the moon's orbit widens, Kepler-style, from 80 to 124 units of radius as the period runs 1 s to 32 s, carrying the moon outward (scale of the orbit, position of the moon).
foam: spray marks fly off both tips of the bulge, none to about 16, densest at the tip facing the moon (count).
scale: the beads on the pitch-class ring fill for the scale's notes and empty for the rest, 5 to 7 of 12 filled, so each scale is a distinct pattern round the ring (count and shade on fixed parts).
cells.risks: Real tides have two bulges per lunar day; a spheroid points both ends, so one player period is half a moon orbit, which a physicist would notice and a player won't. The moon turns once per period on a long period it barely moves; it needs to be stepped. Scale lives on fill state of 12 beads; maj and min differ by two or three beads, which is close to shade-only and must also change the ring (e.g. scale notes sit on the ring, others step in). Orbits as concentric ellipses invite the Saturn/target-ring look craft warns about; the hidden earth helps. The spheroid silhouette is a mutable outline re-keyed on tide turns and as the moon moves (its axis turns), so throttle it. Muted: the moon goes hollow and the spheroid relaxes to a sphere.
cells.alt: Ebb, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The moon on its orbit drawing the sea out into a bright spheroid round a dashed, hidden earth, with the twelve pitch classes as beads on a ring between them

machines.name: Ferry
machines.description: A track-control player on aux track 12: a ferry runs a route between ports (the held chord's tones), dwells at each port before it plays it, and swell holds it up on the way.
machines.soundsLike: No sound of its own: it plays the target track's engine. Hold a chord and it walks the chord's tones one at a time in a set order, an arpeggio with a timetable; swell makes the calls late and uneven, like a boat pushed off schedule.

intake.subject: a ferry working a timetable between ports that are the held chord's tones, calling at them in route order, held up by swell, and waiting at each for the dwell before it plays that tone.
intake.controlSource: new (the DSP is the control code I'm writing)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 1 warning.

ranking.note: closest to the machine's own rule, every control on the main subject, most authored.
best picture of history and swell, but loses the ferry.
most recognisable, weakest control distribution.
good dwell image, weak story, graticule noise.
the stretch doesn't earn it.

cells.subject: Survey sheets of each port's harbour stacked diagonally in the order the route calls at them, the front sheet the port the ferry is berthed at, its berth drawn as long as the dwell.
controls: route: the order the sheets stack in, read from the port names on their edges (C4 E4 G4 C5 for up, reversed for down); position of each sheet in the stack.
ports: how many sheets are stacked, 2 to 8 (6 visible, the deepest two hidden behind the sixth with a count), so the stack grows up and to the right; count.
swell: the depth contours on the front sheet wander off their smooth lines and the ferry swings on its berth; shape of the contours.
dwell: the dashed berth on the pier lengthens from 16 px at 1/32 to 42 px at 1/2; shape of the berth.
cells.risks: Stretch, and it mostly doesn't fit. P4 is a stack the sound scans through continuously; a player steps, so each note becomes a slide change that swaps the whole front sheet, the opposite of P4's cheap shade-only layers. The case for it: the ports are an ordered set like wavetable frames and the route is a scan order through them, so a stack is a literal picture of route x ports. But route then rides on text labels on the sheet edges, which is reading, not seeing, and swell and dwell sit on one small sheet. The front sheet's coast and contours are generic (every port is the same drawing), so nothing about C4 vs G4 is shown. Muted: the front sheet drops back into the stack's grey.
cells.cleanNote: Generated by `clean.py` (model and helpers imported from `../sketch.py`, which I didn't touch). Defaults: route up, 4 ports, swell 0, dwell 1/8. Lint: 0 errors, 0 warnings. Not picked yet, so it stays in the pass folder.
cells.alt: Ferry, cleaned variant 5: Survey sheets of each port's harbour stacked diagonally in the order the route calls at them, the front sheet the port the ferry is berthed at, its berth drawn as long as the dwell

cells.subject: A ferry drawn in side elevation, with centreline, waterline and hidden hull lines, riding a receding sea mesh above a timing diagram of its timetable, one pulse per port at the port's pitch.
controls: route: reorders the pulses in the timing diagram, so the strip's contour becomes a rising stair (up), a falling stair (down), a peak (shtl), a zigzag (cross) or a scatter (tramp); shape of the strip trace.
ports: how many pulse heights the timetable cycles through before it repeats, 2 to 8, each new port a taller pulse (the chord's next tone); count on the strip.
swell: the sea mesh lifts into waves that grow toward the viewer and the hull heels up to 9 degrees, while each pulse slips late in its slot; rotation of the figure, shape of the field.
dwell: the timetable's slot length, from 32 slots a bar at 1/32 down to 2 at 1/2, so the pulses widen and thin out; count and width on the strip.
cells.risks: The figure (the ferry) carries only swell; route, ports and dwell all live in a 28 px strip, so three of four controls sit in the smallest part of the screen and the player's eye lands on the one that does least. The ferry is a figure people recognise, which edges toward an illustration rather than a picture of the rule; it must not gain portholes, flags or wake. At dwell 1/32 the strip is 32 pulses 12 px apart, about the hatching floor. Muted state not drawn yet: proposed as the hull outline dropping from #CDCDCD to #646464 and the strip going dashed, never shade alone.
cells.alt: Ferry, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A ferry drawn in side elevation, with centreline, waterline and hidden hull lines, riding a receding sea mesh above a timing diagram of its timetable, one pulse per port at the port's pitch

cells.subject: An X-Y oscilloscope graticule with one tilted orbit per octave around the root, the chord's tones as points placed by pitch class, the route traced from point to point, and the beam spot as the ferry.
controls: route: which arcs of the orbits the trace lights and in which direction, so up runs forward round each orbit, down runs back, shtl doubles back, cross jumps and flashes the far point, tramp lights a scatter; shape of the links.
ports: how many points sit on the orbits, filling the inner orbit then stepping out an octave at a time to the third orbit, 2 to 8 points; count, plus which orbits light (shade as second cue).
swell: the orbit traces ripple like a noisy beam, nine lobes per turn whose depth grows with swell; shape of the orbits.
dwell: the size of the beam spot burnt in at the port it dwells on, 3 px at 1/32 to 9 px at 1/2; scale of the ferry.
cells.risks: An oscilloscope is the language P3 warns drifts into saying nothing new; here the graticule carries no data and costs 70+ static lines. Placing ports by pitch class makes C, E and G cluster on one side of each orbit, so with a triad the orbits are mostly empty and the eye reads a lopsided cluster. Pitch class on an orbit is the chord's structure, not the ferry's route, so the 'ferry on a route between ports' story is the weakest here. Close to meikyu-orrery in pattern; the scope framing is what keeps it from being a copy. Muted: beam spot drops to a hollow ring and the trace stops lighting.
cells.alt: Ferry, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: An X-Y oscilloscope graticule with one tilted orbit per octave around the root, the chord's tones as points placed by pitch class, the route traced from point to point, and the beam spot as the ferry

cells.subject: A bay in plan like a textbook figure: piers along the shore spaced by the interval between chord tones, each pier head inside a dashed capture ring the ferry must enter and wait in before it plays, and numbered legs of the route arcing across the water.
controls: route: the numbered legs redraw between piers in the new order, so up is a run of short hops with one long return, cross is a fan of wide arcs, tramp is a tangle; shape of the legs.
ports: how many piers stand on the shore, 2 to 8, spaced by pitch so a new octave stretches the chord across the bay; count of piers and position of each.
swell: each leg's line roughens into a wave whose height grows with swell, the ferry visibly pushed off its course; shape of the legs.
dwell: the radius of every capture ring, 9 px at 1/32 to 31 px at 1/2, the ring being the time the ferry is held before it plays; scale of the rings.
cells.risks: The rings overlap at 8 ports with dwell above about 1/4 (a minor third puts piers 36 px apart, rings reach 62 px wide); cap ring radius by pier spacing or accept the overlap. Leg numbers and pier names are static text but change with route and ports, so on the device they are text slots (up to 9), not artwork. A capture ring scaled by dwell reads as 'how long', which is a stretch of P13's 'what's inside plays'; the honest twin is that the ferry only plays once inside. Muted: legs go dashed and the ferry hull hollow.
cells.alt: Ferry, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A bay in plan like a textbook figure: piers along the shore spaced by the interval between chord tones, each pier head inside a dashed capture ring the ferry must enter and wait in before it plays, and numbered legs of the route arcing across the water

cells.subject: The timetable woven as cloth and drawn in flat elevation: one band per voyage stacked from the newest at the foot to three older ones above, a slab on each warp thread raised to the pitch of the port it played, so locked stops form straight columns and swell shows as slabs pushed late.
controls: route: the skyline each band's slabs make, a stair up, a stair down, a peak, a zigzag or a scatter; shape across every row.
ports: how many distinct slab heights the skyline uses before it repeats, 2 to 8, so the stair gets longer and finer; count of levels.
swell: slabs slip right off their threads by a different amount in every band, breaking the straight columns that a calm sea weaves; position, and the only control that makes rows differ.
dwell: how many warp threads fit one bar, 32 at 1/32 down to 2 at 1/2, so threads and slabs spread apart and grow wider; count of threads.
cells.risks: At swell 0 every band is identical, so the rest frame is four copies of one skyline: honest, but repetitive, and it says 'history' only once swell is up. At dwell 1/32 there are 32 threads 12.6 px apart with slabs 7.6 px wide, dense but above the hatching floor; slab count is 3 x 32 + front row, far over the node budget, so short dwells need flat-top slabs or fewer rows shown. There is no ferry in the drawing, only its timetable; the subject sentence carries the ferry, the picture doesn't. Muted: the front band stops weaving and its datum goes dashed.

machines.name: Flock
machines.description: A note player on aux track 12: a small flock flies over a two-octave pitch field and each bird plays the scale degree under it as it crosses into a new cell. Cohesion pulls the notes into a cluster, speed sets how often they come, scatter lets birds break off.
machines.concept: A flock over a pitch field: birds play the pitch under them; cohesion clusters notes, speed sets density.
machines.soundsLike: Eight birds steer the instrument track it controls with short phrases that bunch into close clusters or spread into wide, wandering lines; the result is a gently shifting arpeggio whose register drifts with the flock. Faster birds cross more cells, so more notes; scatter lets a few birds break away for stray notes outside the cluster.

intake.subject: a small flock of birds flying over a two-octave pitch field, each bird sounding the scale degree under it as it crosses into a new cell.
intake.controlSource: new (the DSP is the boids model I'm specifying; no port)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings (one note: trackControl runs on aux track 12; show mute on the page, handled above).

scores.effect: pitch range of the phrase collapses from two octaves to two or three neighbouring degrees: from wandering lines to a repeated cluster
note density from one note every four beats per bird to four a beat (16×): the most obvious change on the track
at 0 nothing; past ~30 % stray notes outside the cluster, frequent by 100; subtle at the low end
changes which notes sound, not how many or where; clear on a change between pent and chr, smaller between neighbouring modes

ranking.note: the cleanest fit of pattern, language and machine; every control moves part of one picture.
the most explanatory of cohesion, at the cost of density and redraw.
the most immediate image, but a stretch with icon and spacing risks.
good history, but no birds.
the orrery is a stand-in the flock doesn't share.

directions.angle: a cutaway of the object at work, so the inside explains it
the mark or trace the process leaves behind
one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand

ranking.note: closest to how the OP-XY draws (calm, precise, physical). The trace is this machine's alone, and every control moves the prints.
explains the pitch field best. The cutaway does real work; it needs thinning for chr.
the clearest control mapping and the most charm. Bird overlap and the music-box read are the risks.
a strong image, but one bird for eight voices is a stretch.
well drawn, but the most generic idea and the weakest bright-element read.

cells.subject: The pitch field charted as a conic atlas sheet, scale degrees as meridians and loudness as parallels, with the flock plotted over it as one asterism whose stars carry proper-motion vectors.
controls: cohere: the asterism's spread over the chart (uniform scale about the flock's centre, about 2x across the range): at 0 the stars span most of the sheet, at 100 they knot into a few neighbouring meridians.
speed: each star's proper-motion vector, the distance flown in one beat (shape: 6 px at 0.25 to 32 px at 4.00), with the strip's raised marks as the second cue.
scatter: outlying stars leave the asterism and its join lines drop (position, up to ~60 px off the group's centre), so stray notes land far from the cluster.
scale: how many meridians the sheet ruled (count: 11 for penta, 25 for chrom over two octaves), each labelled octave meridian staying put.
risks: chrom rules 25 meridians across ~360 px, ~14 px apart at the bottom and closer near the top; fine for spacing but the field gets loud, so meridians may need to fade toward the top.
Stars are 3-5 px; at 1:1 the asterism is small against the chart and the brightest element only by a little. Bigger stars or a dimmer field in the frames pass.
The strip is near-dashboard; it earns its place only if it's the note response (raised marks on play) rather than a permanent meter.
Muted: needs its own cue (stars hollow, vectors hidden), not just dimmer greys.
cells.alt: Flock, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The pitch field charted as a conic atlas sheet, scale degrees as meridians and loudness as parallels, with the flock plotted over it as one asterism whose stars carry proper-motion vectors

cells.subject: A plan-view orrery in schematic drafting: birds circle the flock's centre of gravity on four orbits, and a graduated two-octave rim reads off, by a dashed leader, the pitch each bird's bearing points at.
controls: cohere: the angular sector the birds gather in, with its dimension arc and span in semitones on the rim (position along the orbits, about 160 deg of travel from 0 to 100).
speed: the trailing link behind each planet along its orbit, one beat of travel (shape: 6 deg at 0.25 to ~90 deg at 4.00).
scatter: birds step off their orbits inward and outward (radial position, up to one orbit spacing ~30 px), so leaders hit the rim out of order.
scale: tick count on the graduated rim (count: 10 for penta to 24 for chrom), labelled octaves fixed.
risks: P12's own weakness: the centre of gravity does nothing but sit there; the orbits are a stand-in for the flock, not its rule. Birds don't orbit their centroid in a boids model, they travel.
Pitch as a bearing around a circle wraps c5 onto c3; the rim has a seam the player has to learn.
The rim's front edge sits at y ~205, against the bottom of the body; there's no room for a strip and a wider sector pushes leaders off screen at the front.
Eight leaders plus four orbits plus the rim is a lot of hairline; at 1:1 the dashed leaders read as noise. Leaders may only appear on note.
Lint warns on 1.0 px stroked outlines (orbits, title block): hairlines by craft.md, but they're at the edge of what the panel holds.
cells.alt: Flock, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: A plan-view orrery in schematic drafting: birds circle the flock's centre of gravity on four orbits, and a graduated two-octave rim reads off, by a dashed leader, the pitch each bird's bearing points at

cells.subject: A storage scope plotting every bird's pitch against time as a stepped phosphor trace, with cohesion drawn as two capture cursors that the traces are pulled between as they reach the present.
controls: cohere: the gap between the two capture cursors and its delta readout (position: about 22 semitones apart at 0, 3 at 100, ~150 px of travel), and the traces' older ends sit further outside it.
speed: steps per trace, one each time a bird crosses a cell (count: ~1 step every 4 beats at 0.25, 4 a beat at 4.00, so 1 to 20 risers across the screen).
scatter: some traces escape the cursors in the newest division and their beam spots land outside, drawn dimmer (position of the trace ends, up to the full pitch axis).
scale: the degree ticks on the pitch rail and the step heights every trace can take (count: 11 to 25 levels), octave ticks fixed.
risks: Language risk named in P3: this is an oscilloscope, and an oscilloscope is the cliché. The capture cursors are what make it P13 rather than a trace; if they don't lead, it's a plot.
The capture is a reading of cohesion, not a mechanism: cohere pulls birds toward the centre, it doesn't gate notes the way meikyu's Dens does. Honest but weaker than meikyu's twin.
Eight stepped traces cross each other; at 1:1 the middle division is busy. Persistence greys help; at speed 4 (20 risers each) it will be hatching.
Traces are history, so they scroll while playing: eight mutable outlines would be needed and only four paths exist. Each trace has to be built from translated riser/tread nodes, which is costly.
cells.alt: Flock, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A storage scope plotting every bird's pitch against time as a stepped phosphor trace, with cohesion drawn as two capture cursors that the traces are pulled between as they reach the present

cells.subject: The flock's last four bars woven as a book figure: warp threads are the scale's pitches, one weft row per bar recedes behind the newest, and a raised slab stands wherever birds played that pitch in that bar.
controls: cohere: how many neighbouring threads the slabs gather on (shape of the row's footprint: across ~9 threads at 0, two or three at 100).
speed: slab height, the number of hits per thread per bar (scale of the slabs, one to four courses).
scatter: lone slabs away from the cluster on far threads (position of outliers, up to the full cloth width).
scale: warp thread count (11 for penta to 25 for chrom), octave threads labelled under the front edge.
risks: Reads as a 3D bar chart at a glance; the typeset furniture (row numbers, caption) is what makes it a figure and it costs text slots.
Loom suits a sequence; a flock has no steps. Rows are bars of what was played, so the rest frame shows history, not the flock itself: no bird is on screen.
Slabs are expensive (two to three faces each, up to ~40 slabs); budget needs flat tops on older rows.
chrom's 25 threads with 0.34-wide slabs crowd to ~3 px gaps at the back row.
The caption's 'fig. 1  last four bars' collapses its double space in the preview.
cells.alt: Flock, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The flock's last four bars woven as a book figure: warp threads are the scale's pitches, one weft row per bar recedes behind the newest, and a raised slab stands wherever birds played that pitch in that bar

cells.subject: Birds on telegraph wires drawn in front elevation: two poles carry one wire per scale degree, every perched bird sounds its wire, and birds in the air are hopping between wires.
controls: cohere: how closely the birds bunch along the span and onto neighbouring wires (position: spacing from ~56 px to ~10 px between birds).
speed: how many birds are off their wires mid-hop at once, each with its dashed hop path (count: none at 0.25 to five of eight at 4.00).
scatter: birds that perch far out on the span and on distant wires, away from the bunch (position, up to the full span).
scale: the number of wires strung between the poles (count: 11 to 25), octave wires labelled at the left pole.
risks: Stretch: P11 is for drum kits, an instrument people know by sight. A player has no instrument. The exception argument is that birds on a wire is already a picture everyone reads as notes on a staff, so the wires work as the 'instrument' and each wire has its own place; that's an analogy, not the pattern's reason, and it may simply not fit.
Bird silhouettes are the icon trap craft.md warns about; the line has to stay a drafted elevation (one outline, hairline wires, no cartoon eyes) or it becomes clip-art.
chrom strings 25 wires 5 px apart: under the 6 px stack spacing in accessibility.md. Chrom would need a two-octave fold or a smaller range.
The poles and insulators are static scenery that does nothing for the sound.
cells.alt: Flock, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: Birds on telegraph wires drawn in front elevation: two poles carry one wire per scale degree, every perched bird sounds its wire, and birds in the air are hopping between wires

cells.subject: The pitch field is a reed bed tuned as a pan pipe, every reed cut open down its front to show the node that stops its air column, and the flock skims the mouths so the bird over a reed blows it.
controls: cohere: the flock's spread over the reed mouths (position, birds drawn toward the flock's centre, from about 300 px across at 0 to 2-3 neighbouring reeds at 100).

speed: each bird's wing sweep and bank (shape, wings swept back and the body tilted further into the dive as speed rises, some wingtip point moving at least 16 px), so fast birds read as stooping across the mouths.
scatter: strays leave the flock and drop toward reeds far from the cluster (position, up to about 150 px off the flock's centre), so stray notes come from far reeds.
scale: how many reeds stand in the bed (count, 11 for pent up to 25 for chr), each cut to show its node at the depth of its pitch, the column halving every octave.
risks: chr is 25 reeds in about 360 px: about 15 px apart, so reeds drop to a radius of 4-5 px and the cutaway window (back-wall hairlines, node ring) may need to lose its hairlines to stay 3 px apart.
Eleven tall open tubes are a lot of repeated outline; the reeds stay at mid greys so the birds and the playing reed read first, but the body is busier than toro or theseus at rest.
Muted: every reed mouth is capped with a lid line (the bed stops sounding) and the birds glide with folded wings; the caps are the cue, not a dimmer grey.
The flock is relaxed apart in the sketch so outlines don't touch; on the device, birds that overlap at high cohere need painter order and black fills to stay legible.
cells.angle: a cutaway of the object at work, so the inside explains it
cells.alt: Flock, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: The pitch field is a reed bed tuned as a pan pipe, every reed cut open down its front to show the node that stops its air column, and the flock skims the mouths so the bird over a reed blows it

cells.subject: A block of snow-covered ploughed field cut open in section, one furrow per scale degree, with the wing prints the flock pressed into the snow each time a bird touched down in a furrow.
controls: cohere: how many furrows the prints spread across (position, the line of prints pulled from most of the block's width at 0 into two or three neighbouring furrows at 100).
speed: how far apart the touch-downs are along the track running back into the field (position and count, more and closer prints at 4.00, a few far-spaced ones at 0.25).
scatter: stray prints pressed into furrows far from the line (position, up to the block's far ends), one per stray note.
scale: how many furrows the section shows (count, 11 ridges in the cut profile for pent, 25 for chr), the receding crest lines following.
risks: Section hatching on the cut soil and the shaded end face is the section convention for a cut solid, not 'inactive'; it uses the same 45-degree hairlines 4 px apart, so it reads as material, but a reviewer may want the end face plain.
Prints at the back of the block are foreshortened to about half height and crowd; at high speed the track needs a cap (about 8 prints visible) or the far ones merge.
History is drawn (old prints stay): it must not become a bar history, so prints fade out by being covered (hatched over with fresh snow) rather than stacking up, and only the newest is bright.
Muted: fresh snow falls over the field: every print is hatched over and the newest loses its bright outline; nothing new is pressed while muted.
cells.angle: the mark or trace the process leaves behind
cells.alt: Flock, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: A block of snow-covered ploughed field cut open in section, one furrow per scale degree, with the wing prints the flock pressed into the snow each time a bird touched down in a furrow

cells.subject: One bird of the flock drawn large and exploded like a model kit, its wings, primaries and tail pulled off the body along assembly axes, with its neighbours cut off by the edges of the frame.
controls: cohere: how far the kit is exploded (position, the wings, primaries and tail pulled out from the body by about 70 px at 0 and nearly seated at 100), and the neighbours at the frame's edge slide further into view as the flock tightens.
speed: the wings' sweep (rotation of each wing about its root, about 35 degrees from spread at 0.25 to swept back at 4.00).
scatter: loose primaries drift away from the wings off their assembly axes (position, up to about 40 px), one per stray note.

scale: how many primaries the wings carry (count, 11 for pent across both wings, low octave on the left wing and high on the right, up to 25 for chr); the one the bird sounds now is the bright feather.
risks: One bird stands for eight voices: the other seven are only the edge silhouettes, so a note from another bird has to show on its edge neighbour (a wingbeat) or the flock reads as one voice.
At chr the primaries are 12-13 per wing; at the wing roots they come closer than 3 px, so the fan needs to open wider or the feathers shorten at chr.
The bright feather is small (about 6 x 60 px); it clears the brightest-element rule but a note on it needs a position or scale flare as well as the shade.
Muted: the kit goes hatched (every part filled with 45-degree hairlines, there but not playing) and the bright feather goes back to grey.
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Flock, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: One bird of the flock drawn large and exploded like a model kit, its wings, primaries and tail pulled off the body along assembly axes, with its neighbours cut off by the edges of the frame

cells.subject: Eight starlings in flight seen from above, each in its own wingbeat, over a ploughed field whose drill rows are the scale's degrees, the birds' shadows falling hatched on the rows below them.
controls: cohere: how tightly the eight birds bunch (position about the flock's centre, from spread across most of the field at 0 to a knot over two or three rows at 100).
speed: the wingbeat pose and spacing along the flight line (shape, wings swept and the line strung out as speed rises, some wingtip point moving at least 16 px).
scatter: strays break from the flock and fly off over far rows (position, up to about 160 px), their shadows going with them.
scale: how many drill rows the field has (count, 11 for pent to 25 for chr, rows closing up toward the headland).
risks: Single-weight contour against the three-weight rule: every bird is drawn at the Line weight (1.5 px) and the rows at Hairline, with no Subject weight; the bright bird is told apart by its grey only, plus the heavier row under it. A reviewer may want the bright bird at the Subject weight.
A bird's row is read from its shadow, not the bird, because of the perspective; the hatched shadows are small (about 30 x 15 px) and at 3 px hatching they're on the edge of reading.
Rows at chr are about 10 px apart at the near edge and about 8 px at the headland, so shadows sit across two rows; the playing row's heavier line resolves it.
Muted: the flock lands: birds drawn with folded wings sitting in the rows, shadows gone.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Flock, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: Eight starlings in flight seen from above, each in its own wingbeat, over a ploughed field whose drill rows are the scale's degrees, the birds' shadows falling hatched on the rows below them

cells.subject: A crank-driven automaton box with eight carved birds on rods that ride a slot over a tuned comb, each rod's pick plucking the tine under it as the crank on the end turns.
controls: cohere: how far apart the rods ride along the slot (position, the birds spread over most of the comb at 0 and gathered over two or three tines at 100).
speed: the crank (rotation, the handle swept round about 270 degrees across the range, and turning while notes play).
scatter: rods lean out of line toward far tines (rotation of each rod about its foot, up to about 25 degrees), so their picks reach stray notes.
scale: how many tines the comb carries (count, 11 for pent to 25 for chr), long and low on the left, short and high on the right.
risks: Hatched mass here hatches the box's front face as shading on a solid body, not as 'inactive'; the hatching stays 4 px apart and mid grey so it doesn't read as a state, but it is the one place a hatch means something else.
Eight birds near the same tines overlap on the rods at high cohere; heights differ (the model's height channel) but carved birds about 40 px long will touch at 100.
The tines are short (6-25 px) and at chr about 11 px apart; the playing tine is told by its heavier outline, and needs a note flare to be found.
Muted: the crank handle is pulled out off its square (position, a visible gap at the boss) and the comb is hatched over, so the birds stand still over a comb that can't sound.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Flock, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: A crank-driven automaton box with eight carved birds on rods that ride a slot over a tuned comb, each rod's pick plucking the tine under it as the crank on the end turns

machines.name: Gears
machines.description: A track-control player on aux track 12: two meshed spur gears, each tooth that meshes plays a note on the target track; the wheels' tooth ratio sets a polyrhythm between their revolutions.
machines.concept: Interlocking gears: each tooth that meshes plays a note, ratios between wheels make polyrhythms.
machines.soundsLike: A note player for another track. Driver wheel A (teeth) meshes with follower B (teeth × ratio); one tooth pair meets per step and plays a note picked from the scale by the two teeth's places on their wheels, so A's revolution against B's is a polyrhythm (3:2 at the default, repeating every 24 steps).

intake.subject: two meshed wheels whose teeth play notes as they meet, the ratio between their sizes drawn as the polyrhythm between their revolutions.
intake.controlSource: new
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 1 warning (plus the trackControl note).

scores.effect: Changes B's cycle against A's: the accent pattern and how long before the phrase repeats (1:1 loops every revolution, 3:1 and 7:5 run long); the melody's shape changes with it
Sets the cycle length and so the melody's range and the downbeat spacing; 3 is a tight ostinato, 16 a long line
From silence through sparse Euclidean hits to every step; the biggest change in the output
Re-colours the pitches; rhythm and contour unchanged

ranking.note: the machine's rule drawn as itself, every control on geometry, a natural muted state.
the right idea for a player (history), but needs thinning to read at 1:1.
clearest single read, best ratio channel, but it's a scope, not gears.
handsome and calm, but the picture doesn't do the machine's job.
doesn't fit; icon risk and the mesh is off screen.

rejected.reason: More literal, focused on the gears themselves. Five new variations.
