cells.subject: The last four revolutions of wheel A woven as cloth in schematic projection, one warp thread per tooth and one row per revolution, with a slab raised at the height of its note wherever a mesh sounded and wheel B's index tooth drawn as a centre line stepping across the rows, so the 3:2 repeat shows as cloth that comes round again every third row.
controls: ratio: wheel B's index centre line changes its stride across the rows (a straight column down the cloth at 1:1, a zigzag every half row at 3:2, one vertex in three rows at 3:1), and the row where the cloth starts repeating moves forward or back (position of the index line's vertices).
teeth: the number of warp threads and slabs across a fixed-width cloth goes from 3 to 16, the thread pitch closing from about 70 to 16 px (count).

mesh: slabs whose teeth are too short to reach sink flat onto their threads in Euclidean order, so every row loses raised slabs evenly from 100 % down to bare threads at 0 (count of raised slabs, eased height).
scale: every slab re-steps its height to the new scale's degree while the rhythm stays put (shape: the profile of the slab tops).
cells.risks: Slabs cost three nodes each: 4 rows x 16 threads x 3 = 192 nodes plus the drive, inside 256 but tight, and weaving a row moves every slab back at once, far over ~20 a frame, so the shift has to be stepped or rows moved as flat tops. Teeth and mesh are both counts (threads vs raised slabs), so mesh's sunk slabs must read as rests (no slab, a knot on the thread), not as low notes. Gears are deterministic, so the cloth never wanders: Loom's point (locked vs generated) collapses into 'it repeats', which is true but thin. The index centre line is a 1.2 px dash-dot over busy slabs and is the weakest read at 1:1. The drive circles at the left are a second, small picture. Muted: the front row stops weaving and drops to wire (no bright tops) and the drive's pitch circles break.
cells.alt: Gears, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The last four revolutions of wheel A woven as cloth in schematic projection, one warp thread per tooth and one row per revolution, with a slab raised at the height of its note wherever a mesh sounded and wheel B's index tooth drawn as a centre line stepping across the rows, so the 3:2 repeat shows as cloth that comes round again every third row

cells.subject: An X-Y scope plot with wheel A's angle on x and wheel B's on y, so the ratio draws itself as one bright Lissajous figure (three lobes across, two down at 3:2) floating over a dim graticule floor, every mesh a bead on the trace and the repeat cycle's notes as a strip of bars along the bottom.
controls: ratio: the figure's shape follows the ratio, from a single ellipse at 1:1 through three-by-two at 3:2 to three loops on one sweep at 3:1 (shape of the figure).
teeth: the beads strung along the trace, one per step of the repeat cycle, and the strip's bars respace from a few to many (count on the figure and in the strip).
mesh: beads whose teeth slip go hollow and shrink to a dot, and their strip bars drop to a 2 px stub, evenly round the cycle (count and size of beads).
scale: the strip's bar heights re-step to the new scale's degrees, the figure untouched (shape of the strip).
cells.risks: P3's warning applies: a Lissajous figure over a graticule is the stock picture of an oscilloscope and reads as a screensaver, not as gears; nothing on screen is a wheel. The trace is ~360 points, so on the device it has to fit four mutable outlines of 64 (256 points), re-keyed only when ratio turns. At 3:1 with 16 teeth the cycle is 48 steps, too many beads for the trace, so beads need a cap or only downbeats. Self-crossings stack beads on each other (24 steps show in ~16 places at 3:2). Strip bars are 4 px wide, right at the part floor. Muted: the beam blanks to a dashed #646464 trace and the beads go hollow.
cells.alt: Gears, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: An X-Y scope plot with wheel A's angle on x and wheel B's on y, so the ratio draws itself as one bright Lissajous figure (three lobes across, two down at 3:2) floating over a dim graticule floor, every mesh a bead on the trace and the repeat cycle's notes as a strip of bars along the bottom

cells.subject: A textbook figure of the gear train as an orrery round one arbor: wheel A an inner orbit of eight tooth stations, wheel B an outer orbit of twelve, a third ring of twelve semitones with the scale's degrees set on it, and the two bright planets crossing the mesh line toward the reader as their teeth play.
controls: ratio: orbit B's radius follows the ratio, lying on top of orbit A at 1:1 and reaching the semitone ring at 3:1, its stations respacing round it (position and scale of orbit B).
teeth: the number of stations on orbit A goes from 3 to 16 and B's follows by the ratio (count).
mesh: stations whose teeth slip drop off their orbit to a small hollow ring just inside it, evenly round the wheel (position plus fill).
scale: the filled dots on the outer semitone ring move to the new scale's degrees (position).
cells.risks: P12's own pitfall in its sharpest form: the arbor does nothing, and two orbits round one centre isn't how gears meet, so the picture keeps the cycle but loses the mesh, the machine's actual rule. Planets advance a station per step, so the orbit turn costs redraw (two planets, cheap) but stations at 16 teeth and 3:1 are 64 dots. Stations are 5 px dots, at the floor; filled vs hollow is close to a shade channel, so mesh leans on the position drop. Typeset labels (a, b, scale, fig. 1) are static and fine; numbering the degrees would need moving text, so the scale ring uses dots. Muted: both planets go hollow and the mesh line lifts away.
cells.alt: Gears, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: A textbook figure of the gear train as an orrery round one arbor: wheel A an inner orbit of eight tooth stations, wheel B an outer orbit of twelve, a third ring of twelve semitones with the scale's degrees set on it, and the two bright planets crossing the mesh line toward the reader as their teeth play

cells.subject: Two spur gears in front elevation on a draughtsman's sheet, centre lines and pitch circles drawn, where each tooth's length is its weight and only teeth long enough to reach across the gap between the wheels engage and play, the tooth meshing now lit at the contact point.
controls: ratio: wheel B's diameter and tooth count grow with the ratio, a twin of A at 1:1 and three times A at 3:1, its centre sliding right to stay in mesh (scale of B, with position).
teeth: wheel A's outline redraws with 3 to 16 teeth and B follows by the ratio (shape).
mesh: the centre distance opens as mesh falls, B sliding up to ~28 px away from A, so shorter teeth stop reaching across the capture line and draw hollow (position).
scale: a plain one-octave keyboard in the lower right dots the scale's notes, set apart because the scale has no twin in the gears (position of the dots).
cells.risks: Fitting both wheels: at 3:1 and 16 teeth B has 48 teeth (192 outline points, past one 64-point path), so A's diameter stays fixed and the module shrinks with teeth, and B is drawn as up to three outline paths or coarser teeth; B three times A also runs off the right edge unless both scale down. Tooth lengths differ by only 5 px, so weight reads near the contact point but not across the wheel. The keyboard is the P13 'no twin' fallback and looks bolted on next to an elevation. Wheels turn a tooth per step: two rotating nodes, cheap. Muted: B slides fully out of mesh, nothing engages, the lit tooth goes dark, the machine's own picture of bypass.
cells.alt: Gears, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: Two spur gears in front elevation on a draughtsman's sheet, centre lines and pitch circles drawn, where each tooth's length is its weight and only teeth long enough to reach across the gap between the wheels engage and play, the tooth meshing now lit at the contact point

cells.subject: Wheel A drawn as a surveyed plot in one-bit ink, a dithered web with each tooth a numbered lot whose flat tone says whether it meshes and a 2 px traverse run out to the lot at the mesh station, beside two survey glyphs: a two-row scale bar for the ratio and a stepped section profile for the scale.
controls: ratio: the scale bar's two rows re-divide into the ratio's two numbers (3 over 2 at 3:2, 1 over 1 at 1:1, 3 over 1 at 3:1) in alternating black and white blocks (shape of the glyph).
teeth: the plot's outline redraws with 3 to 16 lots, renumbered round the boundary (shape of the hero).
mesh: lots whose teeth slip pull their tips in to the root circle and drop from their 50 % tone to black, evenly round the wheel (shape, with tone as the second cue).
scale: the section profile's steps re-rise by the scale's intervals (shape of the glyph).
cells.risks: Stretch, and I'd say plainly it doesn't fit. The case for it: a gear is already a flat, chunky, plan-view object, so one-bit ink needs none of the figurative anatomy that sank toro's bull. Against: a lone cog in a 2 px white outline is the settings icon, which craft.md bans outright; only wheel A is drawn, so the mesh between two wheels, the machine's whole rule, is off screen and the ratio is demoted to a glyph; every outline is #CDCDCD, so there's no one brightest element; dither can't move (the web is static run-length rects, ~600 at 2 px, and the lots are flat greys standing in for dither); the survey language (lots, traverse, scale bar, section) is labels on a cog, not a plan of anything. Muted: the lots go black and the traverse hides.
cells.alt: Gears, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: Wheel A drawn as a surveyed plot in one-bit ink, a dithered web with each tooth a numbered lot whose flat tone says whether it meshes and a 2 px traverse run out to the lot at the mesh station, beside two survey glyphs: a two-row scale bar for the ratio and a stepped section profile for the scale

cells.subject: A small gearbox with its front wall and lid cut away, the cut casing hatched in section, where driver A and follower B stand meshed on their shafts and B carries a twelve-hole index plate pinned at the scale's degrees.
controls: ratio: wheel B's diameter and tooth count grow with the ratio (a twin of A at 1:1, three times A at 3:1), its shaft and bearing boss sliding right along the back wall to stay in mesh, inside a casing whose right wall moves with it (scale of B, with position).
teeth: wheel A's outline redraws with 3 to 16 teeth and B follows by the ratio, the module fixed so the pair grows and shrinks inside the box (shape).

mesh: wheel B slides back along its shaft as mesh falls, its face stepping off A's, and the teeth that no longer overlap (Euclidean order) lose their front-face edge, so at 0 B sits clear behind A (position, about 30 px of axial travel on screen).
scale: the pins in B's index plate move to the new scale's seven of twelve holes, the empty holes left as hairline rings (position/count of pins).
cells.risks: Busiest of the five: casing, bosses, two shafts, two wheels and the plate all carry lines, so the meshing tooth (the brightest edge) has to win against a lot of mid grey at 1:1. Index pins are about 7 px across, at the floor; seen from this camera the plate's holes foreshortening to ovals, and degree 0 needs a mark of its own (a longer slot) to read as the start of the scale without any text. Ratio at 3:1 makes B three times A: the box has to scale with it or B runs into the lid line; budget for the casing is static, but B's outline at 48 teeth is past one 64-point path, so B's teeth would be split across paths or coarsened. Mesh's axial slide is a 3D move and the device can't tilt a node, so B's slid positions are pre-drawn variants or a translation along the projected axis (it's straight, so translation is honest). Muted: B slides fully back off A, the meshing edge goes out.
cells.angle: a cutaway of the object at work, so the inside explains it
cells.alt: Gears, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: A small gearbox with its front wall and lid cut away, the cut casing hatched in section, where driver A and follower B stand meshed on their shafts and B carries a twelve-hole index plate pinned at the scale's degrees

cells.subject: An exploded view of the gear pair with follower B lifted straight up off its arbor and washer, so the faces of both wheels show the grooves the run has scored on them: one short groove per mesh behind the tooth that played, at a radius set by the note it played.
controls: ratio: wheel B grows or shrinks with the ratio and its grooves redistribute (two per tooth at 3:2, one per tooth at 1:1, three per A tooth at 3:1), the arbor and washer below sliding to stay under it (scale of B, plus count of grooves per tooth).
teeth: wheel A redraws with 3 to 16 teeth and the cycle lengthens, so the number of grooves on both faces goes from a handful to dozens (count).
mesh: teeth that slip score nothing, so their grooves drop off the faces in Euclidean order, evenly round both wheels, down to clean faces at 0 (count).
scale: every groove slides inward or outward to its note's new radius, the rhythm untouched, so the faces' rings of grooves re-step (position, radial).
cells.risks: Grooves are short 1.5 px arcs; on A's small web they're 3-4 px apart radially for neighbouring semitones, close to the floor, and on a foreshortened face (this camera is about 35 degrees up) the radial spread compresses by half, so A's grooves are the weakest read. At 16 teeth and 3:1 the cycle is 48 steps: 48 grooves on each wheel, 96 nodes, inside 256 but they'd need to be placed nodes, not path points. The exploded lift hides A's arbor and makes the meshing a matter of the dashed assembly line, so 'meshing' reads as 'goes here' rather than 'turning together'. The note answer: the newest groove brightens (the one brightest element) and the wheels turn a tooth. Muted: B lifts further and the newest groove goes out.
cells.angle: the mark or trace the process leaves behind
cells.alt: Gears, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: An exploded view of the gear pair with follower B lifted straight up off its arbor and washer, so the faces of both wheels show the grooves the run has scored on them: one short groove per mesh behind the tooth that played, at a radius set by the note it played

cells.subject: The point where the two wheels meet, drawn large in one weight of line: wheel A rising from the bottom edge, wheel B coming down from beyond the top, one of B's involute teeth sitting in A's gap at the pitch point, and A's rim notched at the scale's degrees.
controls: ratio: B's rim flattens as the ratio rises (the same curve as A's at 1:1, nearly straight at 3:1) because its centre moves further off the top of the frame (shape: the curvature of B's arc).
teeth: with A's diameter fixed, fewer teeth are bigger teeth, so 3 to 16 teeth run from three huge teeth to a fine row, both wheels re-cut with the same module (shape and count).
mesh: teeth that don't engage are cut back to the root circle in Euclidean order, a flat land where a tooth was, round A and through the visible arc of B (shape).
scale: the notches on A's inner rim move to the new scale's seven of twelve positions, degree 0 straight up under the pitch point (position).
cells.risks: Simplest drawing and the calmest, but the frame shows only part of each wheel: B's centre is above the screen, so its tooth count and the ratio read from curvature and spacing, not from a whole wheel; at 1:1 and 3:2 the curvature difference is modest. The notched ring at A's rim sits mostly in view (A's centre is about 30 px above the bottom edge), so nine of twelve positions show; at 16 teeth the rim moves and the notches with it. Single weight means the brightest element is only a brighter colour on B's contact tooth, not a heavier line. Involute flanks are 16 points a tooth, so B's visible teeth fit in four 64-point paths only if the off-screen teeth are dropped. Muted: B lifts up and out of A's gap, the contact tooth goes grey.
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Gears, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: The point where the two wheels meet, drawn large in one weight of line: wheel A rising from the bottom edge, wheel B coming down from beyond the top, one of B's involute teeth sitting in A's gap at the pitch point, and A's rim notched at the scale's degrees

cells.subject: Two thick spur wheels on a low camera, meshed and lit from the upper left, their shaded flanks hatched in hairlines and their top faces left black, with B's web drilled through at the scale's seven of twelve positions.
controls: ratio: B grows from A's twin at 1:1 to three times A at 3:1, its centre sliding back and right to stay in mesh (scale of B, with position).
teeth: A redraws with 3 to 16 teeth and B follows by the ratio, the faces and hatched flanks re-cut (shape).

mesh: teeth that don't engage are milled down to half the face width, their top faces stepping down so they visibly pass under the other wheel's teeth, in Euclidean order (shape: tooth height along the axis).
scale: B's drilled holes move to the new scale's positions; undrilled positions keep a small spot-face ring (position/count of holes).
cells.risks: The most literal and the most like a stock illustration of 'gears'; the hatching has to stay at 3.2 px spacing on flanks only a few px wide, so some flanks carry two or three lines and the hatch must be re-cut whenever a wheel turns (a moving fill, expensive); on the device the hatching would be static per tooth and the wheels turn by whole teeth. Holes at the scale's degrees sit on B's face, so their positions (not their count) carry the scale; seven drilled to five punched is the difference between scales of seven and five notes (pent shows two more blanks). The brightest edge is B's tooth in A's gap; it sits behind A's teeth and could be lost when A grows. Muted: B lifts off along its axis, its bright tooth goes out.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Gears, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: Two thick spur wheels on a low camera, meshed and lit from the upper left, their shaded flanks hatched in hairlines and their top faces left black, with B's web drilled through at the scale's seven of twelve positions

cells.subject: The hand-cranked gear pair close up as black masses lit only along their upper-left edges, a crank arm and handle on driver A turning spoked follower B, whose twelve spokes stand for the semitones and catch the light at the scale's degrees.
controls: ratio: B grows with the ratio, running off the right edge at 3:1, and turns slower against the crank (scale of B, with position).
teeth: A redraws with 3 to 16 teeth under the crank, B following by the ratio (shape).

mesh: teeth that slip lose their rim light and go dark against the black, in Euclidean order round both wheels (line brightness, with the tooth's tip pulled in to the root so it isn't only a shade change).
scale: B's spokes at the new scale's degrees catch the light (a 1.5 px rim), the others stay a dark hairline (which spokes are lit, by position round the wheel).
cells.risks: Silhouettes rely on rim light, so anything on the shadow side (lower right of every part) is a near-black hairline and the lower half of B is quiet by design; at 1:1 B's shadowed teeth almost vanish. Scale on spokes is the weakest mapping: a spoke per semitone is a convention, not mechanics, and a spoke's lit edge depends on its angle to the light, so as B turns, spokes on the shadow side lose their light whether they're in the scale or not; the spokes would need to be lit by membership, not by angle. The crank and handle are the brightest thing and answer every note (the handle advances a tooth's turn), which is right for 'the thing in the hand' but puts the brightest element on a part no control moves. Muted: the handle drops its light and the crank stops.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Gears, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: The hand-cranked gear pair close up as black masses lit only along their upper-left edges, a crank arm and handle on driver A turning spoked follower B, whose twelve spokes stand for the semitones and catch the light at the scale's degrees

machines.name: Lichen
machines.description: A lichen player on aux track 12: a colony grows across a lattice of scale degrees and registers, spreading into neighbouring cells and dying back from its old centre; every cell it newly grows into plays on another track. Its own track stays silent.
machines.concept: A growth automaton on a scale lattice: cells grow into neighbours and decay; new growth plays.
machines.soundsLike: A melody that creeps outward from wherever it started, in short runs of steps and thirds, thickening as the colony spreads and thinning as its centre dies; it plays another track's instrument. Low decay builds long slow phrases that settle into one region of the lattice; high decay gives scattered flickering bursts.

intake.subject: a colony of lichen growing across a lattice of scale degrees, spreading at its margin and dying back at its old centre, where each cell it newly takes is the note that plays.
intake.controlSource: new (the rule sketched below; no port)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 1 warning (plus the trackControl note, answered above under Intake).

scores.effect: note density: at 0 the colony never spreads and only spores play (about one note a bar); at 100 two notes nearly every tick. The biggest change on the page
phrase life: at 0 the colony fills the lattice and then falls silent (nowhere left to grow); at 100 cells die within a few ticks and the melody comes in short scattered bursts
where phrases restart: subtle while the colony is alive (one new start a bar at the default), decisive when it dies out; at 8 the register jumps every half beat
harmony without changing rhythm: seven-note modes differ by one or two notes, the pentatonics clearly soften it

cells.subject: The lattice wrapped into an orrery drawn as a schematic: each row of the lattice is an orbit round a root sun, each cell a planet on it, the colony a cluster of filled planets that goes hollow as it dies back while this tick's growth lights brightest.
controls: grow: count. Growth links run along and across the orbits from living planets to the cells they take; none at 0, one from every planet on the colony's margin at 100.
decay: scale. Each living planet's diameter is its remaining life, so raising decay shrinks the colony's planets from about 2x to 1x and leaves more small hollow dead ones.
seed: count. Spores wait as hollow bodies on the dashed seed track outside the last orbit, 0 to 8 spaced round it.
scale: position. The long radial root marks on every orbit move to where the scale's octave falls (every 7th degree, every 5th for the pentatonics, so their count changes too).
cells.risks: The sun is the root but nothing moves it (P12's own pitfall). Six nested orbits round a centre lean toward a target, and the back orbits bunch above the sun at tilt 0.4. Wrapping a row into an orbit implies column 12 neighbours column 1, which the model doesn't do: wrap the model or break each orbit at a seam. Between the six seven-note modes the root marks don't move, so scale needs a second mark (half-step seams) or it fails its floor there. 72 planets + 12 orbit runs + links is heavy but under 256 nodes. Muted (mute is this machine's bypass): the planets and orbits drop to hollow mid grey and the links hide; the sun's equator goes.
cells.alt: Lichen, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The lattice wrapped into an orrery drawn as a schematic: each row of the lattice is an orbit round a root sun, each cell a planet on it, the colony a cluster of filled planets that goes hollow as it dies back while this tick's growth lights brightest

cells.subject: A lichen thallus captured on a scope screen: the lattice is the graticule, the colony's growth front is one bright closed trace taking in every cell it crosses, and the dead centre glows inside it as a dimmer afterimage.
controls: grow: shape. The front trace's reach past the living cells swells, hugging them at 0 and bulging most of a cell beyond the margin at 100 (16 px or more at its lobes).
decay: shape. The inner afterglow trace round the dead centre opens out toward the front, so the living band between the two traces thins from a solid patch at 0 to a narrow ring at 100.
seed: count. Spores show as hollow spots on bare graticule away from the colony, 0 to 8.
scale: position. The small root labels on the graticule jump to where each octave's root sits (every 7th or 5th degree); between seven-note modes only half-step markers would move.
cells.risks: Two nested closed traces can read as a contour map or a target. The capture idea is weaker than meikyu's: the front follows the colony rather than deciding what plays. A colony that splits needs more traces than the 4-path limit comfortably allows (front and centre per patch). Each trace re-keys on every tick's growth (a whole-path redraw per tick, not per frame). Scale only has labels to move, the weakest channel on the page. Muted (mute is this machine's bypass): the front trace drops to afterglow grey and the growth spots go hollow; the graticule stays.
cells.alt: Lichen, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: A lichen thallus captured on a scope screen: the lattice is the graticule, the colony's growth front is one bright closed trace taking in every cell it crosses, and the dead centre glows inside it as a dimmer afterimage

cells.subject: The colony's last four ticks woven as cloth in a textbook figure: one warp thread per scale degree in pitch order, a slab raised wherever that degree was alive, this tick at the front with new growth capped bright, so old crust stands as unbroken columns and the growing margin as rows that change.
controls: grow: count. Capped slabs in the front row and new slabs between rows, 0 up to the two-per-tick ceiling, so the cloth fills out sideways.
decay: shape. The solid columns down the cloth break up: at 0 a slab runs all four rows, at 100 most last one row and the cloth goes ragged.
seed: count. Pins with a hollow bead stand at the front edge on the threads where spores will land, 0 to 8.
scale: position. The warp re-spaces by semitone (half steps close up), the octave rules under the cloth move, and the pentatonics drop to five threads an octave.
cells.risks: The loom flattens the lattice to pitch, so where the colony is and its dead centre are lost, and two cells of one degree weave as one slab. Back rows' flat tops are about 6 px at 1:1 and the right of the warp is empty at rest. The caption line is decoration. History of four ticks covers a quarter of a bar, so columns are short at fast clocks. Muted (mute is this machine's bypass): the front slabs drop to wireframe with no caps and the warp dims.
cells.alt: Lichen, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: The colony's last four ticks woven as cloth in a textbook figure: one warp thread per scale degree in pitch order, a slab raised wherever that degree was alive, this tick at the front with new growth capped bright, so old crust stands as unbroken columns and the growing margin as rows that change

cells.subject: A wall in elevation laid in running bond, one stone per lattice cell, with the lichen as a single lobed patch spreading over it: margin lobes are new growth, the old centre cracks into hollow areolae, and a strip at the foot ticks off what each step grew.
controls: grow: shape. The margin lobes push across neighbouring stones (the outline moves up to a stone, about 30 px, at 100) and the strip's ticks stand taller.
decay: count. Dead areolae crack open inside the patch, none at 0 to most of the centre at 100, leaving a ring of living crust.
seed: count. Spore dots on bare stones away from the patch, 0 to 8.
scale: position. The doubled perpend joints that mark the scale's half steps move along each course; the pentatonics have none.
cells.risks: A grey body with a bright outline can read as a stain or a map, not a lichen, and the lobes are a texture on the contour rather than drawn lobes. The half-step joints are hairline doubles and won't clear scale's floor alone. The thallus is one mutable outline re-keyed each tick; a colony that splits needs a second. Running bond is exactly the hex lattice, but nothing on the wall says pitch without labels. Muted (mute is this machine's bypass): the patch fill drops to black, its outline to mid grey, and the strip empties.
cells.alt: Lichen, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: A wall in elevation laid in running bond, one stone per lattice cell, with the lichen as a single lobed patch spreading over it: margin lobes are new growth, the old centre cracks into hollow areolae, and a strip at the foot ticks off what each step grew

cells.subject: A survey sheet in plan and profile: on the left the lattice surveyed as running-bond lots with the colony's boundary run as a traverse, on the right a levelled profile of the pitches its new growth played over the last bar.
controls: grow: count. Stations on the profile (notes per bar) and new lots inside the traverse; at 0 the profile is one long hold, at 100 two stations every tick.
decay: shape. The traverse pulls in and hollow dead lots open inside it; at 100 the boundary is a ragged ring round a dead centre.
seed: count. Trig-point marks on bare lots where spores land, each starting a fresh run of stations on the profile away from the colony's pitches.
scale: position. The profile's levels re-space by the scale's semitones, and the root marks on the plan move to where each octave starts.
cells.risks: Stretch, outside the player column. The case for it: this machine's rule is two-dimensional and its output is a line of pitches, two different shapes, and the profile shows why the melody wanders as the colony moves. Plainly, though, it fits weakly: two halves compete for the eye, the profile is a history list in disguise where categories.md asks a player to draw its rule, and the plan duplicates v4's lattice less beautifully. The trig-point triangle edges toward an icon. Better as a note-response idea than half the screen. Muted (mute is this machine's bypass): the traverse drops to mid grey and the profile stops at a flat hold.
cells.alt: Lichen, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: A survey sheet in plan and profile: on the left the lattice surveyed as running-bond lots with the colony's boundary run as a traverse, on the right a levelled profile of the pitches its new growth played over the last bar

cells.subject: A block of stone carrying the colony as crust, cut open along the start row: the cut face is a section through the crust (its thickness is each cell's age, cortex and rhizines inside) and behind the cut the rest of the colony stands as rounded areolae.
controls: grow: shape. Thin tongues of crust push out from the margin over bare stone, from nothing at 0 to most of a cell (about 30 px) at 100.
decay: rotation. Each dead areola is a hatched remnant with one flake hinged at its back edge; decay tips the flakes up off the stone, 12 degrees at 0 to about 85 at 100, and more of the centre dies.
seed: count. Spores hang above the bare stone with a dashed fall line to where each will land, 0 to 8.

scale: position. Where two neighbouring cells sit a half step apart, the stone between them is cracked: a V-shaped crack down the cut face and a double hairline joint across the top. The cracks move with each mode; the pentatonics have none.
cells.risks: The cut only shows one row in section, so most of the colony is read from the plates behind it; the crack joints on the top face are small at 1:1 and scale's floor needs the cut-face cracks to carry it. Areola prisms sit close to toro-blocks' cubes in silhouette, though they are low rounded plates on a cut block, not a stack. Flakes are pre-drawn variants (a tilt out of the plane can't be a node turn). Muted: the block stays, every crust edge drops to G3 and the born plates lose their bright edge; spores hide.
cells.angle: the machine's own rule as a physical thing: what turning each knob would do to a real object
cells.alt: Lichen, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: A block of stone carrying the colony as crust, cut open along the start row: the cut face is a section through the crust (its thickness is each cell's age, cortex and rhizines inside) and behind the cut the rest of the colony stands as rounded areolae

cells.subject: The colony taken apart into what it is made of, floated in an exploded stack over the bare scale lattice: the stone plate with raised half-step seams at the bottom, the dead centre as a thin hatched sheet, the living crust as one cracked sheet with holes where it died, and this tick's two births lifted clear on their assembly axes.
controls: grow: position. The two cells just born lift out of the living sheet along their dashed axes, a little at 0 to about 40 px higher at 100.
decay: shape. The hatched dead sheet grows and the holes in the living sheet above it open to match.
seed: count. Spores wait at the top of the stack, each with a dashed line down to its cell, 0 to 8.
scale: position. On the stone plate the edge between two cells a half step apart stands up as a short raised ridge; the ridges move with the mode, and the pentatonics have none.
cells.risks: The plate is 72 tiles of hairline and carries a lot of line for a part that only scale changes; the live sheet sits over the dead one, so their overlap needs the camera kept where it is. A hole's far wall can read as a stray cylinder. Lifting births reads well for grow but it also answers every note, so the note response and grow share the lift: grow sets how far, a note sets which. Muted: the stack closes (layers drop back together onto the plate) and nothing is bright.
cells.angle: a cutaway of the object at work, so the inside explains it
cells.alt: Lichen, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: The colony taken apart into what it is made of, floated in an exploded stack over the bare scale lattice: the stone plate with raised half-step seams at the bottom, the dead centre as a thin hatched sheet, the living crust as one cracked sheet with holes where it died, and this tick's two births lifted clear on their assembly axes

cells.subject: Only the trail the colony has left on the stone, one line weight throughout: every birth since the first spore is a line from parent to child, worn through where that cell has died, jogged where it stepped a half step, and the two lines grown this tick are the bright ones.
controls: grow: shape. A probe reaches from each living margin cell towards the free cell furthest from the start, a few px at 0 to about 20 px at 100.
decay: shape. Lines into dead cells are dashed and their gaps open with decay, so at 100 the old centre of the trail is mostly worn away.
seed: count. Small rings mark where spores will land, each with a dashed fall above it, 0 to 8.
scale: shape. A link that moved a half step has a small jog in it; a wider step is a plain bow. Each mode moves the jogs; the pentatonics have none.
cells.risks: At rest it's sparse (about 20 lines) and doesn't say lichen or lattice without the motion; the shape of the trail is the colony's history, not its body, so where the colony is alive has to be read from brightness. The jogs are 9 px features and may sit near scale's floor. A long run grows a dense trail that needs a history limit (the last N births) for the node budget. Muted: every line drops to G3 and the bright births go out.
cells.angle: the mark or trace the process leaves behind
cells.alt: Lichen, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: Only the trail the colony has left on the stone, one line weight throughout: every birth since the first spore is a line from parent to child, worn through where that cell has died, jogged where it stepped a half step, and the two lines grown this tick are the bright ones

cells.subject: One stretch of the colony's margin at large scale, the rest implied past the frame's edges: the living crust as cracked black areolae, the dead centre as a hatched mass behind it, the cell just taken drawn bright, lobes pushing out over the bare stone joints.
controls: grow: shape. Lobes of crust push from each living margin cell into its free neighbours, from a nub at 0 to about 45 px at 100.
decay: count. The hatched dead mass spreads through the old crust, none at 0 to most of the window at 100.
seed: count. Spores lie on the bare stone right of the margin, 0 to 8.
scale: shape. The lattice is stretched by the scale: each cell is as wide as its step to the next degree, so half steps are narrow cells and the stone joints shift with each mode.
cells.risks: Large cells mean the whole lattice is never seen, so where the colony is overall is lost; the window has to follow the newest growth, which is a camera move on every birth (expensive, and it fights the calm). Hatching over a third of the window is a lot of nodes. The stretched lattice is honest but can read as random paving. Muted: the bright cell drops to G4 and the lobes withdraw.
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Lichen, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: One stretch of the colony's margin at large scale, the rest implied past the frame's edges: the living crust as cracked black areolae, the dead centre as a hatched mass behind it, the cell just taken drawn bright, lobes pushing out over the bare stone joints

cells.subject: The lichen itself, a leafy thallus lying on stone drawn as a black silhouette lit along the edges that face the light, its lobes reaching out from the living margin, its old centre crumbling to hatched dead crust, fruiting cups on the cells a half step below their neighbour.
controls: grow: shape. The margin lobes lengthen and branch, from a short fringe at 0 to about 22 px longer at 100.
decay: shape. The hatched dead centre spreads outward through the thallus, nothing at 0 to a crumbling ring at 100.
seed: count. Spores lie on the stone round the thallus, 0 to 8.
scale: position. The fruiting cups (apothecia) sit on living cells whose next degree up is a half step; each mode moves them, the pentatonics have none.
cells.risks: An edge-lit black shape on a black screen depends on the rim; the unlit side disappears, so the thallus can read smaller than it is. Pass 01's v4 was also a literal lichen patch; this one differs in being lobed, unfilled and lit, but the owner may see it as the same idea. The outline is a mutable path that re-keys on every birth and its lit runs need several paths, which presses the four-path limit. Muted: the rim light goes out to a G3 hairline all round.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Lichen, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: The lichen itself, a leafy thallus lying on stone drawn as a black silhouette lit along the edges that face the light, its lobes reaching out from the living margin, its old centre crumbling to hatched dead crust, fruiting cups on the cells a half step below their neighbour

machines.name: Marble
machines.description: A Galton board player on aux track 12: marbles drop through rows of pegs into bins pitched on a scale, and the pile they make is the distribution of notes sent to the target track.
machines.concept: A Galton board: marbles drop through pegs into pitched bins; peg spacing shapes the distribution of notes.
machines.soundsLike: Nothing itself: it runs on aux track 12 (kept silent) and plays the target track. Few rows give a melody that hugs the root, many rows a wandering line with rare wide leaps, always weighted to the middle like a bell.

intake.subject: marbles dropping from a hopper through rows of pegs into bins pitched on a scale, where the pile they build is the distribution of notes the machine plays; the screen draws that board or its pile (which object carries it is the subject pass's question, `passes/01-subject/`).
intake.controlSource: new (the "source" is the player logic below; no port)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings (one note: show the muted state, passing `control::Input.muted` through `Overlay::display`). The one warning seen on the way (`dorian`, 6 characters, over the header column) was fixed by replacing it with `blues`.

scores.effect: from a line pinned to the root and its neighbour to a wide, wandering line with rare far leaps: the whole melodic range

none at 0; ratcheted repeats on more and more notes as it rises, clear but an ornament on the same pitches

cells.subject: The Galton board itself in front elevation, hopper and gate over a triangle of pegs, with each bin a pipe cut to its note's length so its floor sits at its pitch, and the pile of marbles caught in the bins is what plays.
controls: pegs: the number of peg rows in the triangle and bins under it (count, 1 to 12 rows), the pile spreading wider and lower as rows are added.
drop: the hopper gate's two plates slide apart (position, closed slit at 1/1 to a wide throat at 1/32).
bounce: a rebound dimension line rises above the pile tops, how high a marble kicks back before it settles (position, 0 to 24 px), with a ghost marble at its height.
scale: the bin floors step to their pitches, deeper for lower notes (position, 4 px a semitone), so major shows its half steps as short risers and chromatic is an even staircase.
risks: It's the literal machine: no translation for the player to learn, but also no surprise; it lives or dies on the drawing quality of the elevation (hatching, dimensions).
Bounce has no part of its own in a board; the rebound dimension is a drafting device bolted onto the drawing (P13's 'not every control has a twin' pitfall).
Twelve rows of pegs in the same height need a 7 px row pitch: pegs 5 px across with 2 px between, near hatching density.
Pipe floors only span 4 px a semitone, so chromatic versus major moves each floor by 4 to 8 px, under the 24 px floor; the staircase reads, the change between scales may not.
Mute: the gate shuts (plates meet) and the pile greys; a closed gate is a strong physical cue.
cells.cleanNote: Generated by `clean.py` (model and helpers imported from `../sketch.py`, which I didn't touch). Defaults: 6 rows, 1/8, bounce 0, major. Lint: 0 errors, 0 warnings. Not picked yet, so it stays in the pass folder.
cells.alt: Marble, cleaned variant 4: The Galton board itself in front elevation, hopper and gate over a triangle of pegs, with each bin a pipe cut to its note's length so its floor sits at its pitch, and the pile of marbles caught in the bins is what plays

cells.subject: The last four bars woven as cloth on a schematic oblique: each bin is a warp thread, each bar a weft row, and every marble that landed is a slab stacked on its bin's thread, so the bell builds up row by row and drifts back as bars pass.
controls: pegs: the number of warp threads (count, one per bin: 2 threads at 1 row, 13 at 12 rows), with the slabs spreading across them as the bell widens.
drop: the height of every slab stack (shape of each row's profile: one marble a bar barely raises a slab, 32 a bar builds tall ridges), since a stack is the marbles that bar landed.
bounce: a hollow rebound cap lifts above each front-row slab, raised further as bounce rises (position, 0 to 24 px), the loom's 'split' role for a retriggered step.
scale: the warp threads slide to their bins' pitches on a semitone rule (position), so a major scale opens gaps at its whole steps and chromatic packs them evenly.
risks: Eight marbles a bar over seven bins makes sparse, low cloth at the default: the bell is only legible across rows, not in one, and the front row reads as scattered boxes.
Scale moves threads by a few semitone steps (about 21 px a step); the major-to-chromatic change shifts some threads under the 24 px position floor, so scale may need a second cue.
Slabs are three faces each: 13 threads by 4 rows passes the redraw budget fast when a bar rolls back; flat tops for the older rows or three rows instead of four.
Mute (bypass) has no natural place in a cloth; the likely answer is the front row going hollow and the warp stopping, which needs a device check that it reads.
Schematic text (warp, weft, bar −3) is static and must stay; without it this is a bar chart in perspective.
cells.alt: Marble, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The last four bars woven as cloth on a schematic oblique: each bin is a warp thread, each bar a weft row, and every marble that landed is a slab stacked on its bin's thread, so the bell builds up row by row and drifts back as bars pass

cells.subject: The odds of each note as one bright stepped trace over a scope graticule, a pulse standing on every bin at its pitch and as tall as its share of the marbles, with the bar's drops ticking along a strip beneath.
controls: pegs: the trace's shape: one tall pulse pair at 1 row, a wide low bell of up to 13 pulses at 12 rows (shape, the bell's outer pulses move well over 16 px).
drop: the number of marks in the activity strip under the graticule (count, 1 to 32 a bar), one per marble released.
bounce: a second, dimmer channel trace rises under the first, its rebound pulses scaled by bounce and offset right of each bin (scale and position on channel 2), flat at 0.
scale: the pitch ticks on the graticule's baseline and the pulses standing on them slide to the scale's tones (position on the pitch axis, 16 px a semitone).
risks: P3's warning applies here too: a stepped trace on a graticule is the most generic picture of the five and could be any analyser; the scope furniture (ch1 readout, divisions) has to carry the authorship.
It shows the probability, not the marbles: the board itself never appears, so the Galton idea depends on the player already knowing it.
Adjacent semitone bins (b and c in major) put pulses 16 px apart, close to merging at 1:1.
Mute: the trace dims to the channel-off look (flat line at the baseline), a scope's own convention, but a flat line also looks like 'pegs at extreme' to a newcomer; needs a second cue.
cells.alt: Marble, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The odds of each note as one bright stepped trace over a scope graticule, a pulse standing on every bin at its pitch and as tall as its share of the marbles, with the bar's drops ticking along a strip beneath

cells.subject: A radial Galton board seen as an orrery: the hopper is the sun, each peg row is an orbit a marble crosses on its way out, and the bins are planets on the outer orbit placed round the pitch circle, sized by how often they're hit.
controls: pegs: the number of orbits between the sun and the bins (count, 1 to 12 rings), and the planets' sizes redistribute as the bell widens.
drop: the number of marbles waiting on the innermost ring around the sun (count, 1 to 32), one per drop in a bar, the release clock.
bounce: moons appear round each planet, up to three per planet, set further out as bounce rises (count with position), one per rebound retrigger.
scale: the planets move round the outer orbit to their pitch classes, 30° a semitone (position on the orbit), root always at the front.
risks: P12's own weakness: the orbits don't turn for any musical reason here, so the 'cycle' is the pitch circle rather than time; motion would have to be a marble's spiral out, not orbiting.
Off-centre bins at 1/64 odds are 3 px planets at the back of the orbit, at the legibility floor.
Twelve rings at 12 rows bring the front spacing to ~5 px: legal, but the board turns into a hatched dish.
The sun does nothing but release marbles; a second subject (the pitch circle) competes with the first (the board).
Mute: the sun goes hollow and the waiting marbles grey out; shade plus the marbles stepping back off the ring, to check it isn't shade alone.

cells.alt: Marble, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: The Galton board itself in front elevation, hopper and gate over a triangle of pegs, with each bin a pipe cut to its note's length so its floor sits at its pitch, and the pile of marbles caught in the bins is what plays

cells.subject: One marble's fall surveyed as a traverse in plan: from the hopper station it runs leg by leg through columns of peg stations, bearing a station up or down at each, to its lot on a boundary line whose parcels are laid out by pitch.
controls: pegs: the number of legs and station columns in the traverse (count, 1 to 12), the lattice opening wider to the east as rows are added.
drop: the pegs on the chain line along the bottom, one per drop in the bar (count, 1 to 32 between 0 and 1 bar).
bounce: a short rebound spur off the traverse's last station, out past the lot line and back (shape, its end moving 0 to 24 px), the survey's closing leg.
scale: the lot boundaries on the right slide to their pitches, 10 px a semitone (position), and the last leg bends to meet its lot.
risks: Stretch: P3 is an engine pattern for waveforms. The case for it is that a player's screen should draw the rule that picks notes in the same shape, and a marble's path IS that rule, a trace in the literal sense; the case against is that one path shows one outcome, not the distribution, which is the thing the machine is about.
At rest the drawing shows the last marble only, so the bell is invisible until many notes have passed; P3 asks the trace to be the subject, and here the subject is chance.
Scale moves lots by 10 px a semitone: the major-to-chromatic change shifts some lots by only 10 to 20 px, under the 24 px position floor.
Station triangles at 8 px are on the edge of reading as icons; they have to stay hairline, open, survey-plan marks.
Mute: the traverse goes to a dashed, unclosed line (a proposed, not surveyed, route); readable to a surveyor, maybe not to a player.

machines.name: Pendula
machines.description: A pendulum wave on aux track 12: pendulums of slowly different lengths each play a note on the target track as they cross the centre, drifting in and out of phase. Length sets the longest pendulum's swing, count how many hang, swing how wide (and so how hard) they swing, scale which notes they play.
machines.concept: A pendulum wave: pendulums of slowly different lengths each play a note as they cross the centre, drifting in and out of phase.
machines.soundsLike: A cluster of notes released together that unravels into rippling arpeggios, ripples, then chords again as the pendulums realign. Pendulum *i* makes K + *i* half-swings per cycle (K = 16), each crossing of the centre sends one note to the target track.

intake.subject: a row of pendulums of slowly different lengths, each playing its note as it crosses the centre, drifting out of phase and back.
intake.controlSource: new (the source is the DSP I'm writing)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings, one note (the trackControl reminder to show mute, answered above). `resources.display` is still the 1A placeholder; phase 4 sets it.

scores.effect: Ten times slower from 0 to 100: the note rate and the speed of the drift both follow it. Dramatic.
3 to 16 voices: density and pitch range (pentatonic: under an octave to over three). Big.
Velocity of every note, plus slightly shorter gates near 100. Clear, but the pattern stays the same.
Changes the pitch set, not the rhythm; pent → chrom is a big colour change, neighbours are subtle.

cells.subject: A patent sheet of conical pendulums on one spindle, each bob orbiting its own circle whose shadow on the section plane is its swing, so the bobs form an orrery and a crossing of that plane plays.
controls: length: how far the cone of rods drops from the hub and how wide the orbits open with it (scale, 1.6x).
count: how many orbits and bobs ring the spindle (count, 3 to 16).
swing: the cone's half-angle: orbits widen and rise towards the hub as it opens (shape of the stack, 10° to 45°).
scale: which ticks on the base dial are long, one per scale degree of the octave (shape of the dial).
cells.risks: A conical pendulum is a different machine; its projection is the swing, but it asks the player to accept that. Nested ellipses at 16 get dense near the hub. Patent numerals are decoration unless they stay few. The base dial is the weak control, a ring of ticks.

cells.subject: A textbook figure with every pendulum hung from a single pivot on nested swing arcs, where the plumb line is a gate that captures each bob as it crosses and that crossing is the note.
controls: length: the radius of the whole nest of arcs (scale, 90 to 180 px), so longer pendulums hang visibly deeper from the pivot.
count: how many nested arcs and bobs hang from the pivot (count, 3 to 16), the inner arcs packing in towards the pivot.
swing: the angle the arcs open to and the bobs are held at, marked θ at the pivot (rotation, 10° to 45° either side).
scale: the polygon on the pitch-class clock in the lower left (shape), a pentagon for pent up to the full twelve-gon for chrom.
cells.risks: Drawing every pendulum from one pivot is a diagram, not the apparatus; players who know the real row of pendulums may not recognise it. At 16 the inner bobs sit ~7 px apart along the ray and need a smaller bob. At rest every bob sits on one ray, so the drift only shows when playing (it opens into a spiral). The pitch-class clock is a corner figure, the P13 fallback for a control with no twin in the metaphor.
cells.alt: Pendula, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A textbook figure with every pendulum hung from a single pivot on nested swing arcs, where the plumb line is a gate that captures each bob as it crosses and that crossing is the note

cells.subject: A front elevation of the row whose strings run on down as warp threads into a woven cloth, where every crossing of the last four beats is a slab on its thread and the drift shows as diagonals.
controls: length: how far each bob hangs below the beam (position, 55 to 130 px for the longest), the bob line sloping as the real apparatus does.
count: how many strings and warp threads there are (count, 3 to 16).
swing: how high the bobs ride towards the viewer when held back, and how tall each woven slab is (position plus slab height, 4 to 12 px).
scale: the spacing of the threads, set by the scale's intervals so the cloth's gaps are the scale (shape: gaps of 1 to 3 semitones).
cells.risks: Front-on, the swing goes towards the viewer, so swing only reads as the bobs lifting (~26 px at most); a side elevation would show it but splits the subject. Four rows is little history for a pendulum wave's slow pattern; rows are beats, not cycles. Slab rows are expensive (P14) at 16 threads.
cells.alt: Pendula, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: A front elevation of the row whose strings run on down as warp threads into a woven cloth, where every crossing of the last four beats is a slab on its thread and the drift shows as diagonals

cells.subject: A survey plan seen from overhead in which the row lies along a dashed datum on a grid and a bright release board holds every bob on one line, ready to snake across it.
controls: length: the span of every bob's lane across the datum, and so how far the board sits from it (position/scale, ~38 to 70 px).
count: how many lanes cross the datum (count, 3 to 16).
swing: the size of each bob's proportional symbol, how hard it will cross (scale, 3 to 7 px radius).
scale: which ticks stand tall on the two-octave strip along the bottom, with each pendulum's note marked above its tick (count and position in the strip).
cells.risks: Seen from above the pendulum's length is invisible, so length borrows the lane span (which physically also grows with swing); swing is then a symbol size, a map convention rather than a physical part. The grid is ground decoration and costs nothing, but it is the most 'chart-like' of the five.

cells.subject: A swing set in hidden-line isometric with a block rider on every seat and chains of slowly different lengths, whose feet strike a tuned bar on the ground as each rider passes the bottom.
controls: length: the chain lengths, riders hanging lower as it rises (position, ~30 px).
count: how many riders hang from the beam (count, 3 to 16).
swing: how far back the riders are held (rotation of each chain about the beam, 10° to 45°).
scale: the lengths of the tuned bars on the ground, longer for lower notes (shape).
cells.risks: Stretch, and I don't think it earns the exception: the pendulum is already the performer, so a rider adds a character without adding a meaning, and figures invite idle animation and the drawing-quality trap toro hit. The only case for it is warmth: a row of swings reads instantly. A node can't tilt out of the screen's plane, so the swinging riders need pre-drawn poses per angle step, and 16 riders is a crowd.

machines.name: Rain
machines.description: A rain player on aux track 12: drops fall on a roof of pitched tiles at a rate, gusts push them across the tiles, puddles repeat the last notes. It plays another track; its own track stays silent.
machines.concept: Raindrops on a roof of pitched tiles: drops fall at a rate, gusts push them across, puddles repeat the last notes.
machines.soundsLike: Rain has no sound of its own: it plays another track. At low rate it's a sparse, irregular drip of notes from a scale; turned up it becomes a dense patter, and a strong gust turns the scatter into runs that walk up or down the tiles. A full puddle makes the last few notes come back as uneven echoes, so phrases repeat and then dissolve.

intake.subject: a roof of pitched tiles in the rain, where each tile course is a note, each drop that lands plays the course it hits, the wind pushes the drops across the courses, and the gutter holds the last notes to replay them.
intake.controlSource: new (the source is the control code I'm writing: a Poisson drop clock, a scale-quantised pitch walk over the roof's span, and a short note memory for the puddle)
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings (one note: show the muted state, which is carried in the intake row above). Nothing to justify.

scores.effect: A drop every four beats to eight a beat: from sparse drip to a dense patter, the biggest change in how much is played
One repeated note at 0 st to a three-octave scatter at 36: the melody's whole range; clear from about 3 st up
Still air at 0 (random landing); toward ±100 the scatter turns into rising or falling runs. Audible as direction more than as density
Nothing at 0; from ~30 phrases start coming back; at 100 most notes are replays and the line loops before it dissolves
