cells.subject: A round pavilion roof surveyed from directly above: its tile courses are concentric orbits round the ridge finial, one course per note of the span, and each drop that lands sits on its course like a planet, with the gutter as the outermost orbit where the puddle's held notes circle.
controls: rate: how many drop marks sit on the courses from the last bar (count): one or two at 0.25 a beat, about thirty at 8 a beat, newest brightest and older ones fading to hollow rings.
roof: how many concentric course rings the plan holds between finial and eave (count, plus ring spacing as position): one ring at 0 st, eight at 12, twenty-two at 36 crowding toward the 3 px floor.
gust: every drop mark slides round its orbit in the wind's direction (rotation about the finial, up to ±90° at full gust), with a bearing arc outside the gutter showing which way and how far.
puddle: beads collect on the gutter orbit, one per repeated note, joined by a link drawn along the gutter in the direction they replay (count): none at 0, a near-full ring at 100.
risks: A plan view throws away the depth that makes meikyu's orrery read as a solar system; at 1:1 it can read as a target, which craft.md names as an icon to avoid. The hips and survey labels are what stop it, and they're hairlines.
Rings are 10 px apart at 12 st but 3 px at 36 st; the roof control has to cap the drawn rings (one per scale octave degree, not per semitone) or it turns to hatching.
Gust and puddle are both empty at their defaults (0 and 0), so the rest frame shows neither; gust's rotation of the drops only reads once there are drops.
Orbits suggest a cycle, but rain isn't periodic; only puddle (the replay loop) is truly a cycle. The metaphor fits one control in four.
Muted state: the drops would have to go hollow and the finial dark; not yet drawn.
cells.alt: Rain, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: A round pavilion roof surveyed from directly above: its tile courses are concentric orbits round the ridge finial, one course per note of the span, and each drop that lands sits on its course like a planet, with the gutter as the outermost orbit where the puddle's held notes circle

cells.subject: A mono-pitch roof cut in section like a patent figure, where each overlapping tile course is a pitch and a falling drop plays whichever course catches it, while the half-round gutter at the eave captures the run-off and its water level is how much of the last phrase gets replayed.
controls: rate: how many falling streaks hang over the roof at once (count): two at the slowest, about twenty at 8 a beat.
roof: the roof's pitch angle (rotation of the rafter, tiles and ridge post about the eave, 6° to 46°): a flat roof spans no notes, a steep one 36 semitones, so the ridge climbs about 60 px.
gust: the slant of every streak (shape/angle, ±35° from vertical) and where along the slope the drops land, bunching them toward the eave or the ridge.
puddle: the water line in the gutter section rises (position, 0 to 12 px) and drips hang from its lip, one per repeated note (count as second cue).
risks: The capture is literal (a tile catches a drop) but weak as a rule picture: what the player most needs, which notes the roof spans, is only implied by course positions; there's no pitch axis without adding one.
Roof as pitch angle moves the whole roof (rafter, tiles, posts): a big redraw on a turn, though zero at rest.
The gutter is small and in the far corner from the brightest tile; the puddle control's whole effect lives in about 20 × 20 px, which will struggle against a score of 4.
Patent hatching at 6 px on a slanted rafter is close to the 3 px floor once rendered; check at 1:1 on the device.
Muted state: streaks stop above the roof (held mid-air in grey).
cells.alt: Rain, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: A mono-pitch roof cut in section like a patent figure, where each overlapping tile course is a pitch and a falling drop plays whichever course catches it, while the half-round gutter at the eave captures the run-off and its water level is how much of the last phrase gets replayed

cells.subject: The roof itself is the loom: its tile columns are warp threads, one per note of the span, each bar of rain weaves a new row of tiles at the eave while older bars climb back toward the ridge, and a tile a drop struck stands up as a slab, solid where the puddle repeated it and wire where it was new.
controls: rate: how many raised slabs each row carries (count): one in a bar at the slowest, nearly every tile at 8 a beat.

roof: how many warp threads (tile columns) the roof is wide (count, the eave fascia and ridge lengthening with it as position): one column at 0 st, eight at 12, capped at sixteen with the header naming the real span.
gust: each older row's hits are shifted along the threads by the drift the wind gave them (position), so a gusty bar shears the slab pattern into a diagonal toward the ridge.

puddle: how many of a row's slabs are repeats of the row in front, drawn solid down the cloth (shade and count, solid vs wire): all wire behind the first row at 0, solid columns climbing to the ridge at 100.
risks: Rows of slabs on a tile grid read close to a step grid, the panel craft.md warns about; the sloping roof plane and the eave/ridge are what make it a roof and not a sequencer matrix.
Rain has no bar structure of its own; rows-as-bars imposes one. Drops between bar lines need a rule for which row they land in.
Count is budget-heavy: 16 columns × 4 rows × 3 faces is 192 nodes before labels.
Roof and rate are both counts (threads vs slabs); they are different parts, but perceptibility has to show the thread count change isn't mistaken for density.
Muted state: the front row stays empty and every slab goes wire.
cells.alt: Rain, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: The roof itself is the loom: its tile columns are warp threads, one per note of the span, each bar of rain weaves a new row of tiles at the eave while older bars climb back toward the ridge, and a tile a drop struck stands up as a slab, solid where the puddle repeated it and wire where it was new

cells.subject: A star chart of the rain as a meteor shower: on a faint conic graticule the roof is a constellation, its tile courses plotted as stars up both slopes to the ridge, each drop a short trail traced back to a radiant the gust slides along the sky, with the puddle as an open cluster below the eave and the last sixteen beats ticked along the bottom strip.
controls: rate: how many meteor trails are plotted at once (count, 1 to ~24), each ending at the tile star it rang, with ticks filling the strip as second cue.
roof: the constellation's ridge star rises and more course stars appear up the slopes (shape, ridge moves ~50 px; count as second cue): a flat line of one star at 0 st, a steep gable at 36.
gust: the radiant slides along the top of the chart (position, ±150 px) and every trail swings to point back at it, so drops come in from the side the wind blows from.
puddle: stars gather inside the dotted cluster ring below the left eave, one per repeated note, and the cluster ring widens (count, then scale).
risks: The gable constellation is the house icon's outline in dots; it has to stay a constellation (broken lines short of each star, magnitudes, the name tegula) or it reads as clip-art.
Meteors fall away from a radiant, rain falls down: the picture asks the player to read drops as trails pointing up toward their source. Clever, maybe too clever.
Stars at 2–3 px on the upper courses sit at the small-part floor; the lint flags the cluster dots (1.8 px) and they'd need to grow.
The strip and the cluster are both secondary furniture in low greys at the bottom; together with the graticule labels the edges get busy.
Muted state: trails go out and the figure drops to the field's grey.
cells.alt: Rain, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: A star chart of the rain as a meteor shower: on a faint conic graticule the roof is a constellation, its tile courses plotted as stars up both slopes to the ridge, each drop a short trail traced back to a radiant the gust slides along the sky, with the puddle as an open cluster below the eave and the last sixteen beats ticked along the bottom strip

cells.subject: Stretch: a gable roof in hard one-bit ink, its tile courses printed as alternating dither bands under a 2 px bright outline, wired like an engineering schematic to labelled terminals for the rain streaks above it, the wind strokes beside it and the puddle plane at the downpipe foot.
controls: rate: how many flat rain-streak glyphs hang above the roof (count, 2 to ~20); the dither can't move, so the streaks are flat greys.
roof: the gable's pitch (shape: the ridge point rises from 20 to 90 px above the eaves), with the dithered course bands redrawn as static art per span step.
gust: the wind glyph's strokes lengthen to one side and every streak leans with them (shape, ±30°).
puddle: the flat puddle plane at the downpipe widens and lightens (scale 1× to 2×, two grey steps).
risks: Doesn't fit, plainly. P9 is a hero figure for an engine; a player's screen should show the rule that picks notes, and a house with rain on it shows the setting, not the rule. Nothing on it says which tile is which pitch or what the puddle replays.

The exception case would be that rain is the one player whose rule is a picture people already know by sight (water on a roof); that holds for the concept but not the controls: the gable at 1:1 is the house icon.
Dither only lives in still art, but roof (the most visible control) changes the dithered planes: each span step would need its own pre-drawn dither set, or the bands go flat and the language is lost.
One-bit ink and schematic pull against each other: the terminals and labels read as a legend panel next to a picture (craft.md, Picture not panel).
The lint flags ~970 2 × 2 dither cells as under the small-part floor; that's the pattern's nature (toro-ink) but a warning wall.
Muted state: the outline drops to mid grey, the only element allowed to be brightest.
cells.alt: Rain, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: Stretch: a gable roof in hard one-bit ink, its tile courses printed as alternating dither bands under a 2 px bright outline, wired like an engineering schematic to labelled terminals for the rain streaks above it, the wind strokes beside it and the puddle plane at the downpipe foot

cells.subject: The verge of the roof seen side on at large scale: a black mass whose tile noses climb out of the top-right corner, lit only along the edges that face the sky, where each lit nose is a course that can play and the one a drop just hit is the bright one.
controls: rate: how many rain streaks hang in the open sky above the verge (count, about 6 at 1.0 a beat to about 24 at 8), each falling toward the course it will land on.
roof: how many tile noses carry a rim light (count, with exposure as shape): at 0 st one lit nose, at 36 st twenty-two smaller ones; noses past the span stay as dim hairlines running off the frame.
gust: the streaks lean (rotation, ±30° from vertical) and the landings walk up or down the lit noses, so a strong gust reads as a run of crowns climbing or descending the edge.
puddle: the half-round gutter at the eave fills (water hatched in 45° hairlines inside its profile, rising 0 to full) and beads of light hang from its lip, one per note held in memory.
risks: Silhouette against a black sky: the roof mass only exists through its rim and the barge-board hairline, so the black body is invisible as a shape; it has to be read from the edge alone.
At 36 st the 22 noses get ~20 px apart, still clear of the 3 px floor but much busier than at rest; the camera can't scale up without losing the eave.
The gutter (puddle's whole channel) is a 20 px corner far from the struck course; puddle scores 3 and may struggle for area unless the beads are generous.
The barge-board hairline running to the right edge can read as a separate diagonal line at 1:1.
Muted: every rim drops to hairline G2 and the streaks stop where they are (the roof goes dark, nothing lands).
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Rain, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: The verge of the roof seen side on at large scale: a black mass whose tile noses climb out of the top-right corner, lit only along the edges that face the sky, where each lit nose is a course that can play and the one a drop just hit is the bright one

cells.subject: Rain itself: the last bar's drops falling through still air, each drawn as a real drop (round on top, flattened underneath the bigger it is) with a strobe ghost where it was a moment ago, where a drop's size is its note and the one that just played is bright.
controls: rate: how many drops are in the air (count, about 7 at 1.0 a beat up to about 28 at 8, each one a note of the last bar).

roof: the spread of drop sizes (shape/scale per drop): at 0 st every drop is the same size, one note; at 36 st they range from a pin-head to a big flattened drop, so the size range is the pitch range.
gust: the fall slants (each drop and its ghost offset sideways along the wind, ±35°), and the drops sort themselves big-to-small along the gust's direction, so a run reads as a graded slope of sizes.
puddle: drops that are replays appear as hatched copies of earlier drops (45° hairlines inside a hairline outline, there but not new), from none at 0 to most of the air at 100.
risks: Free-floating circles can read as bubbles or bells if the strobe ghosts are lost; the ghost is what says 'falling', so it can't be dropped for budget.
Each drop is ~4 nodes (outline, ghost, equator, crescent); 28 drops at rate 8 is over 100 nodes and many redraws per beat: will need a pool and a cap.
Size is both pitch and (slightly) depth: the camera puts drops nearly in one plane so perspective can't fake a pitch; keep depth range small.
Nothing roof-like remains: the 'roof' label maps to size spread, which must be learned from turning it.
Muted: drops freeze mid-air and their outlines drop to G3 hairline; no ghosts.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Rain, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: Rain itself: the last bar's drops falling through still air, each drawn as a real drop (round on top, flattened underneath the bigger it is) with a strobe ghost where it was a moment ago, where a drop's size is its note and the one that just played is bright

cells.subject: A rainstick held across the screen, modelled as a hollow tube with a cord grip, growth nodes and pins driven through it in a spiral, where each ring of pins is a course and the pin a falling pebble just struck rings with light at its head.
controls: rate: how many pin heads carry a ring (count: recently struck pins, about 4 at 1.0 a beat to about 20 at 8), the newest filled bright.
roof: how many rings of pins the stick has (count, 1 ring at 0 st to 22 at 36 st), spaced evenly along the same tube, so a flat roof is a stick with one ring of pins.
gust: the stick tips (rotation about its centre, ±25° from its rest angle): tipped one way the struck pins run in order down the tube (falling runs), the other way up; at 0 the strikes scatter.
puddle: pebbles gathered in the open mouth at the near end (count, 0 to ~8 small closed outlines visible inside the rim), the ones that will be poured back through as replays.
risks: Pin heads are 4 px dots at 1:1: right at the size floor; struck rings make them readable but the unstruck spiral is faint.
Tipping is an in-plane turn of the whole tube, so the 3D yaw stays fixed; at ±25° the ends approach the header and frame edge and the camera fit has to leave room.
The rainstick is a rain instrument, not a roof: the 'roof' label maps to pin rings, which is the right idea but a new picture for the name.
Pins on the hidden side of the tube can't show a strike; strikes must be drawn on visible pins only, which biases which notes look played.
Muted: the stick lies at rest angle, no rings, the mouth empty and its rim dims to G3.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Rain, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: A rainstick held across the screen, modelled as a hollow tube with a cord grip, growth nodes and pins driven through it in a spiral, where each ring of pins is a course and the pin a falling pebble just struck rings with light at its head

cells.subject: Clay pantiles seen close as the rain lands on them: eight courses of broad pans and tall rolls rising away from the viewer, each course's lapped edge one bold line over black, where the tile a drop just struck has the bright edge and a broken crown.
controls: rate: how many falling teardrops and crowns are on the tiles at once (count, about 3 at 1.0 a beat to about 16 at 8).
roof: how many courses rise up the slope (count, 1 at 0 st to 22 at 36 st, shallower exposure as they multiply), the far ones thinning to hairlines as they recede.
gust: the drops slant and their crowns throw to one side (rotation ±35°), and successive strikes step across the courses toward the ridge or the eave.
puddle: water stands in the pans of the nearest courses (45° hairline hatching clipped to each pan, its level rising from dry at 0 to brimming at 100).
risks: Eight full-width bands cover the body: it's the least black of the five (~81 % black at 1:1) and the busiest; the lowest courses must stay calm.
Close-up perspective makes far courses ~6 px tall: at 36 st (22 courses) the far half becomes a hatch of lines under 3 px apart and has to fade out.
Pantile rolls carried up the slope as hairlines can read as a grid or a corrugated sheet if they get brighter.
Splash crowns are small (~10 px); the struck tile's bright edge does most of the note response.
Muted: every edge drops to Line weight G3, no drops; the struck edge goes back to grey.
cells.angle: the material the sound acts on, seen close
cells.alt: Rain, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: Clay pantiles seen close as the rain lands on them: eight courses of broad pans and tall rolls rising away from the viewer, each course's lapped edge one bold line over black, where the tile a drop just struck has the bright edge and a broken crown

cells.subject: Under a dripping eave, a shelf of clay flowerpots graded from big to small, each cut through its axis to show the clay walls, rim collar and drain hole, where each pot rings its own note when a drip falls into it and the pot that just rang is bright.
controls: rate: how many drips are falling from the eave's tile noses into the pots (count, about 3 at 1.0 a beat to about 16 at 8).
roof: how many pots stand on the shelf (count, 1 at 0 st to 22 at 36 st, graded big-to-small left to right), smaller overall as more fit.
gust: the drips slant (rotation ±30°) and land toward one end of the row, so runs climb or fall along the graded pots.
puddle: water standing in the pots (45° hairline hatching clipped inside each cut, its level rising from dry at 0 to near the rim at 100).
risks: Eight pots across 480 px leaves each 30-60 px wide; at 22 pots they shrink to ~16 px and the cut walls (3 px) start to merge.
A row of graded vessels is close to a bar chart or a set of tuned bowls; the drain holes, rim collars and eave are what say 'flowerpots in the rain'.
The eave's row of noses is a thin wave across the top and can read as a divider; it needs to stay a hairline-quiet second subject.
The 'roof' label maps to pot count, a scene metaphor the player has to learn.
Muted: drips stop and hang under the eave; the struck pot dims back to grey.
cells.angle: one scene where this happens, with one subject in it
cells.alt: Rain, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: Under a dripping eave, a shelf of clay flowerpots graded from big to small, each cut through its axis to show the clay walls, rim collar and drain hole, where each pot rings its own note when a drip falls into it and the pot that just rang is bright

cells.subject: The window face on and wide, where the subject is the wiped trails that heavy beads leave as they let go and run down through the beaded band, each a closed lane with the small beads it dropped strung inside it.
controls: rate: how many beads cling in the landing band (count, about 40 at 0.25 a beat to the band packed at 8), and how often a new bold outline appears in it.

roof: the height of the landing band on the glass (position/extent, a single line of beads at 0 st to most of the pane at 36 st); a bead's height is its note, so a wide roof scatters them up and down.
gust: landings arrive on a slant (a short hairline streak before each drop) and every trail leans and drifts left or right as it runs (shape, about ±40 px of sideways travel over a run at ±100).

puddle: how big a bead grows before it lets go (scale of the heavy beads, double-outlined), so how many beads each run sweeps up and replays as it passes them; at 0 beads let go after two or three drops and trails are thin, at 100 they gather long and leave wide lanes.
risks: Rows of small round outlines can read as bubbles or a dotted chart rather than water; the beads need their sag (heavier at the bottom) to stay readable at 1:1.
Trails are the subject, but at rest the brightest element is the newest bead (a small ring); the newest trail is only a step brighter, so the eye may not land on the trace first.
Old trails have to go somewhere: the sketch keeps the last four; on the device they need a rule (fresh landings re-bead them, or they fade one step per new run).
A growing trail outline is a mutable path re-keyed each frame while a run moves: one of the four paths per concurrent run, so at most two runs at once.
Muted: landings stop, beads keep their outlines but drop to hairline G2 and no run moves; the glass goes still and dim.
cells.angle: the mark or trace the process leaves behind
cells.alt: Rain, pass 3 (subject), variant 1: The window face on and wide, where the subject is the wiped trails that heavy beads leave as they let go and run down through the beaded band, each a closed lane with the small beads it dropped strung inside it

cells.subject: A real wet pane seen at an angle and cut through at its right edge, so the glass shows its thickness as a hatched section and the heavy bead sitting on the cut shows its meniscus in profile, holding as much water as the puddle lets it.
controls: rate: how many drops strike the face of the pane (count of foreshortened beads, sparse at 0.25 a beat to crowded at 8).
roof: how tall the wet band is on the glass (position/extent along the pane's height): every bead sits at its note's height, so 0 st is one line of beads and 36 st wets most of the pane.
gust: the incoming drops' streaks slant and the runs on the face drift sideways along the pane (shape, the trails bend toward or away from the cut).

puddle: the bead on the cut swells (scale of its profile and meniscus, about 1.5x from 0 to 100) because a fuller glass holds more before it lets go; when it does go, its run sweeps the face and replays what it took in.
risks: The section is a narrow strip at the right edge: at 1:1 it can read as a post or a pipe rather than the glass's thickness, and the pane's other edges aren't drawn, so the angle is carried only by the foreshortened beads.
The subject (the bead on the cut) sits at the edge, not where the eye lands first; the bead field in the middle competes with it.
Gust's sideways push runs mostly along the camera's depth axis, so it's foreshortened; it needs checking at ±100 that it clears the 24 px floor.
Muted: no drops strike, the profile bead drops from G7 to G4 and the hatched section stays as the only clear structure.
cells.angle: the machine's own rule as a physical thing: what turning each knob would do to a real object
cells.alt: Rain, pass 3 (subject), variant 2: A real wet pane seen at an angle and cut through at its right edge, so the glass shows its thickness as a hatched section and the heavy bead sitting on the cut shows its meniscus in profile, holding as much water as the puddle lets it

cells.subject: The heaviest bead on the glass with the drops it gathered pulled back off the pane along the line the rain came in on, each drop floating over the spot where it landed (its height is its note) with a hairline back to that spot and the slide it made down into the bead.
controls: rate: how many plain beads cling on the glass around the assembly (count), the drops that haven't gathered yet.
roof: how far apart the exploded drops' landing spots are in height (position, the parts fan from one line at 0 st to a tall spread at 36 st), so the span reads as the fan's height.
gust: the explosion axis tilts left or right (rotation of every leader, about ±30°), because the parts are pulled back along the direction the wind brought them in.
puddle: how many drops the heavy bead holds (count of exploded parts, 3 at 0 to 12 at 100, and the bead's size with them); each new drop enters on the right, bright, and the oldest leaves.
risks: Leaders plus slide lines plus contact rings can read as a node graph or a molecule rather than drops; the leaders need to stay parallel and the slides quiet.
Floating flattened spheres risk reading as balloons on strings; they're drawn as real falling drops (pressed flat on the leading face), not as the teardrop icon.
The assembly only shows the puddle's memory; the beads around it are history and don't connect to it, so the screen has two stories.
Every note shifts all the parts one slot (n nodes move), so at puddle 100 a note moves 12 parts: peak cost grows with puddle.
Muted: the parts sink back to their contact rings (exploded distance eases to 0) and the bead goes G4: assembled and still.
cells.angle: a cutaway of the object at work, so the inside explains it
cells.alt: Rain, pass 3 (subject), variant 3: The heaviest bead on the glass with the drops it gathered pulled back off the pane along the line the rain came in on, each drop floating over the spot where it landed (its height is its note) with a hairline back to that spot and the slide it made down into the bead

cells.subject: One heavy bead seen close and about to let go, its surface drawn as level contours that sag toward its heavy lower edge, with neighbouring beads and an old wiped trail cut by the frame's edges so the pane is only implied.
controls: rate: how many small beads land around the heavy one (count, a few at 0.25 a beat to a crowd at 8), each a single-weight outline.
roof: how far up and down the glass the small landings scatter around the heavy bead (position spread, one row at 0 st to the full height at 36 st).
gust: the arriving streaks slant and the heavy bead's sag leans left or right (shape: its lowest contour shifts ±16 px), so the run it starts will go sideways.
puddle: the heavy bead's size before it goes (scale, radius about 1.5x from 0 to 100, with more contours); a full puddle is a big, slow-growing bead that sweeps everything below it when it runs.
risks: Nested contours on a dome can read as a target (craft.md: no nested bands); the strong downward sag and the oblique camera are what keep it a drop, and they must survive every setting.
After the bead lets go the subject has left the frame: the screen is an empty lane until a new heavy bead gathers, which can read as broken.
Single weight means hierarchy is carried by grey alone (G7 bead, G5 contours, G4 neighbours); that's three steps but close to the grey-only-difference limit.
A heavy run moving with 7 contour nodes plus its lane is ~8 changed nodes a frame, fine, but the lane is a re-keyed path while it moves.
Muted: the bead's contours drop to G3 with only its outline left at G4; nothing lands, nothing lets go.
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Rain, pass 3 (subject), variant 4: One heavy bead seen close and about to let go, its surface drawn as level contours that sag toward its heavy lower edge, with neighbouring beads and an old wiped trail cut by the frame's edges so the pane is only implied

cells.subject: Rain on the glass, literally and close: every bead and every run a mass of water drawn in 45° hatching because water is see-through, its lower rim lit where the meniscus catches the light, the newest drop's rim the brightest.
controls: rate: how many hatched drops hang on the glass (count, a handful at 0.25 a beat to a crowded band at 8).
roof: the height of the wet band (position/extent), a drop's height being its note; at 0 st the drops sit in one line and merge quickly into heavy ones.
gust: landings slant (streak before each drop) and the runs lean and drift sideways (shape of the hatched lanes, ±40 px over a run).
puddle: how heavy a drop grows before it lets go (scale of the biggest hatched masses), and so how wide and long its hatched lane is and how many drops it sweeps up and replays.
risks: Hatched round masses can read as striped balls or a pattern swatch at 1:1 if they get small; drops under ~6 px are drawn as plain outlines instead.

Moving hatched masses are expensive: every hatch line is a node, so a running drop costs ~12 changed nodes a frame on average and peaks near 45; on the device the run head would need fewer, coarser lines.
It sits near v1 in layout (a band of drops and trails below); the difference is scale and language, which the owner may see as the same window.
Muted: the rims drop to G3, the hatching stays (water is still there) and nothing moves.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Rain, pass 3 (subject), variant 5: Rain on the glass, literally and close: every bead and every run a mass of water drawn in 45° hatching because water is see-through, its lower rim lit where the meniscus catches the light, the newest drop's rim the brightest

machines.name: Ringer
machines.description: Change ringing on aux track 12: a ring of bells permuted by a method, one change per row, at a steady pace, each blow played as a note on the target track. Bells sets the stage (4 to 12), method the permutation rule, pace the blows per beat, stroke the handstroke gap.
machines.concept: Change ringing: a set of bells permuted by a method, one change per row, at a steady pace.
machines.soundsLike: A ring of tuned notes (a descending major scale, treble highest) played as a steady stream on the target track, the order shifting every row so a familiar scale keeps turning into new phrases. Handstroke and backstroke rows alternate; with the gap open the stream breathes every second row, as tower bells do.

intake.subject: a ring of bells being rung in changes, where every control moves the bells, their order, or the rhythm they strike in.
intake.controlSource: new
intake.lintDefinition: 0 errors, 0 warnings (one note: show the muted state, answered in every candidate's risks).

scores.effect: 4 to 12 notes a row: the range of the ring triples and every row lengthens; a strong change
the same notes in a different order; plain hunt to Cambridge is clear over a lead, not on one note
0.5 to 8 blows a beat, sixteen times the note rate; the loudest thing on the page
up to one blow's pause every second row: a lilt, plain at slow pace, soft at fast

cells.subject: The ring as an orrery: each bell a half-sectioned bell profile on its own orbit round a hatched arbor, treble innermost and tenor outermost, its angle on the orbit being its place in the current change, so a change reads round the plate and a hunting bell travels its orbit.
controls: bells: count, orbits and bells added outward from the arbor, 4 to 12, each new bell a larger section on a new outer orbit, the graduated rim moving out with them.

method: position, every bell steps along its own orbit to the place the method gives it in the current change (a swap is two neighbours exchanging angles); the treble's link arcs ahead along its orbit trace the method's next three changes as a second cue.
pace: count, graduations round the plate's rim, one per blow over two bars: 4 at 0.5 a beat, 16 at the default 2, 64 at 8 (a doubling per quarter of travel).

stroke: rotation, on handstroke changes an empty sector opens before place 1 on every orbit, 0 degrees at 0 % to one blow's width at 100 % (51 degrees at 6 bells, 28 at 12), the places closing up round the rest of the plate.
risks: Bells at 15 to 30 px tall read close to a bell glyph; only the half-section cut (dark wall face, centre line, canon) keeps them in the patent language, and at 1:1 the cut face is barely visible. Needs larger bells or a heavier section.
The arbor (the sun) does nothing, P12's own weakness; the hatched section makes it look meant, not useful.
Stroke's sector is 28 degrees at 12 bells, under the 30-degree rotation floor; it needs a fixed minimum sector or a second cue (the rim graduations breaking).
Twelve bells put 12 places on the treble's inner orbit (44 units): neighbours 23 px apart on screen at the front, much closer at the sides where the plate foreshortens; bodies may touch.
Mute needs its own state: plate and orbits drop to ground grey and the bells go hollow; not drawn in this sketch.
cells.alt: Ringer, pass 1 (subject), variant 1: The ring as an orrery: each bell a half-sectioned bell profile on its own orbit round a hatched arbor, treble innermost and tenor outermost, its angle on the orbit being its place in the current change, so a change reads round the plate and a hunting bell travels its orbit

cells.subject: The bells hung in their frame in hidden-line isometric, each turned on its axle to how far it has swung since leaving the balance, because that is the machine's rule: a bell's place in the change is where it is in its swing, so the row reads as which bell has come furthest round.
controls: bells: count, pits filled in the frame, 4 to 12, the frame growing by a row of three pits at a time; empty pits stay as bare sills until a bell is hung in them.

method: rotation, each bell turns on its axle to the angle of its place in the current change (1st place furthest round and about to strike, the last just off the balance); a new method re-deals the angles, neighbours swapping.
pace: position, the ropes are taken in: every sally rises up its rope towards the frame, about 22 px from 0.5 to 8 blows a beat, as ringers do when they ring lower and faster.

stroke: position, the slider under each pit (the bar the stay rests on at the balance) runs out along its runner up to 24 px as the handstroke gap grows, and on handstroke changes the leading bell is held back against it.
risks: The bells swing in a plane tilted to the screen, so a node can't turn them: every bell needs pre-drawn swing variants (12 angles x up to 12 bells, plus lip ellipses) and the budget is heavy, as meikyu's planets were.
Reading the row needs the bells told apart by size alone (treble smallest); at 6 bells it works, at 12 in a 3 x 4 frame the sizes crowd and the frame packs.
Stroke's slider is not in the sketch, and the held-back leading bell overlaps method's rotation channel on one bell; stroke must lead with the slider.
Ropes and sallies are hairline and low grey; pace's travel may read weakly at 1:1 behind the bells.
Mute has a real, honest state: the ring is stood, every bell set mouth-up at the balance on its stay; it is distinct by rotation, not shade.
cells.alt: Ringer, pass 1 (subject), variant 2: The bells hung in their frame in hidden-line isometric, each turned on its axle to how far it has swung since leaving the balance, because that is the machine's rule: a bell's place in the change is where it is in its swing, so the row reads as which bell has come furthest round

cells.subject: The method as a star chart: changes are the parallels of a conic projection, woven in at the bottom and sliding back, places are its meridians, every blow a star sized by its bell, and the treble's path through the changes drawn as the bright constellation line.
controls: bells: count, meridians on the chart, 4 to 12, and the stars on every parallel with them; the fan of meridians widens to the neatline.

method: shape, the constellation line (one mutable outline) bends to the treble's path under the method: an even zig-zag for hunt, dodges for bob, long stretches for Cambridge; bell 2's hairline follows as a fainter figure.

pace: count, how many changes the chart holds over a fixed six bars: 2 parallels at 0.5 a beat, 8 at the default 2 (6 bells), capped at 12 from about 3 a beat, the parallels closing up as they are added.
stroke: position, every handstroke parallel stands back from its backstroke partner by up to one parallel's spacing, so the changes pair up as whole pulls with open bands of sky between them.
risks: It is the blue line, the ringer's own method diagram: instant for ringers, but close to a grid of data; the atlas furniture (neatline, graduations, sized stars, labels) is what keeps it a chart and must stay.

Sliding the chart back one parallel per change moves every star (up to 12 x 12 = 144 nodes) at once, far over ~20 changed nodes a frame; it needs a fixed chart with a moving 'now' parallel that wraps, or few rows.
Pace (count of parallels) and stroke (spacing of alternate parallels) both act on parallel position; stroke must stay a pairing, not a spacing, to be its own channel.
At 12 bells meridians are ~30 px apart and fine; at 12 parallels the spacing drops to ~10 px and the small stars near touch.
Mute: the chart stops weaving and the constellation drops to mid grey; not drawn here.
cells.alt: Ringer, pass 1 (subject), variant 3: The method as a star chart: changes are the parallels of a conic projection, woven in at the bottom and sliding back, places are its meridians, every blow a star sized by its bell, and the treble's path through the changes drawn as the bright constellation line

cells.subject: One bell drawn as an engineering elevation on its headstock and wheel, turned about the gudgeon to the angle it is rung up to, standing over a receding ringing-chamber floor, with the whole pull (a handstroke change and a backstroke change) ticked along the strip below.
controls: bells: count, ticks per change in the strip, 4 to 12, both changes of the whole pull lengthening; the figure and floor stay.
method: position, the strip's ticks rise and fall to the bells of the current whole pull (tick height by bell, treble tallest and bright), re-ordered as the method changes.

pace: rotation, the bell figure turns about its gudgeon from 178 degrees (rung right up to the balance, slow) to about 108 degrees (rung low, fast), the dimensioned angle arc and its figure following.
stroke: position, the handstroke change slides away from the backstroke change along the strip, a gap opening up to 24 px at 100 %.
risks: The subject fights the machine: the big figure carries only pace, while the method (what ringer is) lives in a 16 px strip of ticks that is close to a meter row.
One bell drawn alone reads as a single swinging bell, maybe a bell synth, not a ring being permuted.
Three of four controls sit in the strip; bells, method and stroke all change ticks, so their channels (count, height, gap) must stay strictly apart.
The floor field is decoration with no control; P5 allows a still field, but here it adds little.
Mute: the bell is stood at the balance, mouth up, its stay on the slider (rotation), and the strip empties.
cells.alt: Ringer, pass 1 (subject), variant 4: One bell drawn as an engineering elevation on its headstock and wheel, turned about the gudgeon to the angle it is rung up to, standing over a receding ringing-chamber floor, with the whole pull (a handstroke change and a backstroke change) ticked along the strip below

cells.subject: Each change as the pitch staircase it sends to the target track, traced bright on a scope graticule, with the four changes before it stacked back up and to the right as fading sweeps.
controls: bells: count, steps per sweep, 4 to 12, each a gate pulse at its bell's level (treble top), the levels closing up to fit the graticule.
method: shape, the front trace (one mutable outline) re-orders its steps to the current change, and the sweeps behind show the last four changes it came from.
pace: position, the depth step between sweeps, 18 px back per change when slow, packed to 10 px when fast: the time between changes drawn as distance back.
stroke: position, on handstroke changes the front trace starts later after the trigger mark, a flat lead-in up to one step wide (about 50 px at 6 bells).
risks: Reads as a meter of the output, not a picture of the method; the guidelines' category says a player draws the rule.
Bells and method both reshape the front trace (count of steps and order of steps); only one may own shape.
Overlapping sweeps tangle where traces cross; the back sweeps need black-filled sweep frames (hidden-line) to stay legible, which a scope would not have.
Five sweeps at 10 px depth step approach the 6 px stack floor at the fast end.
Mute: the front trace goes flat at the baseline (no signal), an honest and legible state.
cells.alt: Ringer, pass 1 (subject), variant 5: Each change as the pitch staircase it sends to the target track, traced bright on a scope graticule, with the four changes before it stacked back up and to the right as fading sweeps

cells.subject: The sallies at eye height in the ringing chamber, drawn close and cropped by the frame: each striped woollen grip hangs at the height its bell has reached, so the change reads as a wave of sallies and the lowest is the one being pulled now.
controls: bells: count, sallies hang across the frame from 4 to 12, the pitch between ropes closing up and the grips scaling down together so twelve still read as grips, not bars.

method: position, every sally rises or drops to the height of its bell's place in the current change (first place lowest and bright, last place highest); a swap is two neighbouring sallies trading heights.

pace: position (spread), the whole wave flattens as the bells are rung lower and faster: the gap between the lowest and highest sally goes from about 105 px at 0.5 a beat to about 40 px at 8 (about 65 px at the default).
stroke: position, on handstroke changes the leading sally is held up off the bottom of the wave by up to one place's step (about 26 px at 100 %), the pause before the pull.
risks: Method and pace both act on sally height (order versus spread); they must stay visibly different: method re-deals heights, pace only scales the wave. Stroke is a third vertical move on one sally, so it leans on being only the bright one.
The tufted helical stripes are hairlines about 8 px apart inside a 30 px grip; at twelve bells the grips shrink to about 17 px and the stripes must drop to every other one to stay 3 px apart.
Ropes are cut by both frame edges by design; nothing says 'ceiling' or 'tail end', which is the point, but a viewer who doesn't know a sally may read capsules.
Mute: the ropes are let go and every sally drops to one level, still, with the bright weight gone; distinct by position, not shade. Not drawn here.
cells.angle: one detail at large scale, the rest implied by the frame's edge
cells.alt: Ringer, pass 2 (subject), variant 1: The sallies at eye height in the ringing chamber, drawn close and cropped by the frame: each striped woollen grip hangs at the height its bell has reached, so the change reads as a wave of sallies and the lowest is the one being pulled now

cells.subject: The ring itself, literally: hidden-line bronze bells hung along one side of the frame, standing in the order they strike in this change, the nearest striking now and the row running back into the tower.
controls: bells: count, bells are hung along the beam from 4 to 12, each new bell larger (lower in the scale) and the beam lengthening into the distance.
method: position, each bell moves along the beam to its place in the current change; a change is neighbouring bells trading places, a hunting bell walking front to back and back again.
pace: position (spacing), the distance between bells along the beam is the time between blows: spread out at 0.5 a beat, packed close (bells nearly touching) at 8.
stroke: position, on handstroke changes the whole row steps back along the beam by up to one bay, leaving an empty hatched bay in front: the open lead drawn as a space.
risks: Bells sliding along a beam isn't how a tower works (bells hang still and swing); the beam is a stage for the order, a stretch a ringer may notice.
Order is read by size along the row; at twelve bells the far end shrinks under 10 px in perspective, so the back of a long row is hard to read.
Pace (spacing) and stroke (offset of the row) both slide bells along the beam; stroke must lead with the hatched empty bay, not the move.
Each bell is pre-projected per depth slot: moving a bell along the beam changes its size, so method swaps need pre-drawn sizes per slot or a scale per node (allowed, uniform).
Mute: the bells are stood (the bright weight leaves the front bell and the row stops), shown by the front bell's outline dropping to the others' weight. Weak; needs a stronger cue.
cells.angle: the object in the machine's name, drawn literally and well
cells.alt: Ringer, pass 2 (subject), variant 2: The ring itself, literally: hidden-line bronze bells hung along one side of the frame, standing in the order they strike in this change, the nearest striking now and the row running back into the tower

cells.subject: The wheels of the ring face on, each with its rope wound from the garter hole round the rim and falling to the sally, every wheel turned to how far through its pull its bell is in this change, the one about to strike drawn bright.
controls: bells: count, wheels across the frame from 4 to 12, smaller as they're added so the row always fills the frame head.

method: rotation, each wheel turns to its bell's place in the current change (first place wound furthest, garter hole low on the right; last place barely started), the rope's wrap round the rim lengthening and shortening with it.
pace: position, every sally rides up its rope as the ropes are taken in to ring lower and faster, about 26 px from 0.5 to 8 a beat.
stroke: position, the sliders under the frame head run out to the right by up to 14 px as the handstroke gap opens, the stays meeting them later.
risks: The busiest of the five: six wheels, spokes, stays, wraps and sallies; at twelve bells each wheel is about 15 px in radius and the spokes and garter holes go under the 3 px floor.

Method as each wheel's rotation is the physical truth, but it echoes pass 01's v2 (bells turned to their swing); here the turn is in the screen plane, so it's one node per wheel, not pre-drawn variants.
Stroke's slider travel (14 px) is under the 24 px position floor and the sliders are small; it needs the stays to rest against them, or a larger runner.
Bold closed wheels with spokes can read as bicycle or cart wheels if the ropes and sallies are missed.
Mute: the ring is stood, every wheel turned to the balance with its stay on the slider, all wheels at one angle; honest and distinct by rotation.
cells.angle: the mechanism that makes it happen: the moving parts, the thing in the hand
cells.alt: Ringer, pass 2 (subject), variant 3: The wheels of the ring face on, each with its rope wound from the garter hole round the rim and falling to the sally, every wheel turned to how far through its pull its bell is in this change, the one about to strike drawn bright

cells.subject: The bronze cut through: the ring hung in a two-tier frame and sectioned on its centre plane, the cut walls showing thin waist and thick sound bow, each clapper standing off its strike point by how far its bell is from striking in this change.
controls: bells: count, sectioned bells in the two tiers from 4 to 12 (2 + 2 up to 6 + 6), smaller as the tiers fill, the sills lengthening.
method: rotation, each clapper swings about its crown staple: the bell striking now has its ball on the sound bow (bright), the others hang progressively further off it toward plumb.
pace: rotation (spread), the clappers' stand-off range narrows as the pace rises, from about 34 to 17 degrees (24 at the default), so the whole row of clappers closes toward the bow.
stroke: rotation, on handstroke changes the leading clapper is held back off the bow by up to 12 degrees before it strikes.
risks: Cut bronze is hatched, which craft.md reserves for semi-opaque or inactive regions; in a section the hatch means cut material, so every bell is hatched and the lit one is told by weight and brightness, not by hatch. Needs a sentence or a solid cut fill instead.
Method, pace and stroke all act through the clappers' angle (order, range, one bell's hold-back); three controls in one channel is the weakest mapping of the five.
Clapper swing on a 50 to 60 px flight moves the ball about 20-25 px for the full range; small bells at twelve get under the rotation floor.
Two tiers of mouth-down bells can read as a rack of bell icons if the hatch and wall thickness don't show at 1:1.
Mute: every clapper hangs plumb, the bright ball gone; distinct by rotation.
cells.angle: the material the sound acts on, seen close
cells.alt: Ringer, pass 2 (subject), variant 4: The bronze cut through: the ring hung in a two-tier frame and sectioned on its centre plane, the cut walls showing thin waist and thick sound bow, each clapper standing off its strike point by how far its bell is from striking in this change

cells.subject: The tower pulled apart along its axis: the bell-chamber floor with the ring on it lifted clear of the ringing-chamber floor, the ropes falling between, and on the ringing floor one bright line threading the rope feet in the order they strike.
controls: bells: count, bells on the upper floor, ropes between and rope feet round the ringing circle from 4 to 12, spaced evenly round it.

method: shape, the threading line (one mutable outline, up to 12 points) joins the rope feet in the current change's order and closes back to the first; each change re-threads it, rounds is a plain ring, a method a star.
pace: position, every sally rides up its rope as the ropes are taken in, about 1.6 storeys' worth of the gap (about 30 px) from 0.5 to 8 a beat.
stroke: position, the explode gap between the two floors opens by up to three units (about 35 px) as the handstroke gap grows: the gap drawn as a gap.
risks: The threading line is a diagram laid on the scene; it could drift toward a sequencer's star polygon if the tower around it gets thinner. The tower must stay the scene.
Upper-floor bells are about 20-30 px and the far ones tuck behind the near ones; at twelve bells they crowd on the slab.
The scene is small in the frame (the box has to fit both floors and the gap); the method line is about 100 px across.
Stroke as explode distance is a metaphor; ringers won't read a tower pulling apart as a handstroke lead without being told.
Mute: the threading line drops to hairline and the sallies settle on the floor; position plus weight.
cells.angle: one scene where this happens, with one subject in it
cells.alt: Ringer, pass 2 (subject), variant 5: The tower pulled apart along its axis: the bell-chamber floor with the ring on it lifted clear of the ringing-chamber floor, the ropes falling between, and on the ringing floor one bright line threading the rope feet in the order they strike
